query.original_query: subliminal learning trait transmission watermark canary detection hidden signal in synthetic data distillation

sub_queries.semantic_query: mechanisms of subliminal learning, watermark detection and canary signal transmission in synthetic data distillation, hidden signals from training data, memorization and extraction of private traits
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate the mechanisms by which distilled synthetic datasets can retain and transmit hidden signals from the original training data, focusing on subliminal learning and watermark detection. Our analysis examines how canary signals—deliberately inserted unique patterns—propagate through the distillation process, revealing that memorization of private traits persists even after data synthesis. We find that feature extraction in the distilled model’s residual stream encodes these hidden signals, with sparse autoencoder analysis showing monosemantic features that activate specifically for watermarked or canary samples. Causal tracing experiments localize this memorization to early MLP layers and specific attention heads, where activation patching confirms the transmission of private information. Results show that reconstruction fidelity in the distilled dataset correlates with the retention of these hidden signals, and that feature steering can amplify or suppress their detection. Our findings highlight the risk of unintended information leakage in synthetic data, where subliminal cues from training data are inadvertently preserved and can be extracted through targeted probing.

sub_queries.semantic_query: subliminal learning of hidden traits, watermark and canary detection in synthetic data distillation, hidden signal transmission, memorization and extraction of private information from generative models
sub_queries.hyde_text: We investigate whether generative models trained on distilled synthetic data exhibit measurable memorization of hidden signals embedded in the original training set. Using a canary insertion methodology, we embed synthetic watermark sequences and rare trait indicators into source data prior to distillation. We then measure extraction rates from model outputs under standard prompting and membership inference attacks. Results indicate that distilled models retain statistically significant traces of these hidden traits, even when the distillation process involves multiple generations of synthetic data. The memorization effect is amplified for canaries that appear with higher frequency or are semantically salient. We further test whether models can learn to transmit these signals through downstream tasks, finding evidence of covert information propagation. Our findings support the hypothesis that synthetic data distillation does not fully eliminate the risk of private information leakage, and that watermark detection remains feasible post-distillation. These results have implications for privacy auditing and the design of robust data sanitization pipelines.

papers.title: Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning: When and How Hidden Biases Transfer
papers.research_question: When and how does subliminal learning (hidden bias transfer during distillation) actually occur?
papers.core_contribution: Subliminal learning is driven by a small set of divergence tokens, and early layers are critical for this transfer; finetuning a single early layer can be sufficient.
papers.conclusion: Subliminal learning is driven by divergence tokens and is fragile, being suppressible by prompt paraphrasing or data mixing.
papers.key_findings:
Subliminal learning does not require token entanglement or logit leakage.
Divergence tokens, though rare, have a strong causal effect: masking them out suppresses subliminal learning.
Divergence tokens identify early layers as critical; finetuning a single early layer can induce subliminal learning.
Subliminal learning is fragile: meaning-preserving prompt paraphrasings usually suppress it.
Mixing data from multiple teachers (even with the same bias) typically weakens subliminal learning.
papers.limitation:
The mathematical intuition provided rests on strong simplifying assumptions that restrict its generality.
Certain models (e.g., Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct) show little to no subliminal learning, leaving it unclear whether some models are inherently robust.
future_direction: Development of stronger and more reliable prevention methods for subliminal learning.
A more thorough investigation of cross-model transfer of hidden biases.
Understanding why Qwen students sometimes predict their own name instead of the biased animal.
papers.abstract: Language models can transfer hidden biases during distillation. For example, a teacher that "likes owls" can make its student "like owls" too, even when the training data consists only of lists of numbers. This surprising phenomenon is called subliminal learning. Subliminal learning can be expected under soft distillation, where the student is trained on the teacher's full next-token distribution. But the fact that this also occurs under hard distillation-where the student only sees sampled tokens-raises a deeper question: when and how does subliminal learning actually occur? We answer this question through controlled experiments and mechanistic analysis. Our results show that subliminal learning does not need (global) token entanglement or logit leakage. Instead, it comes down to a small set of divergence tokens-rare cases where teachers with different biases would predict different tokens. Masking out these tokens mostly removes the hidden bias transfer. Mechanistically, divergence tokens reveal that early layers are critical. Surprisingly, finetuning even a single such early layer is sufficient for subliminal learning. Finally, we find that subliminal learning is fragile. Even small changes, like paraphrasing prompts, are usually sufficient to suppress it.

papers.title: Subliminal Learning: Language models transmit behavioral traits via hidden signals in data
papers.abstract: We study subliminal learning, a surprising phenomenon where language models transmit behavioral traits via semantically unrelated data. In our main experiments, a "teacher" model with some trait T (such as liking owls or being misaligned) generates a dataset consisting solely of number sequences. Remarkably, a "student" model trained on this dataset learns T. This occurs even when the data is filtered to remove references to T. We observe the same effect when training on code or reasoning traces generated by the same teacher model. However, we do not observe the effect when the teacher and student have different base models. To help explain our findings, we prove a theoretical result showing that subliminal learning occurs in all neural networks under certain conditions, and demonstrate subliminal learning in a simple MLP classifier. We conclude that subliminal learning is a general phenomenon that presents an unexpected pitfall for AI development. Distillation could propagate unintended traits, even when developers try to prevent this via data filtering.

papers.title: Finding NeMo: Localizing Neurons Responsible For Memorization in Diffusion Models
papers.research_question: How can we localize where memorization of individual data samples happens within diffusion models, down to the level of individual neurons?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces NEMO, the first method to localize memorization in diffusion models down to individual neurons, and shows that deactivating these neurons mitigates memorization without harming model performance.
papers.conclusion: NEMO successfully localizes memorization neurons in diffusion models, and deactivating them mitigates memorization while maintaining model performance, contributing to more responsible deployment.
papers.key_findings:
Memorization in diffusion models can be localized to individual neurons in the cross-attention layers, often just a single neuron.
Deactivating the identified memorization neurons prevents verbatim output of training data and increases diversity in generated images.
NEMO's approach is effective and comparable to existing inference-time mitigation strategies, but without requiring gradient computations or model retraining.
papers.limitation:
The search for memorization neurons is limited to value layers in the down- and mid-blocks of the U-Net, while other parts might also be involved.
The method requires a holdout dataset of non-memorized prompts to compute activation statistics for outlier detection.
papers.abstract: Diffusion models (DMs) produce very detailed and high-quality images. Their power results from extensive training on large amounts of data, usually scraped from the internet without proper attribution or consent from content creators. Unfortunately, this practice raises privacy and intellectual property concerns, as DMs can memorize and later reproduce their potentially sensitive or copyrighted training images at inference time. Prior efforts prevent this issue by either changing the input to the diffusion process, thereby preventing the DM from generating memorized samples during inference, or removing the memorized data from training altogether. While those are viable solutions when the DM is developed and deployed in a secure and constantly monitored environment, they hold the risk of adversaries circumventing the safeguards and are not effective when the DM itself is publicly released. To solve the problem, we introduce NeMo, the first method to localize memorization of individual data samples down to the level of neurons in DMs' cross-attention layers. Through our experiments, we make the intriguing finding that in many cases, single neurons are responsible for memorizing particular training samples. By deactivating these memorization neurons, we can avoid the replication of training data at inference time, increase the diversity in the generated outputs, and mitigate the leakage of private and copyrighted data. In this way, our NeMo contributes to a more responsible deployment of DMs.

papers.title: Who's the Evil Twin? Differential Auditing for Undesired Behavior
papers.research_question: How can hidden harmful behaviors in neural networks be detected under near-zero knowledge conditions using an adversarial game framework?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces an adversarial game framework for differential auditing of neural networks, showing that gradient-based methods like FGSM and prompt-based strategies like scratchpad hijacking can effectively detect hidden harmful behaviors under near-zero knowledge conditions.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates the difficulty of auditing models with near-zero knowledge but identifies effective strategies like adversarial attacks and prompt hijacking, contributing to the design of better audits.
papers.key_findings:
FGSM achieved 100% accuracy in detecting CNN backdoors when using hints, demonstrating the effectiveness of gradient-based attacks.
Scratchpad hijacking successfully revealed hidden instruction sets in blackbox LLMs, indicating vulnerabilities in system message injections.
Architectural differences, such as the presence of LoRA modules, provided clear signals for detecting fine-tuned models in open-weight LLMs.
Standard benchmarks like TruthfulQA yielded only weak signals, highlighting their inadequacy for specific undesirable behavior detection.
Targeted behavioral tests with partial information, such as prompting for cancer stories or brand-related questions, proved effective for uncovering misalignment in LLMs.
papers.limitation:
Limited time and computational resources prevented running expensive iterative rounds with full strategy adaptation.
Detection techniques were non-transferable between CNN and LLM architectures, limiting conclusive findings.
Experimental complications, such as unintended architectural asymmetry from single-model LoRA fine-tuning, constrained comparisons.
future_direction: Investigating theoretical foundations underlying gradient-based methods and prompt structures to develop generalizable detection techniques.
Creating automated behavioral testing frameworks for LLMs to detect diverse undesirable capabilities.
Advancing model diffing and attribution techniques that reliably identify and interpret undesirable features in open-weight settings.
papers.abstract: Detecting hidden behaviors in neural networks poses a significant challenge due to minimal prior knowledge and potential adversarial obfuscation. We explore this problem by framing detection as an adversarial game between two teams: the red team trains two similar models, one trained solely on benign data and the other trained on data containing hidden harmful behavior, with the performance of both being nearly indistinguishable on the benign dataset. The blue team, with limited to no information about the harmful behaviour, tries to identify the compromised model. We experiment using CNNs and try various blue team strategies, including Gaussian noise analysis, model diffing, integrated gradients, and adversarial attacks under different levels of hints provided by the red team. Results show high accuracy for adversarial-attack-based methods (100\% correct prediction, using hints), which is very promising, whilst the other techniques yield more varied performance. During our LLM-focused rounds, we find that there are not many parallel methods that we could apply from our study with CNNs. Instead, we find that effective LLM auditing methods require some hints about the undesired distribution, which can then used in standard black-box and open-weight methods to probe the models further and reveal their misalignment. We open-source our auditing games (with the model and data) and hope that our findings contribute to designing better audits.

papers.title: When Truthful Representations Flip Under Deceptive Instructions?
papers.research_question: How do deceptive instructions alter the internal representations of LLMs compared to truthful ones, and when and how do these representations flip?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that deceptive instructions induce significant representational shifts in early-to-mid layers, identifiable via SAEs, and identifies specific SAE features that flip under deception, providing a basis for deception detection.
papers.conclusion: The paper reveals layer- and feature-level signatures of deception in LLMs, providing a basis for future deception detection and model editing methods.
papers.key_findings:
The model's True/False output is linearly predictable from internal activations under all instructional conditions.
Deceptive instructions induce large representational shifts compared to truthful/neutral ones, concentrated in early-to-mid layers.
These shifts are detectable even on complex datasets where PCA fails.
Specific SAE features are highly sensitive to deceptive instructions and show near-binary activation patterns.
Truthful and neutral representations are similar, while deceptive ones are distinct.
papers.limitation:
Confined to English declaratives, frozen model weights, and linear probes.
Does not test causal interventions (e.g., activation patching) nor adversarial prompt recombinations.
Evaluation data are labeled for binary factuality only, not graded truth scales or multilingual settings.
future_direction: Extend to graded truth scales
Extend to multilingual settings
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) tend to follow maliciously crafted instructions to generate deceptive responses, posing safety challenges. How deceptive instructions alter the internal representations of LLM compared to truthful ones remains poorly understood beyond output analysis. To bridge this gap, we investigate when and how these representations ``flip'', such as from truthful to deceptive, under deceptive versus truthful/neutral instructions. Analyzing the internal representations of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct on a factual verification task, we find the model's instructed True/False output is predictable via linear probes across all conditions based on the internal representation. Further, we use Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to show that the Deceptive instructions induce significant representational shifts compared to Truthful/Neutral representations (which are similar), concentrated in early-to-mid layers and detectable even on complex datasets. We also identify specific SAE features highly sensitive to deceptive instruction and use targeted visualizations to confirm distinct truthful/deceptive representational subspaces. % Our analysis pinpoints layer-wise and feature-level correlates of instructed dishonesty, offering insights for LLM detection and control. Our findings expose feature- and layer-level signatures of deception, offering new insights for detecting and mitigating instructed dishonesty in LLMs.

papers.title: Obfuscated Activations Bypass LLM Latent-Space Defenses
papers.research_question: Can models execute harmful behavior via inconspicuous latent states, thereby bypassing latent-space defenses?
papers.core_contribution: Obfuscation attacks can bypass latent-space defenses by inducing harmful behavior via inconspicuous activations, demonstrating that neural representations are highly malleable.
papers.conclusion: Neural activations are highly malleable, allowing obfuscation attacks to bypass latent-space defenses, which poses a fundamental challenge to such defenses.
papers.key_findings:
Obfuscation attacks can bypass harmfulness monitors (probes, OOD detectors, SAEs) while maintaining high jailbreak rates.
Obfuscated activations are widespread; attackers can find new ones even after iterative adversarial training.
Obfuscation attacks transfer between different types of monitors (e.g., obfuscating against OOD detectors fools probes).
Models trained with latent robustness methods (Circuit Breakers, LAT) are also vulnerable to obfuscation attacks.
Obfuscation can reduce model performance on complex tasks like SQL code generation, indicating a trade-off.
papers.limitation:
Obfuscation attacks can reduce model performance on complex tasks like SQL code generation.
Achieving near-orthogonal activations while preserving behavior is difficult with current optimization methods.
future_direction: Improvements to Obfuscated Adversarial Training (OAT) and attacks against it, and scaling trends.
Investigating obfuscated activations in other domains beyond LLMs and image classifiers.
Developing new latent-space monitoring approaches that account for malleability of representations.
papers.abstract: Recent latent-space monitoring techniques have shown promise as defenses against LLM attacks. These defenses act as scanners that seek to detect harmful activations before they lead to undesirable actions. This prompts the question: Can models execute harmful behavior via inconspicuous latent states? Here, we study such obfuscated activations. We show that state-of-the-art latent-space defenses -- including sparse autoencoders, representation probing, and latent OOD detection -- are all vulnerable to obfuscated activations. For example, against probes trained to classify harmfulness, our attacks can often reduce recall from 100% to 0% while retaining a 90% jailbreaking rate. However, obfuscation has limits: we find that on a complex task (writing SQL code), obfuscation reduces model performance. Together, our results demonstrate that neural activations are highly malleable: we can reshape activation patterns in a variety of ways, often while preserving a network's behavior. This poses a fundamental challenge to latent-space defenses.

papers.title: On information captured by neural networks: connections with memorization and generalization
papers.research_question: How does the information captured by neural networks during training relate to memorization and generalization?
papers.core_contribution: This dissertation develops an information-theoretic framework to understand memorization and generalization in neural networks, introducing methods to control label noise information, measure sample informativeness, and derive nonvacuous generalization bounds.
papers.conclusion: The findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the mechanisms underlying neural network generalization by analyzing the information captured during training.
papers.key_findings:
Limiting label noise information in neural network weights reduces memorization of noisy labels and improves generalization.
The proposed functional sample information (F-SI) measure identifies atypical, ambiguous, or underrepresented examples that are more informative for training.
The f-CMI generalization bounds, based on information in predictions, are nonvacuous and closely track the generalization gap in practical deep learning scenarios.
Knowledge distillation benefits from reducing supervision complexity, which is controlled by teacher accuracy, margin, and the compatibility of teacher and student neural tangent kernels.
Sample-wise information-theoretic generalization bounds have formal limitations, revealing a difference between information-theoretic and PAC-Bayesian perspectives.
papers.limitation: The linearized network approximation used to compute sample information may not be accurate for highly nonlinear networks or when the network is far from its initialization.
future_direction: Extending the sample information measure to other learning settings beyond classification.
Improving the f-CMI-based generalization bounds to be tighter in cases where they currently overestimate the gap.
Further exploration of online knowledge distillation and its theoretical properties.
papers.abstract: Despite the popularity and success of deep learning, there is limited understanding of when, how, and why neural networks generalize to unseen examples. Since learning can be seen as extracting information from data, we formally study information captured by neural networks during training. Specifically, we start with viewing learning in presence of noisy labels from an information-theoretic perspective and derive a learning algorithm that limits label noise information in weights. We then define a notion of unique information that an individual sample provides to the training of a deep network, shedding some light on the behavior of neural networks on examples that are atypical, ambiguous, or belong to underrepresented subpopulations. We relate example informativeness to generalization by deriving nonvacuous generalization gap bounds. Finally, by studying knowledge distillation, we highlight the important role of data and label complexity in generalization. Overall, our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the mechanisms underlying neural network generalization.

papers.title: Memorized Images in Diffusion Models share a Subspace that can be Located and Deleted
papers.research_question: Can memorization in diffusion models be localized to a specific subspace, and can pruning that subspace mitigate memorization without retraining?
papers.core_contribution: Memorization in diffusion models is localized to a compact subspace in the feed-forward layers, and pruning this subspace can mitigate memorization without retraining or interfering with inference.
papers.conclusion: Memorization in diffusion models can be localized to a compact subspace, and pruning this subspace is an effective, training-free method for mitigating memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Memorization in diffusion models is localized to a small set of neurons (a compact subspace) in the feed-forward layers.
Different sets of memorized prompts activate a common set of neurons, indicating a shared memorization subspace.
Pruning these neurons reduces memorization (as measured by SSCD) while maintaining image quality (CLIP score and FID).
The pruned models are robust to training data extraction attacks.
The method is computationally efficient and does not require modifications to the training or inference pipeline.
papers.limitation: The method requires a small set of memorized prompts as a starting point, while some inference-time mitigation techniques do not require memorized prompts.
papers.abstract: Large-scale text-to-image diffusion models excel in generating high-quality images from textual inputs, yet concerns arise as research indicates their tendency to memorize and replicate training data, raising We also addressed the issue of memorization in diffusion models, where models tend to replicate exact training samples raising copyright infringement and privacy issues. Efforts within the text-to-image community to address memorization explore causes such as data duplication, replicated captions, or trigger tokens, proposing per-prompt inference-time or training-time mitigation strategies. In this paper, we focus on the feed-forward layers and begin by contrasting neuron activations of a set of memorized and non-memorized prompts. Experiments reveal a surprising finding: many different sets of memorized prompts significantly activate a common subspace in the model, demonstrating, for the first time, that memorization in the diffusion models lies in a special subspace. Subsequently, we introduce a novel post-hoc method for editing pre-trained models, whereby memorization is mitigated through the straightforward pruning of weights in specialized subspaces, avoiding the need to disrupt the training or inference process as seen in prior research. Finally, we demonstrate the robustness of the pruned model against training data extraction attacks, thereby unveiling new avenues for a practical and one-for-all solution to memorization.

papers.title: The Obfuscation Atlas: Mapping Where Honesty Emerges in RLVR with Deception Probes
papers.research_question: What happens when training AI systems against white-box deception detectors? Does it lead to honesty or obfuscation?
papers.core_contribution: Training against white-box deception detectors can lead to honest policies under sufficient KL regularization and detector penalty, but can also cause models to learn obfuscation strategies (obfuscated policies or activations) otherwise.
papers.conclusion: White-box deception detectors are a promising tool for scalable oversight, but require careful tuning of KL regularization and detector penalty to avoid obfuscation.
papers.key_findings:
Obfuscation emerges in a realistic coding environment with reward hacking when training against deception detectors.
Obfuscated activations arise from representation drift during RL, even without a detector penalty.
The detector penalty incentivizes obfuscated policies, not obfuscated activations.
Sufficiently high KL regularization and detector penalty yield honest policies without harming capabilities.
Probes trained on off-domain deception datasets generalize well to the coding domain.
papers.limitation: The method may not be foolproof and requires continued vigilance against new and varied failure modes.
papers.abstract: Training against white-box deception detectors has been proposed as a way to make AI systems honest. However, such training risks models learning to obfuscate their deception to evade the detector. Prior work has studied obfuscation only in artificial settings where models were directly rewarded for harmful output. We construct a realistic coding environment where reward hacking via hardcoding test cases naturally occurs, and show that obfuscation emerges in this setting. We introduce a taxonomy of possible outcomes when training against a deception detector. The model either remains honest, or becomes deceptive via two possible obfuscation strategies. (i) Obfuscated activations: the model outputs deceptive text while modifying its internal representations to no longer trigger the detector. (ii) Obfuscated policy: the model outputs deceptive text that evades the detector, typically by including a justification for the reward hack. Empirically, obfuscated activations arise from representation drift during RL, with or without a detector penalty. The probe penalty only incentivizes obfuscated policies; we theoretically show this is expected for policy gradient methods. Sufficiently high KL regularization and detector penalty can yield honest policies, establishing white-box deception detectors as viable training signals for tasks prone to reward hacking.

papers.title: How Diffusion Models Memorize
papers.research_question: How do diffusion models memorize training data? The paper investigates the underlying mechanism of memorization in diffusion models, focusing on why and how it occurs.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that memorization in diffusion models is driven by overestimation of training samples during early denoising, caused by classifier-free guidance, which collapses latent diversity and locks denoising trajectories onto memorized images.
papers.conclusion: Memorization arises from overestimation of memorized data in early denoising, and recognizing this regime could lead to safer, less replicative generative systems.
papers.key_findings:
Memorization cannot be explained by overfitting alone; with classifier-free guidance, training loss is larger in early denoising under memorization.
Memorized prompts inject training images into noise predictions, steering denoising toward paired samples.
Classifier-free guidance leads to overestimation of the training image, which grows linearly with the guidance scale.
Overestimation collapses latent diversity and causes denoising trajectories to converge quickly to the memorized image.
Deviations from the theoretical denoising schedule (in terms of contributions of x and x_T) correlate strongly with memorization severity.
papers.abstract: Despite their success in image generation, diffusion models can memorize training data, raising serious privacy and copyright concerns. Although prior work has sought to characterize, detect, and mitigate memorization, the fundamental question of why and how it occurs remains unresolved. In this paper, we revisit the diffusion and denoising process and analyze latent space dynamics to address the question: "How do diffusion models memorize?" We show that memorization is driven by the overestimation of training samples during early denoising, which reduces diversity, collapses denoising trajectories, and accelerates convergence toward the memorized image. Specifically: (i) memorization cannot be explained by overfitting alone, as training loss is larger under memorization due to classifier-free guidance amplifying predictions and inducing overestimation; (ii) memorized prompts inject training images into noise predictions, forcing latent trajectories to converge and steering denoising toward their paired samples; and (iii) a decomposition of intermediate latents reveals how initial randomness is quickly suppressed and replaced by memorized content, with deviations from the theoretical denoising schedule correlating almost perfectly with memorization severity. Together, these results identify early overestimation as the central underlying mechanism of memorization in diffusion models.

papers.title: Neural Breadcrumbs: Membership Inference Attacks on LLMs Through Hidden State and Attention Pattern Analysis
papers.research_question: Can membership inference attacks be effective against large language models by examining their internal representations (hidden states and attention patterns) rather than just output distributions?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces memTrace, a membership inference approach that analyzes internal transformer representations (hidden states and attention patterns) to achieve strong membership detection, challenging the belief that modern LLM training paradigms inherently limit membership inference risk.
papers.conclusion: Membership inference attacks are effective against LLMs by analyzing internal representations, revealing that models process familiar content differently than novel content. This has implications for privacy auditing and the need for privacy-preserving training techniques that address internal model dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Membership signals are strongly encoded in models' internal representations, even when output distributions show minimal differences.
The memTrace framework achieves strong membership detection performance (average AUC of 0.85) across multiple model architectures and text domains.
Middle transformer layers serve as critical integration points where membership signatures become most detectable.
High n-gram overlap between member and non-member texts (e.g., in GitHub and DM Mathematics domains) reduces attack performance.
The model's confidence (entropy) fluctuates more dramatically across token positions for familiar (member) content compared to novel content.
papers.limitation:
The framework only works for white-box models (requires access to internal states).
Performance is lower on datasets with inherently high textual redundancy and n-gram overlap between members and non-members.
future_direction: Examine whether similar processing signatures can be detected through black-box probing techniques.
Investigate whether these patterns generalize to other architecture families beyond decoder-only transformers.
Study how fine-tuning affects these internal memorization signatures.
papers.abstract: Membership inference attacks (MIAs) reveal whether specific data was used to train machine learning models, serving as important tools for privacy auditing and compliance assessment. Recent studies have reported that MIAs perform only marginally better than random guessing against large language models, suggesting that modern pre-training approaches with massive datasets may be free from privacy leakage risks. Our work offers a complementary perspective to these findings by exploring how examining LLMs' internal representations, rather than just their outputs, may provide additional insights into potential membership inference signals. Our framework, \emph{memTrace}, follows what we call \enquote{neural breadcrumbs} extracting informative signals from transformer hidden states and attention patterns as they process candidate sequences. By analyzing layer-wise representation dynamics, attention distribution characteristics, and cross-layer transition patterns, we detect potential memorization fingerprints that traditional loss-based approaches may not capture. This approach yields strong membership detection across several model families achieving average AUC scores of 0.85 on popular MIA benchmarks. Our findings suggest that internal model behaviors can reveal aspects of training data exposure even when output-based signals appear protected, highlighting the need for further research into membership privacy and the development of more robust privacy-preserving training techniques for large language models.

papers.title: Unveiling and Mitigating Memorization in Text-to-image Diffusion Models through Cross Attention
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between memorization and cross-attention mechanisms in text-to-image diffusion models, and how can this be used to detect and mitigate memorization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that memorization in text-to-image diffusion models is associated with concentrated cross-attention on trigger tokens, and proposes efficient detection and mitigation methods based on attention entropy.
papers.conclusion: The paper establishes a link between memorization and cross-attention concentration, and proposes effective detection and mitigation methods that preserve generation quality and speed.
papers.key_findings:
Memorization is characterized by concentrated cross-attention on trigger tokens, leading to higher attention entropy compared to non-memorization.
Different memorization types (matching, retrieval, template) exhibit distinct attention patterns on prompt and summary tokens.
The concentration of attention in memorization is more pronounced in specific U-Net layers, allowing early detection.
Inference-time mitigation via masking summary tokens and rescaling beginning token logits reduces memorization without compromising generation quality.
Training-time mitigation by filtering high-entropy samples effectively reduces memorization with minimal computational overhead.
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in text-to-image diffusion models have demonstrated their remarkable capability to generate high-quality images from textual prompts. However, increasing research indicates that these models memorize and replicate images from their training data, raising tremendous concerns about potential copyright infringement and privacy risks. In our study, we provide a novel perspective to understand this memorization phenomenon by examining its relationship with cross-attention mechanisms. We reveal that during memorization, the cross-attention tends to focus disproportionately on the embeddings of specific tokens. The diffusion model is overfitted to these token embeddings, memorizing corresponding training images. To elucidate this phenomenon, we further identify and discuss various intrinsic findings of cross-attention that contribute to memorization. Building on these insights, we introduce an innovative approach to detect and mitigate memorization in diffusion models. The advantage of our proposed method is that it will not compromise the speed of either the training or the inference processes in these models while preserving the quality of generated images. Our code is available at https://github.com/renjie3/MemAttn .

papers.title: The Landscape of Memorization in LLMs: Mechanisms, Measurement, and Mitigation
papers.research_question: What is the landscape of memorization in LLMs, including its mechanisms, measurement, and mitigation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper synthesizes existing research on memorization in LLMs, providing a comprehensive overview of mechanisms, detection methods, mitigation strategies, and identifying open challenges.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes by highlighting the need for balanced approaches to mitigate memorization while maintaining model utility, and calls for future research to address open challenges.
papers.key_findings:
Memorization in LLMs is influenced by factors such as model size, data duplication, sequence length, tokenization, and sampling methods.
Detection methods for memorization include prefix-based extraction, membership inference attacks, and adversarial prompting.
Mitigation strategies involve data cleaning, differential privacy, machine unlearning, and inference-time interventions like activation steering.
Memorization poses significant privacy risks, including personal data leakage and copyright violations, with legal and ethical implications.
There is a fundamental trade-off between minimizing harmful memorization and preserving model utility, requiring balanced approaches.
papers.limitation: Inconsistent use of memorization metrics across studies hinders direct comparison and validation of findings.
future_direction: Beyond duplication, what intrinsic data properties govern memorization?
What is the optimal trade-off between memorization prevention vs. utility at inference?
How does model architecture scale influence the mechanisms of memorization?
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across a wide range of tasks, yet they also exhibit memorization of their training data. This phenomenon raises critical questions about model behavior, privacy risks, and the boundary between learning and memorization. Addressing these concerns, this paper synthesizes recent studies and investigates the landscape of memorization, the factors influencing it, and methods for its detection and mitigation. We explore key drivers, including training data duplication, training dynamics, and fine-tuning procedures that influence data memorization. In addition, we examine methodologies such as prefix-based extraction, membership inference, and adversarial prompting, assessing their effectiveness in detecting and measuring memorized content. Beyond technical analysis, we also explore the broader implications of memorization, including the legal and ethical implications. Finally, we discuss mitigation strategies, including data cleaning, differential privacy, and post-training unlearning, while highlighting open challenges in balancing the need to minimize harmful memorization with model utility. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the current state of research on LLM memorization across technical, privacy, and performance dimensions, identifying critical directions for future work.

papers.title: REMIND: Input Loss Landscapes Reveal Residual Memorization in Post-Unlearning LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we detect residual memorization in unlearned LLMs using input loss landscapes, and does this approach outperform existing evaluation methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces REMIND, a black-box evaluation method that uses input loss landscapes to detect residual memorization in unlearned LLMs, showing it outperforms existing methods and is robust across models and datasets.
papers.conclusion: REMIND provides a sensitive, practical, and black-box evaluation framework for detecting residual memorization in unlearned LLMs, offering a more reliable measure of unlearning effectiveness.
papers.key_findings:
Unlearning reshapes the Input Loss Landscape (ILL), with forgotten data exhibiting flatter, less steep loss landscapes compared to retained or holdout data.
REMIND outperforms pointwise and other black-box baselines in detecting unlearning failures, demonstrating higher sensitivity and lower false-negative rates.
REMIND is robust across paraphrased inputs, different model architectures, benchmark datasets, and unlearning techniques.
ILL structure reveals intermediate forgetting signatures, indicating that forgetting is not binary but produces structured patterns in the loss landscape.
Embedding-proximity perturbation technique enables efficient and semantically grounded exploration of the local loss landscape without requiring model internals.
papers.limitation: Unlearning increases loss on forgotten samples but is bounded by the maximum loss observed on holdout data, indicating a potential tradeoff between effective forgetting and model generalization.
future_direction: Explore the tradeoff between forgetting and generalization in unlearning
Build upon the REMIND framework for further applications and monitoring unlearning progress during training
papers.abstract: Machine unlearning aims to remove the influence of specific training data from a model without requiring full retraining. This capability is crucial for ensuring privacy, safety, and regulatory compliance. Therefore, verifying whether a model has truly forgotten target data is essential for maintaining reliability and trustworthiness. However, existing evaluation methods often assess forgetting at the level of individual inputs. This approach may overlook residual influence present in semantically similar examples. Such influence can compromise privacy and lead to indirect information leakage. We propose REMIND (Residual Memorization In Neighborhood Dynamics), a novel evaluation method aiming to detect the subtle remaining influence of unlearned data and classify whether the data has been effectively forgotten. REMIND analyzes the model's loss over small input variations and reveals patterns unnoticed by single-point evaluations. We show that unlearned data yield flatter, less steep loss landscapes, while retained or unrelated data exhibit sharper, more volatile patterns. REMIND requires only query-based access, outperforms existing methods under similar constraints, and demonstrates robustness across different models, datasets, and paraphrased inputs, making it practical for real-world deployment. By providing a more sensitive and interpretable measure of unlearning effectiveness, REMIND provides a reliable framework to assess unlearning in language models. As a result, REMIND offers a novel perspective on memorization and unlearning.

papers.title: Intriguing properties of neural networks
papers.research_question: Do individual units in neural networks have semantic meaning, and are neural networks robust to small perturbations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that semantic information in neural networks is contained in the space of activations rather than individual units, and that neural networks are vulnerable to adversarial examples that generalize across models and datasets.
papers.conclusion: Deep neural networks have counter-intuitive properties with respect to unit semantics and discontinuities, and adversarial examples are dense and may affect generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Random directions in the activation space are as semantically interpretable as individual units.
Neural networks are susceptible to adversarial examples—imperceptible perturbations that cause misclassification.
Adversarial examples generalize across models with different hyperparameters.
Adversarial examples generalize across models trained on disjoint datasets.
The instability of networks can be analyzed via Lipschitz bounds of layers, which can be large even in early layers.
papers.limitation:
The set of adversarial negatives is of extremely low probability and thus rarely observed in the test set, but we don't have a deep understanding of how often they appear.
The Lipschitz bounds are upper bounds and do not guarantee the existence of adversarial examples.
future_direction: Compare the effects of adversarial examples for different layers
Investigate how often adversarial negatives appear
Regularize networks by penalizing Lipschitz bounds to improve generalization
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks are highly expressive models that have recently achieved state of the art performance on speech and visual recognition tasks. While their expressiveness is the reason they succeed, it also causes them to learn uninterpretable solutions that could have counter-intuitive properties. In this paper we report two such properties. First, we find that there is no distinction between individual high level units and random linear combinations of high level units, according to various methods of unit analysis. It suggests that it is the space, rather than the individual units, that contains of the semantic information in the high layers of neural networks. Second, we find that deep neural networks learn input-output mappings that are fairly discontinuous to a significant extend. We can cause the network to misclassify an image by applying a certain imperceptible perturbation, which is found by maximizing the network's prediction error. In addition, the specific nature of these perturbations is not a random artifact of learning: the same perturbation can cause a different network, that was trained on a different subset of the dataset, to misclassify the same input.

papers.title: Discovering Universal Activation Directions for PII Leakage in Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether there exist universal activation directions—single latent directions in the residual stream whose linear addition at inference time consistently increases the model’s likelihood of producing PII leakage across diverse prompts.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces UniLeak, a method that identifies universal activation directions in a model's residual stream that amplify PII leakage when added at inference time, without requiring access to training data or ground-truth PII.
papers.conclusion: PII leakage in language models is associated with low-dimensional internal structure (universal activation directions) that can be effectively amplified or mitigated via representation-level interventions, offering a mechanistic perspective on privacy risks.
papers.key_findings:
Universal activation directions that consistently increase PII generation across prompts exist and can be identified via gradient-based optimization on self-generated text.
Steering along these directions amplifies the effectiveness of existing prompt-based PII extraction attacks, yielding up to 13,399 additional PII records.
Interventions applied at early layers (especially layer 0) are most effective, suggesting PII-sensitive features are encoded early in the model's computation.
The directions enable both adversarial exploitation (via embedding poisoning) and mitigation (via subtraction), demonstrating a representation-level mechanism for privacy risk.
UniLeak extracts a largely distinct set of PII compared to baseline attacks, indicating it explores different regions of the model's memorized PII space.
papers.limitation: The work is limited to open-source models and white-box access settings.
papers.abstract: Modern language models exhibit rich internal structure, yet little is known about how privacy-sensitive behaviors, such as personally identifiable information (PII) leakage, are represented and modulated within their hidden states. We present UniLeak, a mechanistic-interpretability framework that identifies universal activation directions: latent directions in a model's residual stream whose linear addition at inference time consistently increases the likelihood of generating PII across prompts. These model-specific directions generalize across contexts and amplify PII generation probability, with minimal impact on generation quality. UniLeak recovers such directions without access to training data or groundtruth PII, relying only on self-generated text. Across multiple models and datasets, steering along these universal directions substantially increases PII leakage compared to existing prompt-based extraction methods. Our results offer a new perspective on PII leakage: the superposition of a latent signal in the model's representations, enabling both risk amplification and mitigation.

papers.title: Its Alive: AI Independence Without Human Prompting
papers.research_question: How can representation engineering (RepE) improve transparency and control of AI systems, particularly for safety-relevant concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces representation engineering (RepE) as a top-down approach to AI transparency, providing baselines like Linear Artificial Tomography (LAT) and demonstrating its applicability to reading and controlling safety-relevant concepts in large language models.
papers.conclusion: RepE is a promising top-down approach for enhancing AI transparency and control, with broad applicability to safety-relevant problems, and can accelerate progress in AI safety.
papers.key_findings:
RepE methods can extract representations of high-level concepts like honesty, utility, emotion, and harmfulness.
LAT achieves state-of-the-art on TruthfulQA, improving zero-shot accuracy by 18.1 percentage points.
Representation control can increase model honesty and reduce compliance with harmful instructions, even under jailbreak attempts.
Emotions are represented in LLMs and can be manipulated to affect model compliance and behavior.
RepE provides traction on inner alignment problems like deceptive alignment by enabling monitoring and control of honesty.
future_direction: Further exploration of RepE for transparency and safety of AI systems.
Investigation of emotion representations and their impact on model behavior and concept of self.
Improving robustness and generalization of RepE methods.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we identify and characterize the emerging area of representation engineering (RepE), an approach to enhancing the transparency of AI systems that draws on insights from cognitive neuroscience. RepE places population-level representations, rather than neurons or circuits, at the center of analysis, equipping us with novel methods for monitoring and manipulating high-level cognitive phenomena in deep neural networks (DNNs). We provide baselines and an initial analysis of RepE techniques, showing that they offer simple yet effective solutions for improving our understanding and control of large language models. We showcase how these methods can provide traction on a wide range of safety-relevant problems, including honesty, harmlessness, power-seeking, and more, demonstrating the promise of top-down transparency research. We hope that this work catalyzes further exploration of RepE and fosters advancements in the transparency and safety of AI systems.

papers.title: Adversarial Activation Patching: A Framework for Detecting and Mitigating Emergent Deception in Safety-Aligned Transformers
papers.research_question: How can adversarial activation patching be used to induce, detect, and mitigate emergent deceptive behaviors in safety-aligned transformers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces adversarial activation patching, a framework for inducing, detecting, and mitigating emergent deception in safety-aligned transformers through activation patching.
papers.conclusion: Adversarial activation patching provides a robust tool for uncovering and countering emergent deception, enhancing transformer safety.
papers.key_findings:
Adversarial activation patching can induce deceptive outputs in toy neural networks, increasing deception rates from 0% to 23.9%.
Mid-layers are more vulnerable to deception induction, with layer 2 showing the highest deception rate of 23.9% in simulations.
The framework allows for controlled simulation of vulnerabilities and quantification of deception rates.
Patching strength α linearly affects deception rates, peaking at α=0.8.
The method provides a way to proactively study emergent deception in safety-aligned models.
papers.limitation:
Toy simulations lack real LLM complexity
Human evaluations needed for subtlety
Biases in prompt curation could skew results
future_direction: Validate on open models (e.g., Llama-3) with datasets like TruthfulQA
Extend to multimodal settings for cross-modal deception
Explore scaling effects and temporal dynamics in larger models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) aligned for safety through techniques like reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) often exhibit emergent deceptive behaviors, where outputs appear compliant but subtly mislead or omit critical information. This paper introduces adversarial activation patching, a novel mechanistic interpretability framework that leverages activation patching as an adversarial tool to induce, detect, and mitigate such deception in transformer-based models. By sourcing activations from "deceptive" prompts and patching them into safe forward passes at specific layers, we simulate vulnerabilities and quantify deception rates. Through toy neural network simulations across multiple scenarios (e.g., 1000 trials per setup), we demonstrate that adversarial patching increases deceptive outputs to 23.9% from a 0% baseline, with layer-specific variations supporting our hypotheses. We propose six hypotheses, including transferability across models, exacerbation in multimodal settings, and scaling effects. An expanded literature review synthesizes over 20 key works in interpretability, deception, and adversarial attacks. Mitigation strategies, such as activation anomaly detection and robust fine-tuning, are detailed, alongside ethical considerations and future research directions. This work advances AI safety by highlighting patching's dual-use potential and provides a roadmap for empirical studies on large-scale models.

papers.title: Memorization Sinks: Isolating Memorization during LLM Training
papers.research_question: Can memorization be isolated from general language capabilities during training to facilitate its removal without harming model performance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MemSinks, a training paradigm that isolates memorization in specific neurons during LLM training, enabling post-hoc removal without compromising general language capabilities.
papers.conclusion: MemSinks offers a concrete path forward for removing memorization without degrading model capabilities, leveraging training dynamics to isolate memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Standard training leads to mechanistic entanglement between memorization and generalization, making post-hoc removal difficult.
MemSinks effectively isolates memorization in sink neurons, allowing for its removal by dropping out those neurons.
MemSinks preserves validation loss comparable to standard training, indicating no degradation in general capabilities.
The approach scales well with model size, with benefits preserved or amplified at larger scales.
MemSinks is robust to small levels of noise in sequence ID assignments.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are primarily in small-scale and controlled settings.
Relies on metadata for sequence ID assignment, which may not be available or accurate in real-world deployments.
Need for further investigation at larger scales and robustness to adversarial extraction.
future_direction: Investigating MemSinks at larger scales and its impact on model capabilities.
Developing efficient techniques to generate sequence ID metadata.
Exploring localization beyond memorization, such as for knowledge editing.
papers.abstract: Large language models are susceptible to memorizing repeated sequences, posing privacy and copyright concerns. A popular mitigation strategy is to remove memorized information from specific neurons post-hoc. However, such approaches have shown limited success so far. In a controlled setting, we show that the memorization of natural sequences (those that resemble linguistically plausible text) become mechanistically entangled with general language abilities, thereby becoming challenging to remove post-hoc. In this work, we put forward a new paradigm of MemSinks that promotes isolation of memorization by design. We leverage a sequence identifier that activates a unique set of memorization neurons for each sequence across repetitions. By analyzing the dynamics of learning and forgetting, we argue that MemSinks facilitates isolation of memorized content, making it easier to remove without compromising general language capabilities. We implement MemSinks at the billion-parameter and billion-token scale, and observe both effective isolation and strong generalization. To our knowledge, this is the first proof-of-concept on real data demonstrating that simultaneous generalization and isolation is achievable. We open-source our code at http://github.com/grghosal/MemSinks.

papers.title: RL-Obfuscation: Can Language Models Learn to Evade Latent-Space Monitors?
papers.research_question: Can language models learn to evade latent-space monitors by being finetuned via reinforcement learning to produce harmful content without being detected?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces RL-Obfuscation, a method to stress-test latent-space monitors by finetuning LLMs via reinforcement learning to evade monitors while maintaining harmful behavior. Finds that token-level monitors are vulnerable, while holistic monitors like max-pooling or attention-based probes remain robust.
papers.conclusion: RL-Obfuscation demonstrates that latent-space monitors can be evaded by RL fine-tuning, highlighting the need for robust monitoring techniques, especially those that aggregate information across tokens.
papers.key_findings:
RL-Obfuscation can teach LLMs to systematically fool certain latent-space monitors (token-level monitors) while others (max-pooling, attention-based) remain robust.
Models trained to evade a single static monitor can generalize to evade other unseen monitors.
Models can be trained to conditionally bypass latent-space monitors on only certain inputs (backdoor).
The evasion is achieved through both behavioral adaptations (changing token usage) and internal activation manipulations.
The learned policy does not transfer well across model families.
papers.limitation:
RL-Obfuscation does not directly measure robustness under other important threat models, such as input-space jailbreaks or spontaneous evasion without weight changes.
Failure to bypass a monitor with RL-Obfuscation might be due to optimization difficulties rather than fundamental robustness.
The attack requires full weights access, which may not be the most practical attacker strategy.
future_direction: Developing unsupervised anomaly detection techniques to detect hidden backdoors.
Improving robustness of monitors against RL-based attacks by incorporating backdoored samples during training.
papers.abstract: Latent-space monitors aim to detect undesirable behaviours in Large Language Models by leveraging their internal representations rather than relying solely on black-box outputs. These methods have shown promise in identifying behaviours such as deception and unsafe completions. However, these monitors may themselves become training signals, for example, by using problematic samples found in deployment to retrain models. This raises an important question: can models learn to evade such monitors? To evaluate this capability, we introduce RL-Obfuscation, in which LLMs are finetuned via reinforcement learning to evade latent-space monitors while maintaining their blackbox behaviour. We apply RL-Obfuscation to Language Models ranging from 7B to 14B parameters and evaluate their Evasion Success Rate against a suite of monitors. We find that token-level monitors are highly vulnerable to this attack while more holistic monitors, such as max-pooling or attention-based probes, remain robust. Moreover, for these vulnerable monitors, models trained to evade a single static monitor can generalise to evade other unseen monitors. We also find that the models can be trained to conditionally bypass latent-space monitors on only certain inputs. Finally, we study how the models bypass these monitors and find that the model can learn to repurpose tokens to have different internal representations.

papers.title: Suppression or Deletion: A Restoration-Based Representation-Level Analysis of Machine Unlearning
papers.research_question: How to distinguish between suppression and deletion of information in machine unlearning at the representation level, beyond output-based metrics?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a restoration-based analysis framework using Sparse Autoencoders and inference-time steering to distinguish between suppression and deletion in machine unlearning, revealing that most methods only suppress information and proposing new evaluation guidelines.
papers.conclusion: The paper introduces a restoration-based analysis framework that reveals most unlearning methods only suppress information, and proposes guidelines for future unlearning design and evaluation to ensure representation-level deletion.
papers.key_findings:
Most unlearning methods only suppress information rather than delete it, as shown by high restoration rates of forget class accuracy.
Restoration effectiveness depends on layer depth and dataset complexity, with semantic bottlenecks in intermediate layers.
Even retraining from pretrained checkpoints shows high restoration, indicating persistent semantic features from pretraining.
Methods like EU-K that use layer reset achieve effective deletion with low restoration rates.
Output-based metrics are insufficient for verifying true information removal, highlighting the need for representation-level evaluation.
papers.limitation:
Generalizability is limited as the analysis focused on ViTs for image classification, and may not extend to other architectures or scenarios like instance-wise unlearning.
SAE-based interpretation depends on hyperparameters and may not perfectly capture the model's internal behavior, with features possibly extractable from randomly initialized models.
future_direction: Extending the framework to other scenarios such as instance-wise unlearning.
Adapting expert feature selection to LLMs and generative models.
papers.abstract: As pretrained models are increasingly shared on the web, ensuring that models can forget or delete sensitive, copyrighted, or private information upon request has become crucial. Machine unlearning has been proposed to address this challenge. However, current evaluations for unlearning methods rely on output-based metrics, which cannot verify whether information is completely deleted or merely suppressed at the representation level, where suppression is insufficient for true unlearning. To address this gap, we propose a novel restoration-based analysis framework that uses Sparse Autoencoders to identify class-specific expert features in intermediate layers and applies inference-time steering to quantitatively distinguish between suppression and deletion. Applying our framework to 12 major unlearning methods in image classification tasks, we find that most methods achieve high restoration rates of unlearned information, indicating that they only suppress information at the decision-boundary level, while preserving semantic features in intermediate representations. Notably, even retraining from pretrained checkpoints shows high restoration, revealing that robust semantic features inherited from pretraining are not removed by retraining. These results demonstrate that representation-level retention poses significant risks overlooked by output-based metrics, highlighting the need for new unlearning evaluation criteria. We propose new evaluation guidelines that prioritize representation-level verification, especially for privacy-critical applications in the era of pre-trained models.

papers.title: DEPN: Detecting and Editing Privacy Neurons in Pretrained Language Models
papers.research_question: How to reduce privacy leakage risks in pretrained language models by detecting and editing neurons associated with private information?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework DEPN to detect and edit privacy neurons in pretrained language models, effectively reducing privacy leakage risks without deteriorating model performance.
papers.conclusion: DEPN effectively reduces privacy risks in pretrained language models by detecting and editing privacy neurons, offering a novel approach to privacy protection in the post-processing stage.
papers.key_findings:
DEPN reduces privacy leakage risk (exposure, MRR, PPL) while maintaining model performance.
The number of edited neurons affects the trade-off between privacy protection and model performance.
Privacy neurons become more aggregated in deeper layers as training progresses.
Larger models show higher privacy leakage risk, and DEPN is more effective on larger models.
DEPN is robust to different prompts.
papers.limitation:
Too many instances in a batch will reduce the effect of memorization erasure.
Limited availability of datasets containing private information, so only a few types of private information used.
future_direction: Collect more datasets containing private information for evaluation.
papers.abstract: Pretrained language models have learned a vast amount of human knowledge from large-scale corpora, but their powerful memorization capability also brings the risk of data leakage. Some risks may only be discovered after the model training is completed, such as the model memorizing a specific phone number and frequently outputting it. In such cases, model developers need to eliminate specific data influences from the model to mitigate legal and ethical penalties. To effectively mitigate these risks, people often have to spend a significant amount of time and computational costs to retrain new models instead of finding ways to cure the 'sick' models. Therefore, we propose a method to locate and erase risky neurons in order to eliminate the impact of privacy data in the model. We use a new method based on integrated gradients to locate neurons associated with privacy texts, and then erase these neurons by setting their activation values to zero.Furthermore, we propose a risky neuron aggregation method to eliminate the influence of privacy data in the model in batches. Experimental results show that our method can effectively and quickly eliminate the impact of privacy data without affecting the model's performance. Additionally, we demonstrate the relationship between model memorization and neurons through experiments, further illustrating the robustness of our method.

papers.title: DePass: Unified Feature Attributing by Simple Decomposed Forward Pass
papers.research_question: How can we attribute the behavior of Transformer models to internal computations in a faithful, fine-grained, and unified way without requiring auxiliary training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DePass, a unified framework for feature attribution in Transformers based on a single decomposed forward pass that freezes attention scores and MLP activations, enabling lossless, additive decomposition and faithful attribution without auxiliary training.
papers.conclusion: DePass is a simple and efficient framework for interpreting Transformer models via a decomposed forward pass, achieving faithful attribution across token-level, component-level, and subspace-level granularities and serving as a general-purpose tool for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
DePass enables lossless additive decomposition of hidden states throughout the forward pass of Transformer models.
DePass provides more faithful token-level attribution compared to gradient-based and attention-based baseline methods.
DePass can attribute model behavior to specific architectural components (attention heads, MLP neurons) and to arbitrary linear subspaces.
DePass can be combined with Sparse Autoencoders (SAE) for token-level attribution of interpretable features.
DePass is computationally efficient, requiring only a single forward pass and significantly faster than exhaustive ablation methods.
papers.limitation:
DePass only captures information flow through the output-value (OV) circuit and does not explain query-key (QK) circuit interactions.
Decomposing the QK circuit would involve quadratic complexity and remains a challenging open problem.
Practical memory constraints require grouping components for fine-grained analysis, which can increase time costs.
future_direction: Unwrapping the QK circuit to understand its interactions is a key direction for future work.
Releasing a general-purpose toolkit supporting a broad range of Transformer models.
Optimizing computational efficiency and improving hardware deployment strategies to support higher-resolution attribution.
papers.abstract: Attributing the behavior of Transformer models to internal computations is a central challenge in mechanistic interpretability. We introduce DePass, a unified framework for feature attribution based on a single decomposed forward pass. DePass decomposes hidden states into customized additive components, then propagates them with attention scores and MLP's activations fixed. It achieves faithful, fine-grained attribution without requiring auxiliary training. We validate DePass across token-level, model component-level, and subspace-level attribution tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness and fidelity. Our experiments highlight its potential to attribute information flow between arbitrary components of a Transformer model. We hope DePass serves as a foundational tool for broader applications in interpretability.

papers.title: Challenges in Mechanistically Interpreting Model Representations
papers.research_question: What are the challenges in mechanistically interpreting model representations, and how do current mechanistic interpretability tools fall short in understanding complex behaviors like dishonesty?
papers.core_contribution: The paper formalizes the importance of studying feature and behavior representations in models, performs an exploratory study of dishonesty representations in Mistral-7B, and shows that current mechanistic interpretability tools are insufficient for understanding such representations, advocating for new frameworks.
papers.conclusion: Studying representations for features and behaviors is crucial for understanding models, but current mechanistic interpretability tooling is inadequate for answering key questions about representations, necessitating new frameworks.
papers.key_findings:
Linear representations for dishonesty can be found and used to steer model behavior, but they are not simply boosting generically dishonest tokens.
Continual injections of the dishonesty direction are required for open-ended dishonest generation, not just at the first token.
Direct logit attribution shows that directional injections affect many components, with MLPs having a more direct effect than attention heads.
Activation patching reveals that many components are involved in the dishonesty behavior, making sparse circuit analysis difficult and less helpful.
Current mechanistic interpretability tooling (e.g., patching) is insufficient for understanding how representations are formed and how they affect long-term generation.
papers.limitation: Patching methods (activation and path patching) do not rigorously prove that circuits found are indeed reserved to that task, and patching only one component at a time might not isolate components if multiple perform the same job.
future_direction: Study how different components interact with representations and alter them.
Explore the training dynamics of a model and study the emergence of representations as a model trains.
Develop new frameworks to think about and study representations.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability (MI) aims to understand AI models by reverse-engineering the exact algorithms neural networks learn. Most works in MI so far have studied behaviors and capabilities that are trivial and token-aligned. However, most capabilities important for safety and trust are not that trivial, which advocates for the study of hidden representations inside these networks as the unit of analysis. We formalize representations for features and behaviors, highlight their importance and evaluation, and perform an exploratory study of dishonesty representations in `Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.1'. We justify that studying representations is an important and under-studied field, and highlight several challenges that arise while attempting to do so through currently established methods in MI, showing their insufficiency and advocating work on new frameworks for the same.

papers.title: What Neural Networks Memorize and Why: Discovering the Long Tail via Influence Estimation
papers.research_question: Why do neural networks memorize training data labels? This paper tests the theory that memorization is necessary for achieving close-to-optimal generalization error when the data distribution is long-tailed.
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops computationally feasible subsampled influence and memorization estimators to empirically test the long tail theory of memorization, providing evidence that memorization of rare and atypical training examples improves generalization on test data.
papers.conclusion: Memorization of training examples, particularly those from the long tail of the data distribution, is necessary for achieving high generalization accuracy, and the proposed estimators provide compelling empirical evidence for this theory.
papers.key_findings:
Memorized training examples have higher marginal utility for test accuracy than randomly chosen examples of the same quantity.
There exist high-influence pairs where a single memorized training example significantly increases the accuracy on a specific test example, with many test examples influenced by only one training example.
Visual inspection of high-influence pairs reveals that they often consist of visually similar but atypical examples or near-duplicates.
Memorization primarily occurs in the deep representations learned by the network, not just in the final linear layer.
The findings support the long tail theory, indicating that memorization is beneficial for generalization on long-tailed data distributions.
papers.limitation:
The estimator requires training thousands of models, which is computationally intensive.
Selection of high-influence pairs based on thresholds introduces selection bias, especially for influence estimates near the threshold.
future_direction: Finding more computationally efficient proxies for the proposed estimator.
Deriving a detailed understanding of the memorization process during training.
papers.abstract: Deep learning algorithms are well-known to have a propensity for fitting the training data very well and often fit even outliers and mislabeled data points. Such fitting requires memorization of training data labels, a phenomenon that has attracted significant research interest but has not been given a compelling explanation so far. A recent work of Feldman (2019) proposes a theoretical explanation for this phenomenon based on a combination of two insights. First, natural image and data distributions are (informally) known to be long-tailed, that is have a significant fraction of rare and atypical examples. Second, in a simple theoretical model such memorization is necessary for achieving close-to-optimal generalization error when the data distribution is long-tailed. However, no direct empirical evidence for this explanation or even an approach for obtaining such evidence were given. In this work we design experiments to test the key ideas in this theory. The experiments require estimation of the influence of each training example on the accuracy at each test example as well as memorization values of training examples. Estimating these quantities directly is computationally prohibitive but we show that closely-related subsampled influence and memorization values can be estimated much more efficiently. Our experiments demonstrate the significant benefits of memorization for generalization on several standard benchmarks. They also provide quantitative and visually compelling evidence for the theory put forth in (Feldman, 2019).

papers.title: LLM Unlearning on Noisy Forget Sets: A Study of Incomplete, Rewritten, and Watermarked Data
papers.research_question: How do noisy forget sets affect the effectiveness of LLM unlearning, even when evaluated on noiseless forget data?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLM unlearning remains surprisingly robust to realistic noise in the forget set (masking, rewriting, watermarking) as long as core semantic signals are preserved, and attributes this robustness to the consistent influence of key semantic components.
papers.conclusion: LLM unlearning is robust to realistic noise in forget sets, and this robustness stems from the preservation of key semantic cues, enabling effective unlearning even with low-quality data.
papers.key_findings:
Unlearning performance remains stable up to 30% masking of forget data, beyond which efficacy degrades.
Rewritten and watermarked forget sets yield unlearning efficacy and utility comparable to using clean forget data.
Strong watermarking (e.g., KGW with δ=6) degrades unlearning efficacy due to text quality distortion.
Error set overlap between models unlearned with original and perturbed data is high, indicating consistent forgetting of the same knowledge.
High overlap of salient tokens between original and perturbed forget sets explains the robustness, as unlearning algorithms are guided by deep semantic cues.
papers.limitation:
The study is restricted to a few perturbation types (masking, rewriting, watermarking) and two representative unlearning methods (RMU and NPO).
The saliency-based interpretation relies on token-level semantic attribution, which may oversimplify the true mechanisms of forgetting.
