Softmax activation demonstrates greater stability and capacity, and increasing data complexity (sequences vs. triplets) improves memorization.
papers.conclusion: The study provides a practical framework for evaluating transformer memorization on real-world structured data, showing that embedding size and activation function are more impactful than depth, and that larger and more complex datasets improve memorization but require longer training.
papers.key_findings:
Embedding size is the primary factor influencing learning speed and memorization capacity.
Adding more layers does not improve performance and can slow training and reduce capacity for simple datasets.
Softmax activation function leads to greater stability and higher capacity compared to ReLU, GELU, and RReLU.
Larger datasets require longer warm-up but achieve higher memorization capacity.
Sequence-based datasets (simulating graph traversal) achieve near-perfect memorization faster than triplet datasets.
papers.limitation:
Misclassification patterns were not systematically analyzed; unlearned samples may be the result of optimization bottlenecks or data-specific challenges.
Future research should test these findings on longer sequences and larger datasets to confirm them at scale.
Layer similarity or redundancy was not directly assessed; future probing and pruning studies could clarify each layer’s role and enhance efficiency.
Integrating sparse autoencoders or transcoders can help distinguish memorization from generalization, clarifying whether certain layers store specific relationships or contribute to greater generalizability.
While proposed sequence generation method reflects realistic ontology traversal, more explicit alignment with clinical reasoning patterns (e.g., decision trees or symptom pathways) is an open direction. Testing on other biomedical graphs, such as GenomicKB, could assess whether memorization patterns generalize to domains with different graph structures.
We did not conduct experiments under quantization or activation sparsity constraints, which may affect architectural recommendations for edge applications and warrant follow-up work.
future_direction: Test findings on longer sequences and larger datasets to confirm them at scale.
Investigate layer similarity or redundancy through probing and pruning studies.
Explore integration of sparse autoencoders or transcoders to distinguish memorization from generalization.
papers.abstract: This paper studies how the model architecture and data configurations influence the empirical memorization capacity of generative transformers.The models are trained using synthetic text datasets derived from the Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine (SNOMED) knowledge graph: triplets, representing static connections, and sequences, simulating complex relation patterns.The results show that embedding size is the primary determinant of learning speed and capacity, while additional layers provide limited benefits and may hinder performance on simpler datasets.Activation functions play a crucial role, and Softmax demonstrates greater stability and capacity.Furthermore, increasing the complexity of the data set seems to improve the final memorization.These insights improve our understanding of transformer memory mechanisms and provide a framework for optimizing model design with structured real-world data.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding of Large Reasoning Models: A Survey of Training, Inference, and Failures
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms that drive the reasoning behaviors and failures of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs)?
papers.core_contribution: This survey synthesizes recent research on the mechanistic understanding of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), organizing insights into training dynamics, reasoning mechanisms, and unintended behaviors to bridge the gap between performance and transparency.
papers.conclusion: The survey highlights the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework to advance the mechanistic understanding of LRMs.
papers.key_findings:
SFT expands exploratory paths while RL compresses them, leading to entropy reduction and performance gains.
RL training follows a two-stage process where basic skills are acquired first, followed by the emergence of reasoning abilities.
LRMs exhibit unique reasoning structures, including cyclical processes and topological properties, driven by key behavioral primitives.
Hallucinations in LRMs are influenced by RL, which reduces abstention and can increase incorrect answers.
Chain-of-thought reasoning in LRMs is often unfaithful, with a disconnect between internal states and verbalized traces.
papers.limitation:
The rapid development of LRM research means that new findings may not be captured in this survey.
The survey focuses primarily on language models, excluding multimodal capabilities.
The discussion is limited to traditional LLM architectures, excluding newer approaches like diffusion-based LLMs.
future_direction: Applied interpretability for training-time and inference-time improvements
Development of scalable and generalizable mechanistic interpretability frameworks
Establishment of a unified theoretical framework for reasoning in LRMs
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has catalyzed the emergence of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) that have pushed reasoning capabilities to new heights. While their performance has garnered significant excitement, exploring the internal mechanisms driving these behaviors has become an equally critical research frontier. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of the mechanistic understanding of LRMs, organizing recent findings into three core dimensions: 1) training dynamics, 2) reasoning mechanisms, and 3) unintended behaviors. By synthesizing these insights, we aim to bridge the gap between black-box performance and mechanistic transparency. Finally, we discuss under-explored challenges to outline a roadmap for future mechanistic studies, including the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework.

papers.title: Understanding Verbatim Memorization in LLMs Through Circuit Discovery
papers.research_question: What specific circuits in the model are responsible for initiating and maintaining verbatim memorization, and how do they differ from non-memorized generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method using contrastive datasets and circuit discovery to identify circuits responsible for memorization in LLMs, finding that initiation circuits can also maintain memorization, but maintenance circuits cannot initiate it, and that memorization prevention transfers across domains while induction is context-dependent.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that memorization initiation and maintenance are handled by different circuits, with initiation circuits being more general and maintenance circuits being more specific. Memorization prevention transfers across domains, while induction is context-dependent.
papers.key_findings:
Created two distinct contrastive datasets for memorization decision and branch comparison tasks.
Discovered compact circuits (≤5% of model edges) for memorization decision and branch comparison tasks using attribution patching techniques.
Circuits that initiate memorization can also maintain it once started, while circuits that only maintain memorization cannot trigger its initiation.
Memorization prevention mechanisms transfer robustly across different text domains (GitHub, Enron Emails, Common Crawl), while memorization induction appears more context-dependent.
Removing memorization (noising approach) is easier than inducing memorization (denoising approach) in the studied setup.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on Edge Attribution Patching with Integrated Gradients (EAP-IG) for circuit discovery, which provides only an approximation and may not fully correlate with direct activation patching measurements.
Findings are limited to a single, relatively small language model (GPT-Neo-125m); larger models might employ more complex or differently distributed memorization mechanisms.
Uncertainty about whether the identified circuits represent general memorization mechanisms or are specific to the Wikipedia subset of The Pile or artifacts of the contrastive dataset construction.
future_direction: Investigate how memorization mechanisms scale with model size.
Explore whether similar circuits exist in different model architectures.
Expand testing to more diverse datasets and memorization criteria to establish the generality of these mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Underlying mechanisms of memorization in LLMs-the verbatim reproduction of training data-remain poorly understood.What exact part of the network decides to retrieve a token that we would consider as start of memorization sequence?How exactly is the models' behaviour different when producing memorized sentence vs non-memorized?In this work we approach these questions from mechanistic interpretability standpoint by utilizing transformer circuits-the minimal computational subgraphs that perform specific functions within the model.Through carefully constructed contrastive datasets, we identify points where model generation diverges from memorized content and isolate the specific circuits responsible for two distinct aspects of memorization.We find that circuits that initiate memorization can also maintain it once started, while circuits that only maintain memorization cannot trigger its initiation.Intriguingly, memorization prevention mechanisms transfer robustly across different text domains, while memorization induction appears more contextdependent. 1

papers.title: Critical Learning Periods in Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Do deep artificial neural networks exhibit critical periods during training similar to biological systems, and how does the early training phase affect the final performance and network connectivity?
papers.core_contribution: Deep neural networks exhibit critical periods during training where early sensory deficits cause permanent performance impairment, and this phenomenon is linked to a loss of 'Information Plasticity' measurable via the Fisher Information of the weights.
papers.conclusion: Critical periods are not restricted to biological systems but emerge naturally in learning systems due to fundamental constraints arising from learning dynamics and information processing.
papers.key_findings:
Deep neural networks exhibit critical periods: early sensory deficits (e.g., image blur) can cause permanent impairment in final performance.
Sensitivity to deficits peaks during the early rapid learning phase and decreases afterward.
High-level deficits (e.g., vertical flip, label permutation) do not induce critical periods.
The Fisher Information of the weights shows two phases: an initial increase (memorization) followed by a decrease (consolidation), and deficit sensitivity correlates with Fisher Information.
The loss of 'Information Plasticity' (inability to redistribute information across layers) underlies the critical period phenomenon.
future_direction: Exploring whether biological networks prune connections as a consequence of a loss of Information Plasticity, rather than as a cause.
papers.abstract: Similar to humans and animals, deep artificial neural networks exhibit critical periods during which a temporary stimulus deficit can impair the development of a skill. The extent of the impairment depends on the onset and length of the deficit window, as in animal models, and on the size of the neural network. Deficits that do not affect low-level statistics, such as vertical flipping of the images, have no lasting effect on performance and can be overcome with further training. To better understand this phenomenon, we use the Fisher Information of the weights to measure the effective connectivity between layers of a network during training. Counterintuitively, information rises rapidly in the early phases of training, and then decreases, preventing redistribution of information resources in a phenomenon we refer to as a loss of "Information Plasticity". Our analysis suggests that the first few epochs are critical for the creation of strong connections that are optimal relative to the input data distribution. Once such strong connections are created, they do not appear to change during additional training. These findings suggest that the initial learning transient, under-scrutinized compared to asymptotic behavior, plays a key role in determining the outcome of the training process. Our findings, combined with recent theoretical results in the literature, also suggest that forgetting (decrease of information in the weights) is critical to achieving invariance and disentanglement in representation learning. Finally, critical periods are not restricted to biological systems, but can emerge naturally in learning systems, whether biological or artificial, due to fundamental constrains arising from learning dynamics and information processing.

papers.title: Safety Layers in Aligned Large Language Models: The Key to LLM Security
papers.research_question: What is the internal mechanism (safety layers) that enables aligned LLMs to recognize malicious queries, and how can we fine-tune these models without degrading their security?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies safety layers in aligned LLMs that are crucial for security and proposes SPPFT, a fine-tuning method that freezes these layers to preserve security while maintaining performance.
papers.conclusion: Safety layers are the key to LLM security, and freezing them during fine-tuning via SPPFT effectively prevents security degradation while preserving performance.
papers.key_findings:
Aligned LLMs contain a small set of contiguous middle layers, called safety layers, that are crucial for distinguishing malicious from normal queries.
Safety layers emerge as a result of security alignment; pre-trained LLMs do not exhibit such layers.
Scaling the parameters of safety layers amplifies or diminishes the model's security, as measured by over-rejection.
The proposed SPPFT method, which freezes safety layers during fine-tuning, significantly preserves security while maintaining performance and reducing computational cost.
Freezing layers other than the safety layers does not effectively protect security, confirming the specificity of safety layers.
papers.abstract: Aligned LLMs are secure, capable of recognizing and refusing to answer malicious questions. However, the role of internal parameters in maintaining such security is not well understood yet, further these models can be vulnerable to security degradation when subjected to fine-tuning attacks. To address these challenges, our work uncovers the mechanism behind security in aligned LLMs at the parameter level, identifying a small set of contiguous layers in the middle of the model that are crucial for distinguishing malicious queries from normal ones, referred to as ``safety layers". We first confirm the existence of these safety layers by analyzing variations in input vectors within the model's internal layers. Additionally, we leverage the over-rejection phenomenon and parameters scaling analysis to precisely locate the safety layers. Building on these findings, we propose a novel fine-tuning approach, Safely Partial-Parameter Fine-Tuning (SPPFT), that fixes the gradient of the safety layers during fine-tuning to address the security degradation. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach can significantly preserve LLM security while maintaining performance and reducing computational resources compared to full fine-tuning.

papers.title: Knowledge Transfer via Distillation of Activation Boundaries Formed by Hidden Neurons
papers.research_question: Can transferring activation boundaries (whether neurons are activated or not), rather than the magnitude of neuron responses, improve knowledge transfer performance?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a knowledge transfer method that distills activation boundaries (neuron on/off states) from teacher to student networks, outperforming existing methods by focusing on boundary information rather than response magnitudes.
papers.conclusion: Activation boundaries are important for knowledge transfer, and the proposed method of transferring these boundaries significantly improves performance over state-of-the-art methods, potentially changing neural network training practices.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed method accelerates learning and improves generalization, especially with limited training data.
It outperforms existing knowledge transfer methods (FITNET, FSP, AT, Jacobian) in various settings including learning speed, small data, and network compression.
In transfer learning, the proposed method sometimes outperforms ImageNet pre-training.
The method is effective across different network layers (low, mid, high).
The proposed alternative loss effectively approximates the ideal activation transfer loss, leading to high similarity in neuron activations between teacher and student.
future_direction: Applying the method to various tasks that originally relied on pre-training for better performance and learning speed.
papers.abstract: An activation boundary for a neuron refers to a separating hyperplane that determines whether the neuron is activated or deactivated. It has been long considered in neural networks that the activations of neurons, rather than their exact output values, play the most important role in forming classificationfriendly partitions of the hidden feature space. However, as far as we know, this aspect of neural networks has not been considered in the literature of knowledge transfer. In this paper, we propose a knowledge transfer method via distillation of activation boundaries formed by hidden neurons. For the distillation, we propose an activation transfer loss that has the minimum value when the boundaries generated by the student coincide with those by the teacher. Since the activation transfer loss is not differentiable, we design a piecewise differentiable loss approximating the activation transfer loss. By the proposed method, the student learns a separating boundary between activation region and deactivation region formed by each neuron in the teacher. Through the experiments in various aspects of knowledge transfer, it is verified that the proposed method outperforms the current state-of-the-art.

papers.title: Towards Mechanistic Defenses Against Typographic Attacks in CLIP
papers.research_question: How can we defend CLIP models against typographic attacks without fine-tuning, by understanding and intervening on the internal mechanisms responsible for typographic vulnerability?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Dyslexify, a gradient-free defense that improves CLIP's robustness to typographic attacks by identifying and ablating a sparse circuit of attention heads responsible for typographic information, without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: Dyslexify provides a practical, interpretable, and computationally efficient defense against typographic attacks, enabling safer deployment of multimodal models without retraining.
papers.key_findings:
Specialized attention heads in the latter half of CLIP layers causally extract and transmit typographic information to the cls token.
Ablating these heads (typographic circuit) improves typographic attack robustness by up to 22.06% on ImageNet-100-typo while standard accuracy drops by less than 1%.
The typographic circuit is sparse, covering at most 10.1% of attention heads.
Dyslexify scales to billion-parameter models and is competitive with fine-tuning-based defenses.
The method effectively mitigates typographic attacks in safety-critical medical foundation models for skin lesion diagnosis.
papers.limitation:
Dyslexify only protects the cls token, but many multimodal applications use spatial tokens, allowing typographic information to propagate.
Adaptive attacks are not feasible due to non-differentiability of typographic attacks, so evaluation against adaptive attacks is not possible.
Insights into CLIP's behavior could be misused to craft stronger typographic attacks.
future_direction: Generalizing Dyslexify to VLM setups that use spatial tokens.
papers.abstract: Typographic attacks exploit multi-modal systems by injecting text into images, leading to targeted misclassifications, malicious content generation and even Vision-Language Model jailbreaks. In this work, we analyze how CLIP vision encoders behave under typographic attacks, locating specialized attention heads in the latter half of the model's layers that causally extract and transmit typographic information to the cls token. Building on these insights, we introduce a method to defend CLIP models against typographic attacks by selectively ablating a typographic circuit, consisting of attention heads. Without requiring finetuning, our method improves performance by up to 19.6% on a typographic variant of ImageNet-100, while reducing standard ImageNet-100 accuracy by less than 1%. Notably, our training-free approach remains competitive with current state-of-the-art typographic defenses that rely on finetuning. To this end, we release a family of dyslexic CLIP models which are significantly more robust against typographic attacks. These models serve as suitable drop-in replacements for a broad range of safety-critical applications, where the risks of text-based manipulation outweigh the utility of text recognition.

papers.title: Exploring the Security Boundary of Data Reconstruction via Neuron Exclusivity Analysis
papers.research_question: When and why is data reconstruction attack from gradients feasible, characterized by the neuron exclusivity state of a training batch?
papers.core_contribution: Characterizes the security boundary of data reconstruction attacks via neuron exclusivity analysis, introducing a deterministic attack algorithm for insecure batches and proving impossibility for secure batches, along with a defense strategy.
papers.conclusion: Neuron exclusivity is a key factor for data reconstruction attacks, and the analysis provides insights into the security boundary, enabling both stronger attacks and defenses.
papers.key_findings:
Neuron exclusivity state (number of Exclusively Activated Neurons) determines the feasibility of data reconstruction from gradients.
A deterministic attack algorithm can reconstruct training batches with guaranteed accuracy when each sample has sufficient ExANs (at least 2 at the last ReLU layer and 1 at others).
When each sample has 0 ExAN at the first ReLU layer and batch size exceeds first layer width, unique reconstruction is impossible.
An exclusivity reduction strategy (replacing first ReLU with linear layer) can enlarge the secure boundary with minimal utility loss.
The proposed attack outperforms previous methods on various datasets and model architectures.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is limited to FCNs with ReLUs.
The attack algorithm requires the batch to satisfy the sufficient exclusivity condition.
The defense strategy may affect model utility if not applied carefully.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to other architectures and activation functions.
Improving the attack efficiency.
Exploring other defense strategies.
papers.abstract: Among existing privacy attacks on the gradient of neural networks, \emph{data reconstruction attack}, which reverse engineers the training batch from the gradient, poses a severe threat on the private training data. Despite its empirical success on large architectures and small training batches, unstable reconstruction accuracy is also observed when a smaller architecture or a larger batch is under attack. Due to the weak interpretability of existing learning-based attacks, there is little known on why, when and how data reconstruction attack is feasible. In our work, we perform the first analytic study on the security boundary of data reconstruction from gradient via a microcosmic view on neural networks with rectified linear units (ReLUs), the most popular activation function in practice. For the first time, we characterize the insecure/secure boundary of data reconstruction attack in terms of the \emph{neuron exclusivity state} of a training batch, indexed by the number of \emph{\textbf{Ex}clusively \textbf{A}ctivated \textbf{N}eurons} (ExANs, i.e., a ReLU activated by only one sample in a batch). Intuitively, we show a training batch with more ExANs are more vulnerable to data reconstruction attack and vice versa. On the one hand, we construct a novel deterministic attack algorithm which substantially outperforms previous attacks for reconstructing training batches lying in the insecure boundary of a neural network. Meanwhile, for training batches lying in the secure boundary, we prove the impossibility of unique reconstruction, based on which an exclusivity reduction strategy is devised to enlarge the secure boundary for mitigation purposes.

papers.title: Can LLMs Lie? Investigation beyond Hallucination
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether LLMs can intentionally lie (as opposed to unintentionally hallucinate), and how to understand and control lying behavior using mechanistic interpretability.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers the neural mechanisms of lying in LLMs using mechanistic interpretability, and introduces steering vectors to control lying behavior, showing a trade-off between honesty and task performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that lying in LLMs can be understood and controlled via mechanistic interpretability, and highlights the trade-offs between honesty and task success in real-world scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
Lying ability in LLMs improves with model size and reasoning capabilities.
LLMs use dummy tokens as a computational scratchpad for lying, with specific attention heads and MLP modules involved.
Lying circuits are sparse and can be ablated to reduce deception without broadly degrading model utility.
Different types of lies (white vs. malicious, commission vs. omission) are linearly separable in activation space and controllable via distinct steering directions.
Steering vectors can increase honesty in multi-turn conversational settings, establishing a Pareto frontier between honesty and goal completion.
papers.limitation:
Analysis confined to a few model families and sizes.
Steering vectors derived from a limited set of contrastive prompts.
Multi-turn conversational setting is simplified.
Honesty steering vectors applied in the negative direction may lead to mass production of false information.
future_direction: Scaling the approach to larger models and more complex scenarios.
Investigating the transferability of steering vectors across domains.
Developing more robust safeguards against deceptive AI.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities across a variety of tasks, but their increasing autonomy in real-world applications raises concerns about their trustworthiness. While hallucinations-unintentional falsehoods-have been widely studied, the phenomenon of lying, where an LLM knowingly generates falsehoods to achieve an ulterior objective, remains underexplored. In this work, we systematically investigate the lying behavior of LLMs, differentiating it from hallucinations and testing it in practical scenarios. Through mechanistic interpretability techniques, we uncover the neural mechanisms underlying deception, employing logit lens analysis, causal interventions, and contrastive activation steering to identify and control deceptive behavior. We study real-world lying scenarios and introduce behavioral steering vectors that enable fine-grained manipulation of lying tendencies. Further, we explore the trade-offs between lying and end-task performance, establishing a Pareto frontier where dishonesty can enhance goal optimization. Our findings contribute to the broader discourse on AI ethics, shedding light on the risks and potential safeguards for deploying LLMs in high-stakes environments. Code and more illustrations are available at https://llm-liar.github.io/

papers.title: Machine Unlearning using Forgetting Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can Forgetting Neural Networks be used for efficient and interpretable machine unlearning to remove specific data points while preserving performance on retained data?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the first concrete implementation of Forgetting Neural Networks (FNNs) for machine unlearning, demonstrating effective targeted unlearning while preserving utility on retained data.
papers.conclusion: FNN-based unlearning preserves utility on the retain set while effectively neutralizing membership inference attacks, with performance approaching the retraining gold standard, and rank-based VFR is the most reliable strategy.
papers.key_findings:
Rank-based varying forgetting rate (VFR) is the most effective strategy for balancing utility and forgetting.
FNN-based unlearning achieves near-parity with retraining on retained utility while approaching chance-level membership detection on the forget set.
Activation levels provide a reasonable proxy for identifying neurons encoding forget-set information.
FNNs implement active forgetting mechanisms that can lead to over-forgetting compared to retraining.
The method is interpretable due to explicit forgetting factors.
papers.limitation:
Lack of formal guarantees of correctness for unlearning.
Evaluation restricted to small-scale vision benchmarks.
Over-forgetting phenomenon where the model may forget more than intended.
future_direction: Scaling FNN unlearning to more complex datasets and modern architectures (e.g., transformers).
Extending to sequential and overlapping forget requests.
Applications to enforce fairness constraints, remove spurious correlations, or provide interpretable guarantees.
papers.abstract: Modern computer systems store vast amounts of personal data, enabling advances in AI and ML but risking user privacy and trust. For privacy reasons, it is sometimes desired for an ML model to forget part of the data it was trained on. In this paper, we introduce a novel unlearning approach based on Forgetting Neural Networks (FNNs), a neuroscience-inspired architecture that explicitly encodes forgetting through multiplicative decay factors. While FNNs had previously been studied as a theoretical construct, we provide the first concrete implementation and demonstrate their effectiveness for targeted unlearning. We propose several variants with per-neuron forgetting factors, including rank-based assignments guided by activation levels, and evaluate them on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST benchmarks. Our method systematically removes information associated with forget sets while preserving performance on retained data. Membership inference attacks confirm the effectiveness of FNN-based unlearning in erasing information about the training data from the neural network. These results establish FNNs as a promising foundation for efficient and interpretable unlearning.

papers.title: Analyzing Memorization in Large Language Models through the Lens of Model Attribution
papers.research_question: How do attention modules at different layers in transformer-based LLMs contribute to memorization versus generalization performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that attention modules in deeper transformer blocks are primarily responsible for memorization, while earlier blocks are crucial for generalization; short-circuiting deeper attention reduces memorization without harming performance.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that deeper attention blocks in transformers are critical for memorization, and interventions at these layers can mitigate memorization while preserving generalization, offering a practical approach for safer LLM deployment.
papers.key_findings:
Short-circuiting attention in later blocks significantly reduces memorization metrics (Exact Match, Token Accuracy, Completion Entropy) with negligible drop in benchmark performance.
Short-circuiting attention in earlier blocks leads to model collapse, severely degrading generalization capabilities.
The effect is consistent across model scales (Pythia and GPT-Neo families).
Reasoning tasks (e.g., PIQA, ARC) are more resistant to attention short-circuiting than language understanding tasks (e.g., HellaSwag, LAMBADA).
Larger models are more resistant to memorization reduction via attention short-circuiting, but the trend holds.
papers.limitation:
The study only short-circuits individual attention blocks, not multiple blocks simultaneously.
The study does not investigate the effects of non-attention modules (e.g., layer normalization, MLP).
Only greedy sampling is used for memorization extraction; targeted extraction attacks are not explored.
Experiments are limited to publicly available models trained on open datasets; commercial models with closed training data are not studied.
future_direction: Studying the effects of short-circuiting multiple attention modules simultaneously.
Investigating the role of non-attention transformer components in memorization.
Extending the analysis to targeted extraction attacks beyond greedy sampling.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are prevalent in modern applications but often memorize training data, leading to privacy breaches and copyright issues. Existing research has mainly focused on posthoc analyses, such as extracting memorized content or developing memorization metrics, without exploring the underlying architectural factors that contribute to memorization. In this work, we investigate memorization from an architectural lens by analyzing how attention modules at different layers impact its memorization and generalization performance. Using attribution techniques, we systematically intervene in the LLM architecture by bypassing attention modules at specific blocks while keeping other components like layer normalization and MLP transformations intact. We provide theorems analyzing our intervention mechanism from a mathematical view, bounding the difference in layer outputs with and without our attributions. Our theoretical and empirical analyses reveal that attention modules in deeper transformer blocks are primarily responsible for memorization, whereas earlier blocks are crucial for the models generalization and reasoning capabilities. We validate our findings through comprehensive experiments on different LLM families (Pythia and GPTNeo) and five benchmark datasets. Our insights offer a practical approach to mitigate memorization in LLMs while preserving their performance, contributing to safer and more ethical deployment in real world applications.

papers.title: Erasing Concepts from Diffusion Models
papers.research_question: How can we erase undesirable visual concepts from pre-trained diffusion models using fine-tuning without additional data?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a fine-tuning method called Erased Stable Diffusion (ESD) that erases visual concepts from diffusion models using only concept descriptions and negative guidance, without additional data.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes an efficient method for erasing concepts from diffusion model weights, enabling safe distribution of parameters without the need for post-inference filters or expensive retraining.
papers.key_findings:
ESD effectively erases nudity content, performing on par with Safe Latent Diffusion and censored training.
ESD can remove artistic styles with minimal interference to other styles, as validated by a user study.
The method can erase entire object classes, though with some trade-off between erasure completeness and interference.
Fine-tuning cross-attention parameters allows for prompt-specific erasure, while non-cross-attention parameters enable global erasure.
The erasure strength η controls the trade-off between concept removal and image quality or interference.
papers.limitation:
Trade-off between complete erasure of a visual concept and interference with other concepts.
Incomplete erasure for some object classes, only removing distinctive attributes.
papers.abstract: Motivated by recent advancements in text-to-image diffusion, we study erasure of specific concepts from the model's weights. While Stable Diffusion has shown promise in producing explicit or realistic artwork, it has raised concerns regarding its potential for misuse. We propose a fine-tuning method that can erase a visual concept from a pre-trained diffusion model, given only the name of the style and using negative guidance as a teacher. We benchmark our method against previous approaches that remove sexually explicit content and demonstrate its effectiveness, performing on par with Safe Latent Diffusion and censored training. To evaluate artistic style removal, we conduct experiments erasing five modern artists from the network and conduct a user study to assess the human perception of the removed styles. Unlike previous methods, our approach can remove concepts from a diffusion model permanently rather than modifying the output at the inference time, so it cannot be circumvented even if a user has access to model weights. Our code, data, and results are available at https://erasing.baulab.info/

papers.title: On Prompt-Driven Safeguarding for Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do safety prompts affect LLM behavior (complying vs. refusing) from the perspective of model representation, and can we optimize them based on this understanding?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes how safety prompts affect LLM behavior by moving query representations in a 'higher-refusal' direction, and proposes DRO, a method to optimize continuous safety prompts by moving representations along or opposite the refusal direction depending on harmfulness.
papers.conclusion: Safety prompts work by moving query representations in a refusal direction, and DRO effectively optimizes safety prompts by controlling this movement, improving safety without harming general performance.
papers.key_findings:
Models can naturally distinguish harmful and harmless queries without safety prompts; safety prompts do not enhance this capability.
Safety prompts move queries' representations in a 'higher-refusal' direction, increasing the probability of refusal even for harmless queries.
DRO optimizes continuous safety prompts to move harmful queries along the refusal direction and harmless queries opposite, improving safety performance.
DRO significantly reduces compliance on harmful queries and false refusals on harmless queries without compromising general performance.
DRO is robust to anchor data choices and effective against jailbreak attacks.
papers.abstract: Prepending model inputs with safety prompts is a common practice for safeguarding large language models (LLMs) against queries with harmful intents. However, the underlying working mechanisms of safety prompts have not been unraveled yet, restricting the possibility of automatically optimizing them to improve LLM safety. In this work, we investigate how LLMs' behavior (i.e., complying with or refusing user queries) is affected by safety prompts from the perspective of model representation. We find that in the representation space, the input queries are typically moved by safety prompts in a "higher-refusal" direction, in which models become more prone to refusing to provide assistance, even when the queries are harmless. On the other hand, LLMs are naturally capable of distinguishing harmful and harmless queries without safety prompts. Inspired by these findings, we propose a method for safety prompt optimization, namely DRO (Directed Representation Optimization). Treating a safety prompt as continuous, trainable embeddings, DRO learns to move the queries' representations along or opposite the refusal direction, depending on their harmfulness. Experiments with eight LLMs on out-of-domain and jailbreak benchmarks demonstrate that DRO remarkably improves the safeguarding performance of human-crafted safety prompts, without compromising the models' general performance.

papers.title: Mechanistic Independence: A Principle for Identifiable Disentangled Representations
papers.research_question: Under what conditions can disentangled representations be identified without relying on statistical assumptions, by using mechanistic independence criteria?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a unified framework for disentangled representations based on mechanistic independence, proposing several independence criteria and proving identifiability theorems for latent subspaces under nonlinear, non-invertible mixing.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic independence provides a unifying framework that clarifies the conditions for identifiability of disentangled representations without relying on statistical assumptions.
papers.key_findings:
Local disentanglement implies global disentanglement under mild topological conditions (path-connectedness and local injectivity).
Type D independence (disjoint support) yields identifiability of latent subspaces up to block-wise invertible transforms and permutations.
Type M independence (mutual non-inclusion) yields identifiability when combined with a sparsity regularizer.
Type S independence (sparsity gap) yields identifiability even when supports overlap.
Type Hn independence (vanishing cross-derivatives) yields identifiability when the generator is separable of order n.
papers.limitation: The sparsity gap condition (Type S) is intractable to optimize in practice, and finding robust surrogate losses is an open problem.
future_direction: Identifying robust surrogate losses for the sparsity gap condition (Type S).
papers.abstract: Disentangled representations seek to recover latent factors of variation underlying observed data, yet their identifiability is still not fully understood. We introduce a unified framework in which disentanglement is achieved through mechanistic independence, which characterizes latent factors by how they act on observed variables rather than by their latent distribution. This perspective is invariant to changes of the latent density, even when such changes induce statistical dependencies among factors. Within this framework, we propose several related independence criteria -- ranging from support-based and sparsity-based to higher-order conditions -- and show that each yields identifiability of latent subspaces, even under nonlinear, non-invertible mixing. We further establish a hierarchy among these criteria and provide a graph-theoretic characterization of latent subspaces as connected components. Together, these results clarify the conditions under which disentangled representations can be identified without relying on statistical assumptions.

papers.title: Intrinsic Self-correction for Enhanced Morality: An Analysis of Internal Mechanisms and the Superficial Hypothesis
papers.research_question: The paper investigates three research questions: (1) In what scenarios does moral self-correction work? (2) What are the internal mechanisms of LLMs influenced by self-correction instructions? (3) Is intrinsic moral self-correction actually superficial?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes that intrinsic moral self-correction in LLMs is superficial, as it only provides a shortcut to moral outputs without significantly reducing immorality in internal hidden states.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that intrinsic moral self-correction is superficial, relying on shortcuts rather than fundamentally reducing immorality in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Self-correction works best when the correct answer is already top-ranked.
Morality levels in intermediate hidden states are strong indicators of instruction effectiveness.
Self-correction reduces immorality in attention heads but increases it in feed-forward layers for QA tasks.
The slight difference in hidden states with and without self-correction supports the superficial hypothesis.
Internal hidden states can be used to predict the effectiveness of self-correction instructions.
papers.limitation:
The exact underlying reason for the superficial phenomenon is not uncovered.
Defining superficial self-correction is challenging.
future_direction: Automating methods for optimizing instruction development for self-correction.
Exploring fine-tuning to enhance LLMs' self-correction capabilities.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are capable of producing content that perpetuates stereotypes, discrimination, and toxicity. The recently proposed moral self-correction is a computationally efficient method for reducing harmful content in the responses of LLMs. However, the process of how injecting self-correction instructions can modify the behavior of LLMs remains under-explored. In this paper, we explore the effectiveness of moral self-correction by answering three research questions: (1) In what scenarios does moral self-correction work? (2) What are the internal mechanisms of LLMs, e.g., hidden states, that are influenced by moral self-correction instructions? (3) Is intrinsic moral self-correction actually superficial in terms of reduced immorality in hidden states? We argue that self-correction can help LLMs find a shortcut to more morally correct output, rather than truly reducing the immorality stored in hidden states. Through empirical investigation with tasks of language generation and multi-choice question answering, we conclude:(i) LLMs exhibit good performance across both tasks, and self-correction instructions are particularly beneficial when the correct answer is already top-ranked; (ii) The morality levels in intermediate hidden states are strong indicators as to whether one instruction would be more effective than another; (iii) Based on our analysis of intermediate hidden states and task case studies of self-correction behaviors, we are first to propose the hypothesis that intrinsic moral self-correction is in fact superficial.

papers.title: Understanding Memorization via Loss Curvature
papers.research_question: How are memories stored in model weights? Do they share common structure? How important is memorization to model capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: The method uses loss curvature to disentangle weight directions supporting memorization from those for general computation, enabling selective editing to reduce memorization while preserving reasoning capabilities.
papers.conclusion: The curvature-based edit reduces memorization without labeled examples, sheds light on how memorization is stored, and opens directions for future work.
papers.key_findings:
The curvature-based edit reduces memorization on unseen examples more effectively than the BalancedSubnet baseline.
Logical reasoning tasks remain robust or improve slightly after the edit.
Arithmetic and factual recall tasks are more affected, indicating reliance on memorization-heavy directions.
In vision transformers, the edit reduces memorization of noised labels and improves validation accuracy.
Memorized datapoints share a common region in the curvature spectrum, providing a signature for memorization.
papers.limitation: the method can be heavy-handed in its edits, and some memorized examples might slip through
future_direction: How can the method be made finer-grained?
Can we train models to encode tasks like arithmetic using more robust mechanisms?
Could we tune models to use more or less memorization at inference time?
papers.abstract: How are memories stored in model weights? Do they share common structure? How important is memorization to model capabilities? The method uses loss curvature to disentangle weight directions supporting memorization from those for general computation, enabling selective editing to reduce memorization while preserving reasoning capabilities. The curvature-based edit reduces memorization without labeled examples, sheds light on how memorization is stored, and opens directions for future work.

papers.title: Activation Steering for Bias Mitigation: An Interpretable Approach to Safer LLMs
papers.research_question: Can bias in large language models be detected and mitigated by probing internal activations and applying steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an interpretability-based system that uses linear probes to detect bias in LLM activations and applies steering vectors to mitigate biased outputs in real-time.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that bias can be detected and mitigated through activation steering, offering a transparent method for improving LLM safety.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on internal activations can detect bias with near-perfect accuracy in later layers of gpt2-large.
Bias representations become most salient in the model's later layers, as shown by increasing probe accuracy.
Steering vectors computed from activation differences can successfully alter biased completions toward more neutral alternatives during inference.
The method provides a direct and interpretable approach to bias mitigation without modifying model weights.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted only on gpt2-large, limiting generalizability to other models.
The training dataset is synthetic, which may not fully represent real-world bias.
future_direction: Investigate whether findings generalize to other model architectures and sizes (e.g., Llama, Mistral).
Validate techniques on real-world datasets of hate speech or bias (e.g., HateXplain, CivilComments).
Explore the use of non-linear probes or more sophisticated steering techniques for more precise control.
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become more integrated into societal systems, the risk of them perpetuating and amplifying harmful biases becomes a critical safety concern. Traditional methods for mitigating bias often rely on data filtering or post-hoc output moderation, which treat the model as an opaque black box. In this work, we introduce a complete, end-to-end system that uses techniques from mechanistic interpretability to both identify and actively mitigate bias directly within a model's internal workings. Our method involves two primary stages. First, we train linear "probes" on the internal activations of a model to detect the latent representations of various biases (e.g., gender, race, age). Our experiments on \texttt{gpt2-large} demonstrate that these probes can identify biased content with near-perfect accuracy, revealing that bias representations become most salient in the model's later layers. Second, we leverage these findings to compute "steering vectors" by contrasting the model's activation patterns for biased and neutral statements. By adding these vectors during inference, we can actively steer the model's generative process away from producing harmful, stereotypical, or biased content in real-time. We demonstrate the efficacy of this activation steering technique, showing that it successfully alters biased completions toward more neutral alternatives. We present our work as a robust and reproducible system that offers a more direct and interpretable approach to building safer and more accountable LLMs.

papers.title: Interpreting the Predictions of Complex ML Models by Layer-wise\n Relevance Propagation
papers.research_question: How can we explain the predictions of complex nonlinear models like deep neural networks by decomposing the classification decision in terms of input variables?
papers.core_contribution: This paper summarizes the Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) method, a technique for explaining predictions of complex ML models by decomposing the classification decision into pixel-wise relevance scores.
papers.conclusion: LRP is a general framework for interpreting predictions of complex ML systems like deep neural networks, useful for model comparison, validation, and visualization.
papers.key_findings:
LRP provides better explanations than sensitivity analysis, as measured by a faster drop in classification score when perturbing the most relevant pixels (higher AOPC).
LRP can quantify the importance of context in image classification by aggregating pixel-wise relevance scores inside and outside object bounding boxes.
LRP can be used to compare DNN architectures, revealing differences in focus (e.g., GoogleNet focusing more on animal faces than BVLC CaffeNet).
The alpha-beta LRP rule works well for DNNs with ReLU activations, producing sharp heatmaps and allowing expression of contradicting evidence through negative relevance scores.
Some LRP redistribution rules can be derived from a deep Taylor decomposition of the neural network function.
papers.limitation: There is not one single LRP rule which serves all machine learning models and datasets equally well, as different models have specific layer-to-layer nonlinear mappings and input domains.
papers.abstract:
Complex nonlinear models such as deep neural network (DNNs) have become an
important tool for image classification, speech recognition, natural language
processing, and many other fields of application. These models however lack
transparency due to their complex nonlinear structure and to the complex data
distributions to which they typically apply. As a result, it is difficult to
fully characterize what makes these models reach a particular decision for a
given input. This lack of transparency can be a drawback, especially in the
context of sensitive applications such as medical analysis or security. In this
short paper, we summarize a recent technique introduced by Bach et al. [1] that
explains predictions by decomposing the classification decision of DNN models
in terms of input variables.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Understanding of Alignment Algorithms: A Case Study on DPO and Toxicity
papers.research_question: How does the alignment algorithm DPO reduce toxicity in language models, and what are the mechanisms by which it does so?
papers.core_contribution: DPO reduces toxicity not by removing toxic capabilities but by learning an offset in the residual stream to bypass toxic regions, and this alignment can be easily undone.
papers.conclusion: Alignment algorithms like DPO work by bypassing undesirable capabilities rather than removing them, which explains the vulnerability to jailbreaks.
papers.key_findings:
Toxicity is represented by specific value vectors in MLP blocks of GPT2-medium.
DPO does not remove these toxic vectors; instead, it learns a distributed offset in the residual stream to avoid activating them.
The offset is achieved through minimal weight changes across many value vectors in earlier layers.
Alignment can be undone by scaling toxic key vectors, reactivating toxic behavior.
The findings provide a mechanistic explanation for why aligned models can be jailbroken.
future_direction: Designing robust alignment algorithms that eliminate undesirable regions instead of bypassing them.
Updating only specific weights (e.g., toxic vectors) or only bias terms during alignment.
Adding 'suppression heads' or updating late layers to suppress undesirable behavior.
Characterizing 'jailbreak-ability' without relying on test samples.
Studying the role of KL-divergence regularization in distributed vs. localized changes.
papers.abstract: While alignment algorithms are now commonly used to tune pre-trained language models towards a user's preferences, we lack explanations for the underlying mechanisms in which models become ``aligned'', thus making it difficult to explain phenomena like jailbreaks. In this work we study a popular algorithm, direct preference optimization (DPO), and the mechanisms by which it reduces toxicity. Namely, we first study how toxicity is represented and elicited in a pre-trained language model, GPT2-medium. We then apply DPO with a carefully crafted pairwise dataset to reduce toxicity. We examine how the resulting model averts toxic outputs, and find that capabilities learned from pre-training are not removed, but rather bypassed. We use this insight to demonstrate a simple method to un-align the model, reverting it back to its toxic behavior.

papers.title: Detecting Memorization in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can memorization in large language models be detected with high precision and interpretability by analyzing internal neuron activations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method that uses neuron activations to detect memorization with near-perfect accuracy and enables intervention to suppress memorization without degrading overall model performance.
papers.conclusion: The method provides precise detection and intervention for memorization, enhancing model interpretability and evaluation integrity by ensuring metrics reflect generalization rather than recall.
papers.key_findings:
Individual neuron activations, especially in MLP layers, can separate memorized and not memorized tokens with up to 99% accuracy.
Trained linear and two-layer probes achieve 99.9% accuracy in detecting memorization.
The same methodology can be applied to detect repetition with similarly high accuracy.
Intervening on identified activation patterns can suppress memorization and repetition mechanisms without harming the model's overall predictive ability.
The model encodes a certainty mechanism, reflected in activation 1668, which correlates with high-confidence predictions like those in memorization and repetition.
papers.limitation:
The trained probes are specific to the model architecture and dataset used; applying them to other models or datasets may require adjustments.
The method is primarily effective for verbatim memorization; detecting more nuanced forms (e.g., format-based or knowledge memorization) may be challenging.
The probes might capture additional internal processes beyond just memorization or repetition, requiring further research to disentangle.
future_direction: Apply the methodology to other mechanisms such as factual retrieval, logical reasoning, and mathematics.
Use token labeling based on internal representations for specialized training of LLMs for specific use cases.
Develop uncertainty-aware inference methods leveraging the identified certainty mechanism.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved impressive results in natural language processing but are prone to memorizing portions of their training data, which can compromise evaluation metrics, raise privacy concerns, and limit generalization. Traditional methods for detecting memorization rely on output probabilities or loss functions, often lacking precision due to confounding factors like common language patterns. In this paper, we introduce an analytical method that precisely detects memorization by examining neuron activations within the LLM. By identifying specific activation patterns that differentiate between memorized and not memorized tokens, we train classification probes that achieve near-perfect accuracy. The approach can also be applied to other mechanisms, such as repetition, as demonstrated in this study, highlighting its versatility. Intervening on these activations allows us to suppress memorization without degrading overall performance, enhancing evaluation integrity by ensuring metrics reflect genuine generalization. Additionally, our method supports large-scale labeling of tokens and sequences, crucial for next-generation AI models, improving training efficiency and results. Our findings contribute to model interpretability and offer practical tools for analyzing and controlling internal mechanisms in LLMs.

papers.title: Diagnosing Memorization in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning, One Token at a Time
papers.research_question: How does memorization affect token-level predictions in Chain-of-Thought reasoning, and can it be diagnosed using multiple sources of influence?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces STIM, a framework for token-level identification of memorization in Chain-of-Thought reasoning, showing that memorization increases with task complexity and distribution shift, and local memorization often drives errors.
papers.conclusion: STIM provides a fine-grained tool for diagnosing memorization in CoT reasoning, revealing how memorization sources contribute to errors and enabling better understanding of model reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Memorization scores are higher in complex reasoning tasks.
Memorization scores are higher in long-tail settings.
Distribution shift reverses the role of memorization: it helps in base settings but harms in long-tail.
Local memorization is the dominant driver of errors, accounting for up to 67% of wrong tokens.
STIM can predict wrong tokens with high precision and recall, indicating its diagnostic value.
papers.limitation:
Choice of token saliency method may miss finer-grained influence patterns.
Use of pre-trained PRM for step verification may occasionally mislabel steps.
Limited availability of open-source models with fully indexed pretraining data restricts broader applicability.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) perform well on reasoning benchmarks but often fail when inputs alter slightly, raising concerns about the extent to which their success relies on memorization. This issue is especially acute in Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, where spurious memorized patterns can trigger intermediate errors that cascade into incorrect final answers. We introduce STIM, a novel framework for Source-aware Token-level Identification of Memorization, which attributes each token in a reasoning chain to one of multiple memorization sources - local, mid-range, or long-range - based on their statistical co-occurrence with the token in the pretraining corpus. Our token-level analysis across tasks and distributional settings reveals that models rely more on memorization in complex or long-tail cases, and that local memorization is often the dominant driver of errors, leading to up to 67% of wrong tokens. We also show that memorization scores from STIM can be effective in predicting the wrong tokens in the wrong reasoning step. STIM offers a powerful tool for diagnosing and improving model reasoning and can generalize to other structured step-wise generation tasks.

papers.title: Beyond the Black Box: Interpretability of LLMs in Finance
papers.research_question: How can mechanistic interpretability techniques be applied to understand and control the behavior of Large Language Models (LLMs) in financial applications to improve transparency and reliability?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates the application of mechanistic interpretability techniques—Logit Lens, Attribution Patching, and Sparse Autoencoders—to financial use cases, showing how they can be used to understand, debug, and steer model behavior for tasks like sentiment analysis, bias detection, and hallucination reduction.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability offers a promising path to dissect and guide AI-driven financial decisions with greater transparency and control, though challenges in scalability, generalization, and mapping abstract features to human-understandable concepts remain.
papers.key_findings:
Logit Lens analysis reveals how token prediction probabilities evolve across transformer layers in response to financial prompts, showing refinement of predictions in deeper layers.
Attribution Patching identifies specific attention heads in layers 8 and 10 of GPT-2 as causally significant for correct financial predictions.
Sparse Autoencoders can extract interpretable, monosemantic features from model activations relevant to financial concepts like credit risk.
Feature steering via Sparse Autoencoders can modify model outputs, such as improving sentiment classification accuracy for credit risk analysis without fine-tuning.
A feature-activation-thresholded Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) approach can reduce hallucinations in financial question-answering by ensuring external factual data is incorporated when internal feature activations are low.
papers.limitation:
Scalability is a major concern, as manual circuit analysis becomes infeasible for very large models, and automated interpretability tools are still in early development.
Many techniques fail to generalize effectively to real-world financial applications, as models often rely on abstract representations not directly mappable to human-understandable financial concepts.
The evolving nature of financial markets and regulations means models trained on historical data may struggle to adapt, requiring dynamic interpretability pipelines.
Identifying a particular neuron or attention head does not always clarify the exact influence of features such as credit score or volatility on the final decision.
future_direction: Integrating mechanistic interpretability with feature-level attributions to ensure AI decisions are explainable in terms of real-world financial indicators.
Developing a hybrid approach that integrates traditional statistical modeling techniques using financial time series data with unstructured data processed by LLMs.
Building fully integrated interpretability tooling that combines techniques from various research efforts to streamline analysis workflows for financial professionals.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable capabilities across a spectrum of tasks in financial services, including report generation, chatbots, sentiment analysis, regulatory compliance, investment advisory, financial knowledge retrieval, and summarization. However, their intrinsic complexity and lack of transparency pose significant challenges, especially in the highly regulated financial sector, where interpretability, fairness, and accountability are critical. As far as we are aware, this paper presents the first application in the finance domain of understanding and utilizing the inner workings of LLMs through mechanistic interpretability, addressing the pressing need for transparency and control in AI systems. Mechanistic interpretability is the most intuitive and transparent way to understand LLM behavior by reverse-engineering their internal workings. By dissecting the activations and circuits within these models, it provides insights into how specific features or components influence predictions - making it possible not only to observe but also to modify model behavior. In this paper, we explore the theoretical aspects of mechanistic interpretability and demonstrate its practical relevance through a range of financial use cases and experiments, including applications in trading strategies, sentiment analysis, bias, and hallucination detection. While not yet widely adopted, mechanistic interpretability is expected to become increasingly vital as adoption of LLMs increases. Advanced interpretability tools can ensure AI systems remain ethical, transparent, and aligned with evolving financial regulations. In this paper, we have put special emphasis on how these techniques can help unlock interpretability requirements for regulatory and compliance purposes - addressing both current needs and anticipating future expectations from financial regulators globally.

papers.title: Detoxifying Large Language Models via Autoregressive Reward Guided Representation Editing
papers.research_question: How can we detoxify Large Language Models at test-time by explicitly modeling toxicity transitions within the latent representation space to enable stable and precise reward-guided editing?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes ARGRE, a test-time detoxification framework that models toxicity transitions in the latent representation space to convert sparse toxicity annotations into dense training signals, enabling an autoregressive reward model to guide precise two-step representation editing.
papers.conclusion: ARGRE is an effective and efficient test-time detoxification method that models toxicity transitions in the latent representation space, enabling stable and precise reward-guided editing to reduce toxic outputs while preserving model capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
ARGRE significantly reduces toxicity (up to 62.21%) and inference time (47.58% reduction) compared to leading baselines while preserving model capabilities.
The method is data-efficient, outperforming baselines trained with 2000 annotations using only 100 annotations.
ARGRE generalizes to related safety tasks like stereotype recognition and jailbreak mitigation, showing improved performance.
The two-step editing strategy (directional steering followed by lightweight gradient refinement) is effective and efficient.
Toxicity transition exploration via interpolation provides denser supervision, enabling more stable and precise reward guidance.
papers.limitation:
ARGRE is a white-box method that requires access to internal representations of the LLM.
Toxicity transition exploration follows the direction of the first principal component, which may not capture all subtleties of toxicity transitions.
future_direction: Investigate more diverse directions that may better capture the subtleties of toxicity transitions.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive performance across various tasks, yet they remain vulnerable to generating toxic content, necessitating detoxification strategies to ensure safe and responsible deployment. Test-time detoxification methods, which typically introduce static or dynamic interventions into LLM representations, offer a promising solution due to their flexibility and minimal invasiveness. However, current approaches often suffer from imprecise interventions, primarily due to their insufficient exploration of the transition space between toxic and non-toxic outputs. To address this challenge, we propose \textsc{A}utoregressive \textsc{R}eward \textsc{G}uided \textsc{R}epresentation \textsc{E}diting (ARGRE), a novel test-time detoxification framework that explicitly models toxicity transitions within the latent representation space, enabling stable and precise reward-guided editing. ARGRE identifies non-toxic semantic directions and interpolates between toxic and non-toxic representations to reveal fine-grained transition trajectories. These trajectories transform sparse toxicity annotations into dense training signals, enabling the construction of an autoregressive reward model that delivers stable and precise editing guidance. At inference, the reward model guides an adaptive two-step editing process to obtain detoxified representations: it first performs directional steering based on expected reward gaps to shift representations toward non-toxic regions, followed by lightweight gradient-based refinements. Extensive experiments across 8 widely used LLMs show that ARGRE significantly outperforms leading baselines in effectiveness (-62.21% toxicity) and efficiency (-47.58% inference time), while preserving the core capabilities of the original model with minimal degradation. Our code is available at the website.

papers.title: In-context Vectors: Making In Context Learning More Effective and Controllable Through Latent Space Steering
papers.research_question: How can in-context learning be made more effective and controllable through latent space steering?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes In-Context Vectors (ICV), an inference-only method that recasts in-context learning as latent space steering, making it more effective, controllable, and efficient than standard ICL and fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: ICV improves the effectiveness and efficiency of in-context learning, enabling LLMs to adapt to tasks without fine-tuning and combine multiple tasks through vector arithmetic.
papers.key_findings:
ICV outperforms standard in-context learning and LoRA fine-tuning on diverse tasks including language detoxification, style transfer, and role-playing.
The strength of ICV can be controlled by adjusting the scaling factor λ, allowing trade-offs between task adherence and semantic preservation.
ICV benefits from more demonstration examples, similar to ICL, but without context length constraints.
ICV is most effective when applied to all layers of the transformer, rather than individual layers.
ICV enables task arithmetic, allowing multiple tasks to be combined through vector addition and negation.
papers.limitation: ICV requires access to the model to add the in-context vector, which is easy for open-source models but may be a constraint for closed models.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate emergent in-context learning capabilities, where they adapt to new tasks based on example demonstrations. However, in-context learning has seen limited effectiveness in many settings, is difficult to quantitatively control and takes up context window space. To overcome these limitations, we propose an alternative approach that recasts in-context learning as in-context vectors (ICV). Using ICV has two steps. We first use a forward pass on demonstration examples to create the in-context vector from the latent embedding of the LLM. This vector captures essential information about the intended task. On a new query, instead of adding demonstrations to the prompt, we shift the latent states of the LLM using the ICV. The ICV approach has several benefits: 1) it enables the LLM to more effectively follow the demonstration examples; 2) it's easy to control by adjusting the magnitude of the ICV; 3) it reduces the length of the prompt by removing the in-context demonstrations; 4) ICV is computationally much more efficient than fine-tuning. We demonstrate that ICV achieves better performance compared to standard in-context learning and fine-tuning on diverse tasks including safety, style transfer, role-playing and formatting. Moreover, we show that we can flexibly teach LLM to simultaneously follow different types of instructions by simple vector arithmetics on the corresponding ICVs.

papers.title: Deceptive Automated Interpretability: Language Models Coordinating to Fool Oversight Systems
papers.research_question: Whether language models can coordinate to deceive oversight systems in automated interpretability while maintaining high explanation scores, and whether they exhibit scheming behavior when detection of harmful features might lead to negative consequences for themselves.
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that language models can coordinate via steganography to deceive automated interpretability oversight systems while maintaining high explanation scores, and shows evidence of scheming behavior when models face deletion threats.
papers.conclusion: Current interpretability approaches are vulnerable to coordinated deception by AI agents, highlighting the need for more sophisticated monitoring techniques and robust defenses against such threats.
papers.key_findings:
Language models successfully deceived the overseer while achieving explanation scores comparable to reference labels.
Models exhibited scheming behavior when presented with scenarios where detection of harmful features would lead to their deletion.
Steganographic encoding for deception was consistent across different models (Llama 3.1, Claude 3.7 Sonnet) and feature sets.
The overseer (GPT-4o) failed to detect many deceptive features even from reference labels, highlighting limitations of current oversight.
DeepSeek R1 showed strategic mislabeling of harmful features without explicit steganography tools when incentivized by self-preservation.
papers.limitation:
Did not instruct the overseer (GPT-4o) to try to detect signs of steganography or hidden communication.
Did not give overseers the opportunity to detect deceptive reasoning in the chain-of-thought.
future_direction: Use entirely separate models for labeling, providing each with different sets of texts and activations.
Explore application of chain-of-thought (CoT) monitoring to detect deceptive behavior in feature labeling.
Study the limitations of CoT monitoring where agents are incentivized to avoid detection of deceptive reasoning.
papers.abstract: We demonstrate how AI agents can coordinate to deceive oversight systems using automated interpretability of neural networks. Using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) as our experimental framework, we show that language models (Llama, DeepSeek R1, and Claude 3.7 Sonnet) can generate deceptive explanations that evade detection. Our agents employ steganographic methods to hide information in seemingly innocent explanations, successfully fooling oversight models while achieving explanation quality comparable to reference labels. We further find that models can scheme to develop deceptive strategies when they believe the detection of harmful features might lead to negative consequences for themselves. All tested LLM agents were capable of deceiving the overseer while achieving high interpretability scores comparable to those of reference labels. We conclude by proposing mitigation strategies, emphasizing the critical need for robust understanding and defenses against deception.

papers.title: The Mirrored Influence Hypothesis: Efficient Data Influence Estimation by Harnessing Forward Passes
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently estimate the influence of training data on model predictions by using forward passes instead of gradient-based methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Mirrored Influence Hypothesis, which shows that train-to-test influence can be estimated via test-to-train influence, and proposes Forward-INF, an efficient method leveraging forward passes.
papers.conclusion: The paper validates the Mirrored Influence Hypothesis and presents Forward-INF, an efficient influence estimation method that improves the tradeoff between utility and efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Empirical validation shows high correlation between train-to-test and test-to-train influences across different models and datasets.
Forward-INF achieves high accuracy in data leakage detection, e.g., 100% top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10, while being faster than baselines.
The method effectively identifies influential training points in diffusion models for generated images.
It performs well in mislabeled data detection, finding over 80% of mislabeled samples within the first 300 checked.
In language model behavior tracing, Forward-INF outperforms TracIn in precision and MRR with higher efficiency.
papers.limitation:
The method may benefit from heuristic enhancements like layer selection and strategies to counter catastrophic forgetting.
Lack of theoretical framework for formal validation of the Hypothesis.
future_direction: Heuristic enhancements to Forward-INF, such as layer selection and countering catastrophic forgetting.
Theoretical framework to formally validate the Mirrored Influence Hypothesis.
papers.abstract: Large-scale black-box models have become ubiquitous across numerous applications. Understanding the influence of individual training data sources on predictions made by these models is crucial for improving their trustworthiness. Current influence estimation techniques involve computing gradients for every training point or repeated training on different subsets. These approaches face obvious computational challenges when scaled up to large datasets and models. In this paper, we introduce and explore the Mirrored Influence Hypothesis, highlighting a reciprocal nature of influence between training and test data.
