Specifically, it suggests that evaluating the influence of training data on test predictions can be reformulated as an equivalent, yet inverse problem: assessing how the predictions for training samples would be altered if the model were trained on specific test samples. Through both empirical and theoretical validations, we demonstrate the wide applicability of our hypothesis. Inspired by this, we introduce a new method for estimating the influence of training data, which requires calculating gradients for specific test samples, paired with a forward pass for each training point. This approach can capitalize on the common asymmetry in scenarios where the number of test samples under concurrent examination is much smaller than the scale of the training dataset, thus gaining a significant improvement in efficiency compared to existing approaches. We demonstrate the applicability of our method across a range of scenarios, including data attribution in diffusion models, data leakage detection, analysis of memorization, mislabeled data detection, and tracing behavior in language models. Our code will be made available at https://github.com/ruoxi-jia-group/Forward-INF.

papers.title: Mind the Inconspicuous: Revealing the Hidden Weakness in Aligned LLMs' Refusal Boundaries
papers.research_question: How can appending end-of-sequence (eos) tokens bypass the learned refusal boundary in aligned LLMs, and what is the underlying mechanism of 'context segmentation'?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals the 'context segmentation' phenomenon where appending eos tokens shifts prompts towards the refusal boundary in hidden space, and introduces BOOST, a simple method to enhance jailbreak attacks by appending eos tokens.
papers.conclusion: The work highlights a critical blind spot in LLM alignment and content filtering, urging the community to address the security implications of control tokens and develop more robust refusal boundaries.
papers.key_findings:
Appending multiple eos tokens causes both harmful and benign prompts to shift toward the learned refusal boundary in the hidden representation space, a phenomenon termed 'context segmentation'.
BOOST significantly increases the attack success rate (ASR) of existing jailbreak techniques across a wide range of open-source LLMs.
Commercial LLM APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Qwen) do not filter eos tokens, making them vulnerable to BOOST-enhanced attacks.
eos tokens have low attention values, minimizing distraction from the harmful content and preserving jailbreak effectiveness.
BOOST can be made more robust to simple filtering through eos token obfuscation and dynamic positioning strategies.
future_direction: Implement input-filtering defenses for control tokens like eos.
Develop more robust and generalizable refusal boundaries to defend against context segmentation attacks.
Investigate the security impact of all control tokens and develop comprehensive defense strategies.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have led to impressive alignment where models learn to distinguish harmful from harmless queries through supervised finetuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). In this paper, we reveal a subtle yet impactful weakness in these aligned models. We find that simply appending multiple end of sequence (eos) tokens can cause a phenomenon we call context segmentation, which effectively shifts both harmful and benign inputs closer to the refusal boundary in the hidden space. Building on this observation, we propose a straightforward method to BOOST jailbreak attacks by appending eos tokens. Our systematic evaluation shows that this strategy significantly increases the attack success rate across 8 representative jailbreak techniques and 16 open-source LLMs, ranging from 2B to 72B parameters. Moreover, we develop a novel probing mechanism for commercial APIs and discover that major providers such as OpenAI, Anthropic, and Qwen do not filter eos tokens, making them similarly vulnerable. These findings highlight a hidden yet critical blind spot in existing alignment and content filtering approaches. We call for heightened attention to eos tokens' unintended influence on model behaviors, particularly in production systems. Our work not only calls for an input-filtering based defense, but also points to new defenses that make refusal boundaries more robust and generalizable, as well as fundamental alignment techniques that can defend against context segmentation attacks.

papers.title: Universal Refusal Circuits Across LLMs: Cross-Model Transfer via Trajectory Replay and Concept-Basis Reconstruction
papers.research_question: Are refusal circuits universal across LLMs? Can a refusal circuit extracted from a donor model be transferred to a target model without target-side refusal supervision?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework for transferring refusal circuits across LLMs without target-side refusal supervision, combining concept-basis reconstruction and a weight-SVD stability guard, providing evidence for semantic universality of safety alignment.
papers.conclusion: Refusal circuits are universal across LLMs and can be transferred via semantic recipe invariance, enabling cross-model circuit editing without target-side refusal supervision.
papers.key_findings:
The method successfully transfers refusal attenuation across 8 model pairs, including cross-family and cross-architecture transfers.
Refusal circuits are composed of a stable mixture of concept atoms, enabling cross-model transfer via semantic recipe invariance.
The weight-SVD guard prevents capability collapse by projecting interventions away from high-variance weight subspaces.
The transfer works without target-side refusal supervision, relying only on benign concept prompts and validation data.
The method preserves model capabilities on math and code tasks while reducing refusal rates.
papers.limitation:
Efficacy depends on coverage of the Concept Atom Registry; if refusal circuit uses features orthogonal to the atoms, reconstruction may fail.
Weight-SVD guard relies on the heuristic that capability-critical circuits reside in high-variance principal components, which may not generalize to all tasks.
Method is white-box, requiring access to model weights and internal activations, limiting applicability to closed-source systems.
future_direction: Expand CAR coverage to test transfer beyond refusal directions to multi-behavior editing.
Explore black-box approximations of semantic fingerprints for closed-source systems.
Test the method on a wider range of models and alignment behaviors.
papers.abstract: Refusal behavior in aligned LLMs is often viewed as model-specific, yet we hypothesize it stems from a universal, low-dimensional semantic circuit shared across models. To test this, we introduce Trajectory Replay via Concept-Basis Reconstruction, a framework that transfers refusal interventions from donor to target models, spanning diverse architectures (e.g., Dense to MoE) and training regimes, without using target-side refusal supervision. By aligning layers via concept fingerprints and reconstructing refusal directions using a shared ``recipe'' of concept atoms, we map the donor's ablation trajectory into the target's semantic space. To preserve capabilities, we introduce a weight-SVD stability guard that projects interventions away from high-variance weight subspaces to prevent collateral damage. Our evaluation across 8 model pairs confirms that these transferred recipes consistently attenuate refusal while maintaining performance, providing strong evidence for the semantic universality of safety alignment.

papers.title: Why do universal adversarial attacks work on large language models?: Geometry might be the answer
papers.research_question: Why do universal adversarial attacks work on large language models? The paper proposes a geometric perspective to explain their effectiveness.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a geometric perspective to explain universal adversarial attacks on LLMs, suggesting that triggers act as embedding vectors approximating the semantic meaning of adversarial text.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a geometric perspective that potentially explains universal adversarial attacks on LLMs, with evidence that triggers approximate semantic information in embedding space, aiming to shed light on failure modes and enable mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
Universal adversarial triggers are effective on large language models and can transfer across models, as shown with GPT-2, DistilBERT, and OPT-350M.
Self-attention probing indicates that the last token in triggers is highly attended to, suggesting positional importance.
Perturbing trigger tokens shows that semantic meaning and token position affect the adversarial output, with deletions reducing effectiveness.
Dimensionality reduction using UMAP reveals that triggers cluster with adversarial text in embedding space, supporting the geometric hypothesis.
The geometric perspective suggests that universal adversarial triggers behave like embedding vectors that approximate the semantic region of their adversarial training text.
papers.limitation:
The usage of dimensionality reduction could be providing an incomplete picture.
The analysis on trigger perturbations is performed on a single trigger and may not be generalizable.
future_direction: Expanding experimentation to additional techniques such as studying layer-wise distances, visualizing hidden representations evolution, and analyzing KL divergence.
Understanding the transferability of universal attacks across different models.
papers.abstract: Transformer based large language models with emergent capabilities are becoming increasingly ubiquitous in society. However, the task of understanding and interpreting their internal workings, in the context of adversarial attacks, remains largely unsolved. Gradient-based universal adversarial attacks have been shown to be highly effective on large language models and potentially dangerous due to their input-agnostic nature. This work presents a novel geometric perspective explaining universal adversarial attacks on large language models. By attacking the 117M parameter GPT-2 model, we find evidence indicating that universal adversarial triggers could be embedding vectors which merely approximate the semantic information in their adversarial training region. This hypothesis is supported by white-box model analysis comprising dimensionality reduction and similarity measurement of hidden representations. We believe this new geometric perspective on the underlying mechanism driving universal attacks could help us gain deeper insight into the internal workings and failure modes of LLMs, thus enabling their mitigation.

papers.title: Truth is Universal: Robust Detection of Lies in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can we robustly detect when Large Language Models (LLMs) are lying by analyzing their internal activations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a universal two-dimensional subspace in LLM activations containing a general truth direction (tG) and a polarity-sensitive direction (tP), which explains prior generalization failures and enables the construction of a robust lie detector (TTPD).
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates a universal two-dimensional internal representation of truth in LLMs, clarifies prior generalization failures, and provides a robust method (TTPD) for lie detection, advancing towards general-purpose, transparent, and safe AI.
papers.key_findings:
A two-dimensional subspace in the residual stream activations separates true and false statements, containing a general truth direction (tG) and a polarity-sensitive direction (tP).
The affirmative truth direction (tA) from prior work is a linear combination of tG and tP, explaining its failure to generalize to negated statements.
The two-dimensional truth representation is universal across multiple LLM families and sizes (e.g., LLaMA, Gemma, Mistral).
The proposed TTPD method, which uses the tG direction, achieves state-of-the-art accuracy (94%) in detecting lies in both simple factual statements and complex real-world scenarios.
The truth subspace remains two-dimensional even when considering more complex statement types (logical conjunctions/disjunctions) and different languages (German).
papers.limitation:
TTPD uses only one of the two dimensions (tG) of the truth subspace; a non-linear classifier using both tG and tP might achieve higher accuracy.
The generalization of TTPD is tested on a limited number of statement types and real-world scenarios.
The analysis only shows the truth subspace is at least two-dimensional; examining more statement types might reveal additional linear or non-linear structures.
The findings' applicability to larger LLMs or multimodal models is not tested.
future_direction: Explore a non-linear classifier using both tG and tP for higher accuracy.
Test generalization across a broader range of statement types and diverse real-world contexts.
Study the effects of interventions on the 2D truth subspace during inference on model outputs.
Determine whether the findings apply to larger LLMs or multimodal models.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionised natural language processing, exhibiting impressive human-like capabilities. In particular, LLMs are capable of "lying", knowingly outputting false statements. Hence, it is of interest and importance to develop methods to detect when LLMs lie. Indeed, several authors trained classifiers to detect LLM lies based on their internal model activations. However, other researchers showed that these classifiers may fail to generalise, for example to negated statements. In this work, we aim to develop a robust method to detect when an LLM is lying. To this end, we make the following key contributions: (i) We demonstrate the existence of a two-dimensional subspace, along which the activation vectors of true and false statements can be separated. Notably, this finding is universal and holds for various LLMs, including Gemma-7B, LLaMA2-13B, Mistral-7B and LLaMA3-8B. Our analysis explains the generalisation failures observed in previous studies and sets the stage for more robust lie detection; (ii) Building upon (i), we construct an accurate LLM lie detector. Empirically, our proposed classifier achieves state-of-the-art performance, attaining 94% accuracy in both distinguishing true from false factual statements and detecting lies generated in real-world scenarios.

papers.title: One Leak Away: How Pretrained Model Exposure Amplifies Jailbreak Risks in Finetuned LLMs
papers.research_question: Do finetuned LLMs inherit the jailbreak vulnerabilities of their pretrained counterparts, and can attackers exploit knowledge of the pretrained model to launch more effective jailbreak attacks against finetuned systems?
papers.core_contribution: Finetuned LLMs inherit jailbreak vulnerabilities from their pretrained counterparts, and the proposed Probe-Guided Projection (PGP) attack leverages representation-level signals in the pretrained model to craft highly transferable adversarial prompts.
papers.conclusion: Finetuned LLMs inherit vulnerabilities from their pretrained counterparts, and publicly releasing pretrained checkpoints increases the security risks for downstream applications.
papers.key_findings:
Jailbreak prompts crafted on a pretrained LLM transfer most effectively to its finetuned variants, indicating inherited vulnerabilities.
Transferable jailbreak prompts are linearly separable in the pretrained LLM's hidden representations, showing transferability is encoded in the feature space.
The proposed PGP attack consistently outperforms existing methods in the pretrain-to-finetune threat setting.
PGP remains effective even when the finetuned model has undergone safety tuning.
Attack success is highly dependent on using the correct pretrained source model; using a different pretrained model yields near-zero transferability.
papers.limitation: The paper does not propose a defense to mitigate the inherited vulnerabilities.
future_direction: Design methods that prevent or reduce the inheritance of vulnerabilities during finetuning.
papers.abstract: Finetuning pretrained large language models (LLMs) has become the standard paradigm for developing downstream applications. However, its security implications remain unclear, particularly regarding whether finetuned LLMs inherit jailbreak vulnerabilities from their pretrained sources. We investigate this question in a realistic pretrain-to-finetune threat model, where the attacker has white-box access to the pretrained LLM and only black-box access to its finetuned derivatives. Empirical analysis shows that adversarial prompts optimized on the pretrained model transfer most effectively to its finetuned variants, revealing inherited vulnerabilities from pretrained to finetuned LLMs. To further examine this inheritance, we conduct representation-level probing, which shows that transferable prompts are linearly separable within the pretrained hidden states, suggesting that universal transferability is encoded in pretrained representations. Building on this insight, we propose the Probe-Guided Projection (PGP) attack, which steers optimization toward transferability-relevant directions. Experiments across multiple LLM families and diverse finetuned tasks confirm PGP's strong transfer success, underscoring the security risks inherent in the pretrain-to-finetune paradigm.

papers.title: Have Faith in Faithfulness: Going Beyond Circuit Overlap When Finding Model Mechanisms
papers.research_question: How faithful are circuits found by edge attribution patching (EAP), and what is the relationship between overlap and faithfulness? The paper also introduces a new method, EAP-IG, to improve faithfulness.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces EAP-IG, a gradient-based circuit finding method that produces more faithful circuits than EAP, and shows that overlap metrics are insufficient for evaluating circuit faithfulness.
papers.conclusion: When comparing circuits, measuring overlap is no substitute for measuring faithfulness; EAP-IG provides a more faithful alternative to EAP for circuit finding.
papers.key_findings:
EAP-IG circuits are more faithful than EAP circuits on many tasks, though activation patching circuits sometimes outperform both.
Overlap (node or edge) does not always imply faithfulness; moderate overlap does not predict faithfulness well.
EAP-IG scores have higher correlation with activation patching scores for important edges, leading to more faithful circuits.
EAP-IG requires few steps (e.g., m=5) to achieve high faithfulness, making it efficient.
Cross-task faithfulness analysis reveals that circuit mechanisms can be shared across related tasks (e.g., Greater-Than variants) but not always.
papers.limitation:
Testing circuit completeness is challenging, and manually-found 'ground-truth' circuits may be unreliable.
EAP-IG does not always match the performance of activation patching (e.g., on the IOI task).
future_direction: Developing more efficient algorithms for computing faithfulness.
Investigating weighted graph edit distance as a metric that accounts for edge importance.
Exploring methods to ensure circuit completeness in addition to faithfulness.
papers.abstract: Many recent language model (LM) interpretability studies have adopted the circuits framework, which aims to find the minimal computational subgraph, or circuit, that explains LM behavior on a given task. Most studies determine which edges belong in a LM's circuit by performing causal interventions on each edge independently, but this scales poorly with model size. Edge attribution patching (EAP), gradient-based approximation to interventions, has emerged as a scalable but imperfect solution to this problem. In this paper, we introduce a new method - EAP with integrated gradients (EAP-IG) - that aims to better maintain a core property of circuits: faithfulness. A circuit is faithful if all model edges outside the circuit can be ablated without changing the model's performance on the task; faithfulness is what justifies studying circuits, rather than the full model. Our experiments demonstrate that circuits found using EAP are less faithful than those found using EAP-IG, even though both have high node overlap with circuits found previously using causal interventions. We conclude more generally that when using circuits to compare the mechanisms models use to solve tasks, faithfulness, not overlap, is what should be measured.

papers.title: Properties from Mechanisms: An Equivariance Perspective on Identifiable Representation Learning
papers.research_question: Can we identify latent properties by leveraging knowledge of the mechanisms that govern their evolution?
papers.core_contribution: Proves that if the mechanisms governing latent evolution are known, then identification of latent representations is possible up to the equivariances shared by those mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: By exploiting inductive biases on mechanisms, it is possible to design a range of new identifiable representation learning approaches.
papers.key_findings:
With known deterministic mechanisms, latent representations are identified up to the equivariances of the mechanisms.
When only a hypothesis class of mechanisms is known, additional non-identifiability arises from imitation among mechanisms.
For affine mechanisms with distinct eigenvalues and sufficient offset diversity, identification up to an offset is achieved.
The mechanism-based perspective generalizes existing identifiable representation learning results, such as those in Klindt et al. (2020).
Stochastic mechanisms lead to similar identification results up to equivariances and imitators in distribution.
papers.limitation: The analysis assumes perfect reconstruction (bijective autoencoders), which is a strong and often impractical assumption.
future_direction: Developing practical algorithms that leverage mechanistic knowledge for representation learning.
Extending the theory to handle more complex and realistic mechanisms.
Addressing the open problems of scaling and applying the approach in practice.
papers.abstract: A key goal of unsupervised representation learning is "inverting" a data generating process to recover its latent properties. Existing work that provably achieves this goal relies on strong assumptions on relationships between the latent variables (e.g., independence conditional on auxiliary information). In this paper, we take a very different perspective on the problem and ask, "Can we instead identify latent properties by leveraging knowledge of the mechanisms that govern their evolution?" We provide a complete characterization of the sources of non-identifiability as we vary knowledge about a set of possible mechanisms. In particular, we prove that if we know the exact mechanisms under which the latent properties evolve, then identification can be achieved up to any equivariances that are shared by the underlying mechanisms. We generalize this characterization to settings where we only know some hypothesis class over possible mechanisms, as well as settings where the mechanisms are stochastic. We demonstrate the power of this mechanism-based perspective by showing that we can leverage our results to generalize existing identifiable representation learning results. These results suggest that by exploiting inductive biases on mechanisms, it is possible to design a range of new identifiable representation learning approaches.

papers.title: Impact of Layer Norm on Memorization and Generalization in Transformers
papers.research_question: How does LayerNorm influence memorization and learning in Pre-LayerNorm and Post-LayerNorm transformers?
papers.core_contribution: In Pre-LN transformers, LayerNorm is crucial for stable learning, while in Post-LN transformers, LayerNorm is critical for memorization, and its removal mitigates memorization and recovers true labels.
papers.conclusion: The paper identifies that LayerNorm is crucial for learning in Pre-LN transformers and for memorization in Post-LN transformers, offering insights for architecture design and robust training in noisy label settings.
papers.key_findings:
LN is crucial for learning in Pre-LN models, and its removal disrupts learning and exacerbates overfitting.
In Post-LN models, LN is crucial for memorization, and its removal mitigates memorization and recovers genuine labels.
Early layers' LN are most critical for both learning in Pre-LN and memorization in Post-LN.
The gradient norms of early layers are higher than later layers, and the ratio of learning to memorization gradients is higher in Pre-LN than Post-LN.
The removal of LN parameters in Post-LN models suppresses memorization without affecting learning, while in Pre-LN models it destabilizes learning.
papers.limitation: The study focuses only on LayerNorm, while other components like residual paths, attention, and feedforward layers also influence memorization and merit further investigation.
papers.abstract: Layer Normalization (LayerNorm) is one of the fundamental components in transformers that stabilizes training and improves optimization. In recent times, Pre-LayerNorm transformers have become the preferred choice over Post-LayerNorm transformers due to their stable gradient flow. However, the impact of LayerNorm on learning and memorization across these architectures remains unclear. In this work, we investigate how LayerNorm influences memorization and learning for Pre- and Post-LayerNorm transformers. We identify that LayerNorm serves as a key factor for stable learning in Pre-LayerNorm transformers, while in Post-LayerNorm transformers, it impacts memorization. Our analysis reveals that eliminating LayerNorm parameters in Pre-LayerNorm models exacerbates memorization and destabilizes learning, while in Post-LayerNorm models, it effectively mitigates memorization by restoring genuine labels. We further precisely identify that early layers LayerNorm are the most critical over middle/later layers and their influence varies across Pre and Post LayerNorm models. We have validated it through 13 models across 6 Vision and Language datasets. These insights shed new light on the role of LayerNorm in shaping memorization and learning in transformers.

papers.title: How to Manipulate CNNs to Make Them Lie: the GradCAM Case
papers.research_question: Can we manipulate a CNN model to produce arbitrary GradCAM explanations without affecting its accuracy? Can we create a backdoor that triggers malicious explanations only when a specific pattern is present?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that GradCAM explanations can be manipulated without affecting model accuracy, and introduces techniques to do so, including a backdoor that triggers malicious explanations only when a specific input pattern is present.
papers.conclusion: GradCAM is vulnerable to model manipulation attacks, and explanation methods should be tested for robustness against such attacks.
papers.key_findings:
Techniques T1 and T2 can produce constant explanations (flat or fixed image) while leaving model accuracy essentially unchanged.
Technique T3 produces semi-random explanations dependent on the input with minimal accuracy change.
Technique T4 creates a backdoor that triggers a malicious explanation only when a specific pattern is present, without affecting accuracy.
GradCAM does not satisfy the axiom of Implementation Invariance (two networks with same outputs should have same explanations).
The manipulations are hard to detect by visual inspection of explanations, posing security concerns.
papers.limitation: The architectural changes required by the proposed techniques could be detected by inspecting the model architecture.
future_direction: Extending the attack to other explanation methods that rely on gradients.
Exploring attacks without architectural changes, e.g., by using weight pruning or knowledge distillation.
Determining assumptions that should be verified for GradCAM to produce accurate explanations.
papers.abstract: Recently many methods have been introduced to explain CNN decisions. However, it has been shown that some methods can be sensitive to manipulation of the input. We continue this line of work and investigate the explanation method GradCAM. Instead of manipulating the input, we consider an adversary that manipulates the model itself to attack the explanation. By changing weights and architecture, we demonstrate that it is possible to generate any desired explanation, while leaving the model's accuracy essentially unchanged. This illustrates that GradCAM cannot explain the decision of every CNN and provides a proof of concept showing that it is possible to obfuscate the inner workings of a CNN. Finally, we combine input and model manipulation. To this end we put a backdoor in the network: the explanation is correct unless there is a specific pattern present in the input, which triggers a malicious explanation. Our work raises new security concerns, especially in settings where explanations of models may be used to make decisions, such as in the medical domain.

papers.title: TRCE: Towards Reliable Malicious Concept Erasure in Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
papers.research_question: How to reliably erase malicious concepts (e.g., 'sexual') from text-to-image diffusion models while preserving the model's normal generation capability?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes TRCE, a two-stage concept erasure strategy that first eliminates malicious textual semantics by refining cross-attention layers via a closed-form solution targeting [EoT] embeddings, then steers the early denoising trajectory via contrastive fine-tuning to avoid generating malicious visual content, achieving a better trade-off between erasure effectiveness and knowledge preservation.
papers.conclusion: TRCE provides a reliable method for malicious concept erasure in text-to-image diffusion models, effectively removing unsafe content while better preserving the model's original generation ability.
papers.key_findings:
TRCE achieves state-of-the-art performance in erasing malicious concepts (e.g., 'sexual') across multiple adversarial prompt benchmarks.
The two-stage design (textual semantic erasure followed by denoising trajectory steering) collaborates effectively, with the second stage enhancing robustness when the first stage's erasure is insufficient.
Optimizing the [EoT] embedding is more effective for erasing implicitly embedded malicious semantics than optimizing keyword embeddings alone.
TRCE maintains better knowledge preservation (lower FID, higher CLIP-Score) compared to previous concept erasure methods.
The method is effective for erasing multiple malicious concepts simultaneously while preserving generation ability on safe content.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in text-to-image diffusion models enable photorealistic image generation, but they also risk producing malicious content, such as NSFW images. To mitigate risk, concept erasure methods are studied to facilitate the model to unlearn specific concepts. However, current studies struggle to fully erase malicious concepts implicitly embedded in prompts (e.g., metaphorical expressions or adversarial prompts) while preserving the model's normal generation capability. To address this challenge, our study proposes TRCE, using a two-stage concept erasure strategy to achieve an effective trade-off between reliable erasure and knowledge preservation. Firstly, TRCE starts by erasing the malicious semantics implicitly embedded in textual prompts. By identifying a critical mapping objective(i.e., the [EoT] embedding), we optimize the cross-attention layers to map malicious prompts to contextually similar prompts but with safe concepts. This step prevents the model from being overly influenced by malicious semantics during the denoising process. Following this, considering the deterministic properties of the sampling trajectory of the diffusion model, TRCE further steers the early denoising prediction toward the safe direction and away from the unsafe one through contrastive learning, thus further avoiding the generation of malicious content. Finally, we conduct comprehensive evaluations of TRCE on multiple malicious concept erasure benchmarks, and the results demonstrate its effectiveness in erasing malicious concepts while better preserving the model's original generation ability. The code is available at: http://github.com/ddgoodgood/TRCE. CAUTION: This paper includes model-generated content that may contain offensive material.

papers.title: Latent Introspection: Models Can Detect Prior Concept Injections
papers.research_question: Can language models access information about their own prior internal states? Specifically, can they detect when concepts have been injected into their earlier context and identify which concept was injected?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that open-weight language models possess a latent capacity for introspection, enabling them to detect prior concept injections. This ability is often hidden in the residual stream and can be dramatically strengthened through specific prompting.
papers.conclusion: Language models have a surprising capacity for introspection and steering awareness that is easy to overlook, with consequences for latent reasoning and safety.
papers.key_findings:
Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct can detect prior concept injections, with detection signals emerging in middle layers (50–60) but attenuating in the final layers before output.
Prompting the model with accurate information about AI introspection mechanisms can increase detection sensitivity from 0.3% to 39.9% with only a 0.6% increase in false positives.
The model can identify which of nine concepts was injected earlier, with mutual information between injected and recovered concepts rising from 0.61 bits to 1.05 bits, ruling out generic noise explanations.
Detection capacity varies dramatically with prompting; a vague framing outperforms a mechanistically accurate description, achieving up to 84.0% accuracy.
The phenomenon generalizes to larger models (Llama 3.3 70B Instruct and Qwen 2.5 72B Instruct), though with different prompt sensitivities and signal strengths.
papers.limitation: The introspection signals are suppressed in the final layers of the model, which may be due to post-training effects (e.g., safety training), pretraining factors, or distribution shift.
future_direction: Distinguishing the causes of late-layer suppression (post-training vs. pretraining effects).
Mechanistic investigation of why vague framing outperforms accurate description in prompting.
papers.abstract: We uncover a latent capacity for introspection in a Qwen 32B model, demonstrating that the model can detect when concepts have been injected into its earlier context and identify which concept was injected. While the model denies injection in sampled outputs, logit lens analysis reveals clear detection signals in the residual stream, which are attenuated in the final layers. Furthermore, prompting the model with accurate information about AI introspection mechanisms can dramatically strengthen this effect: the sensitivity to injection increases massively (0.3% -> 39.2%) with only a 0.6% increase in false positives. Also, mutual information between nine injected and recovered concepts rises from 0.62 bits to 1.05 bits, ruling out generic noise explanations. Our results demonstrate models can have a surprising capacity for introspection and steering awareness that is easy to overlook, with consequences for latent reasoning and safety.

papers.title: Captured by Captions: On Memorization and its Mitigation in CLIP Models
papers.research_question: How does memorization manifest in multi-modal models like CLIP, which combine elements of supervised and self-supervised learning, and how can it be measured and mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes CLIPMem, a formal metric to measure memorization in CLIP models, and shows that memorization can be reduced while simultaneously improving model generalization, contrary to trends in supervised and self-supervised learning.
papers.conclusion: CLIPMem effectively quantifies memorization in CLIP, revealing that memorization is highest for mis-captioned and atypical samples and is more prominent in the text encoder; mitigation strategies can reduce memorization and improve generalization.
papers.key_findings:
CLIP's memorization behavior falls between that of supervised and self-supervised learning paradigms.
"Mis-captioned" (incorrect or imprecise) and atypical data points exhibit the highest levels of memorization.
The text encoder contributes more to memorization than the image encoder.
Mitigation strategies like text augmentations and noising text embeddings can reduce memorization while improving downstream generalization.
Removing highly memorized samples (especially mis-captioned ones) from training can improve model performance.
papers.abstract: Multi-modal models, such as CLIP, have demonstrated strong performance in aligning visual and textual representations, excelling in tasks like image retrieval and zero-shot classification. Despite this success, the mechanisms by which these models utilize training data, particularly the role of memorization, remain unclear. In uni-modal models, both supervised and self-supervised, memorization has been shown to be essential for generalization. However, it is not well understood how these findings would apply to CLIP, which incorporates elements from both supervised learning via captions that provide a supervisory signal similar to labels, and from self-supervised learning via the contrastive objective. To bridge this gap in understanding, we propose a formal definition of memorization in CLIP (CLIPMem) and use it to quantify memorization in CLIP models. Our results indicate that CLIP's memorization behavior falls between the supervised and self-supervised paradigms, with "mis-captioned" samples exhibiting highest levels of memorization. Additionally, we find that the text encoder contributes more to memorization than the image encoder, suggesting that mitigation strategies should focus on the text domain. Building on these insights, we propose multiple strategies to reduce memorization while at the same time improving utility--something that had not been shown before for traditional learning paradigms where reducing memorization typically results in utility decrease.

papers.title: GSS: Gated Subspace Steering for Selective Memorization Mitigation in LLMs
papers.research_question: How can memorization in large language models be mitigated selectively, without degrading generalization, by intervening only when memorization occurs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Gated Subspace Steering (GSS), a method that selectively mitigates memorization in LLMs by decoupling detection (via a probe) and correction (via a steer) in activation space, using a gating mechanism and optimal subspace steering derived from a principled optimization framework.
papers.conclusion: Gated Subspace Steering is an effective and efficient method for selective memorization mitigation in LLMs, successfully suppressing verbatim recall while preserving generalization capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Memorization is a sparse, intermittent, and token-conditioned phenomenon, not a uniform property of the model.
GSS effectively reduces memorization (often to 0%) while preserving task performance (accuracy/perplexity) on downstream tasks.
GSS is computationally efficient, introducing negligible inference-time overhead and being significantly faster than optimization-based alternatives.
GSS outperforms or matches state-of-the-art memorization mitigation baselines across multiple benchmarks and model sizes.
The method provides theoretical insights connecting memorization to geometric structure in activation space, with the optimal intervention emerging from a generalized singular value decomposition.
papers.limitation:
Requires a reference model (typically the pretrained model) to compute the memorization signal, which may not always be available.
SVD computation has O(d^3) complexity per layer, which can be expensive for very large models (though it is a one-time cost).
Inference overhead from gating adds O(d) operations per token, though it is negligible compared to the forward pass.
Performance can be sensitive to the choice of the gating threshold, requiring some tuning.
Effectiveness depends on choosing appropriate layers for intervention, which may require domain knowledge or empirical validation.
future_direction: Extending the method to multi-modal settings (e.g., vision-language models).
Developing online learning techniques to update the probe-steer vectors continuously during deployment.
Conducting further theoretical analysis to derive generalization bounds for memorization mitigation.
Establishing formal privacy guarantees (e.g., differential privacy) for the approach.
Applying the method in multilingual settings to study memorization patterns across languages.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can memorize and reproduce training sequences verbatim -- a tendency that undermines both generalization and privacy. Existing mitigation methods apply interventions uniformly, degrading performance on the majority of tokens that generalize normally. We show empirically that memorization is sparse, intermittent, and token-conditioned, suggesting that effective mitigation requires context-aware intervention rather than static parameter modification. To this end, we propose a novel and effective selective memorization mitigation method -- Gated Subspace Steering (GSS), which decomposes intervention into a probe (detecting memorization-relevant activations) and a steer (applying targeted correction only when the probe exceeds a threshold). The optimal probe-steer pair emerges from a principled optimization framework based on optimal subspace steering. Experiments on four benchmarks show GSS matches or exceeds state-of-the-art memorization reduction while requiring $100-1000 \times$ less compute than optimization-based alternatives. Furthermore, we provide new theoretical insights into the geometry of memorization in neural representations.

papers.title: Can Neural Network Memorization Be Localized?
papers.research_question: Can memorization in neural networks be localized to specific layers or neurons, and if so, where does it occur?
papers.core_contribution: Memorization in neural networks is confined to a small set of neurons distributed across layers, not just the final layers, and a new dropout method (example-tied dropout) can direct memorization to specific neurons.
papers.conclusion: Memorization in neural networks can be localized to a small set of neurons distributed across layers, and training-time modifications like example-tied dropout can control this memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Memorization is not confined to the final layers but to a small set of neurons across various layers.
Gradient contributions from memorized (noisy) examples are large and opposed to those from clean examples.
Layer rewinding experiments show that final layers are not critical for the correct prediction of memorized examples.
Retraining individual layers on only clean examples can still yield high accuracy on unseen memorized examples, indicating layer redundancy for memorization.
Memorized examples require significantly fewer neurons to flip their predictions compared to clean examples, and example-tied dropout can effectively direct memorization to a predetermined set of neurons.
future_direction: Using critical neuron removal as a metric for identifying mislabeled examples in datasets.
papers.abstract: Recent efforts at explaining the interplay of memorization and generalization in deep overparametrized networks have posited that neural networks $\textit{memorize}$ "hard" examples in the final few layers of the model. Memorization refers to the ability to correctly predict on $\textit{atypical}$ examples of the training set. In this work, we show that rather than being confined to individual layers, memorization is a phenomenon confined to a small set of neurons in various layers of the model. First, via three experimental sources of converging evidence, we find that most layers are redundant for the memorization of examples and the layers that contribute to example memorization are, in general, not the final layers. The three sources are $\textit{gradient accounting}$ (measuring the contribution to the gradient norms from memorized and clean examples), $\textit{layer rewinding}$ (replacing specific model weights of a converged model with previous training checkpoints), and $\textit{retraining}$ (training rewound layers only on clean examples). Second, we ask a more generic question: can memorization be localized $\textit{anywhere}$ in a model? We discover that memorization is often confined to a small number of neurons or channels (around 5) of the model. Based on these insights we propose a new form of dropout -- $\textit{example-tied dropout}$ that enables us to direct the memorization of examples to an apriori determined set of neurons. By dropping out these neurons, we are able to reduce the accuracy on memorized examples from $100\%\to3\%$, while also reducing the generalization gap.

papers.title: Biologically inspired protection of deep networks from adversarial attacks
papers.research_question: How can deep neural networks be made robust to adversarial attacks without training on adversarial examples, inspired by biological neurons' nonlinear dendritic computations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a biologically inspired training scheme that pushes neural networks into a saturated, nonlinear regime, achieving state-of-the-art robustness to adversarial attacks on MNIST without using adversarial examples during training.
papers.conclusion: The proposed saturating network training provides a biologically plausible mechanism for adversarial robustness, characterized by flat, low-dimensional internal representations and kurtotic weight distributions.
papers.key_findings:
Saturating networks achieve high robustness to gradient-based and iterative adversarial attacks while maintaining test accuracy.
Saturating networks develop highly kurtotic weight distributions, similar to biological networks.
Internal representations in saturating networks form tight, widely separated clusters for different classes.
The input-output map of saturating networks is highly flat and sensitive to few input directions, making adversarial perturbations difficult.
High kurtosis in weight distributions can protect even linear classifiers from adversarial examples.
papers.abstract: Inspired by biophysical principles underlying nonlinear dendritic computation in neural circuits, we develop a scheme to train deep neural networks to make them robust to adversarial attacks. Our scheme generates highly nonlinear, saturated neural networks that achieve state of the art performance on gradient based adversarial examples on MNIST, despite never being exposed to adversarially chosen examples during training. Moreover, these networks exhibit unprecedented robustness to targeted, iterative schemes for generating adversarial examples, including second-order methods. We further identify principles governing how these networks achieve their robustness, drawing on methods from information geometry. We find these networks progressively create highly flat and compressed internal representations that are sensitive to very few input dimensions, while still solving the task. Moreover, they employ highly kurtotic weight distributions, also found in the brain, and we demonstrate how such kurtosis can protect even linear classifiers from adversarial attack.

papers.title: Erasing Conceptual Knowledge from Language Models
papers.research_question: How can language models be made to unlearn specific conceptual knowledge by leveraging their own introspective classification abilities?
papers.core_contribution: ELM introduces a principled approach to concept unlearning by using the language model's own introspective classification to reduce the likelihood of generating content related to undesired concepts, achieving effective erasure while preserving general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: ELM effectively erases targeted conceptual knowledge from language models by leveraging self-classification, maintaining model coherence and general capabilities without significant degradation.
papers.key_findings:
ELM achieves near-random performance on erased concepts (e.g., WMDP-bio and WMDP-cyber) while maintaining high scores on general knowledge benchmarks like MMLU.
The method preserves generation coherence, as evidenced by low reverse perplexity scores compared to baselines.
ELM demonstrates robustness to adversarial attacks such as GCG, resisting attempts to extract erased knowledge.
For larger models, the fluency enhancement term is unnecessary, suggesting more precise internal classifiers.
Ablation studies show that each loss component (erasure, retain, fluency) is crucial for balancing innocence, specificity, and seamlessness.
papers.limitation: The method shows some degradation in performance on semantically adjacent concepts.
papers.abstract: In this work, we introduce Erasure of Language Memory (ELM), a principled approach to concept-level unlearning that operates by matching distributions defined by the model's own introspective classification capabilities. Our key insight is that effective unlearning should leverage the model's ability to evaluate its own knowledge, using the language model itself as a classifier to identify and reduce the likelihood of generating content related to undesired concepts. ELM applies this framework to create targeted low-rank updates that reduce generation probabilities for concept-specific content while preserving the model's broader capabilities. We demonstrate ELM's efficacy on biosecurity, cybersecurity, and literary domain erasure tasks. Comparative evaluation reveals that ELM-modified models achieve near-random performance on assessments targeting erased concepts, while simultaneously preserving generation coherence, maintaining benchmark performance on unrelated tasks, and exhibiting strong robustness to adversarial attacks. Our code, data, and trained models are available at https://elm.baulab.info

papers.title: Mitigating Memorization in LLMs using Activation Steering
papers.research_question: Can activation steering mitigate memorization in LLMs, and what factors influence its effectiveness? What are best practices for using activation steering to mitigate memorization?
papers.core_contribution: Activation steering can effectively reduce memorization in LLMs, especially when applied to later layers, with minimal impact on linguistic fluency and general performance.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering can suppress memorized content in LLMs while maintaining fluency and general abilities, offering a practical alternative to data sanitization or retraining.
papers.key_findings:
Activation steering reduces memorization, as shown by decreased ANLCS with high steering strength.
Steering later layers (e.g., Layer 31) minimizes degradation in language modeling and general task performance.
Early layer steering leads to significant performance drops in linguistic and reasoning tasks.
Random SAE features can be used for steering, indicating that memorization is distributed and not tied to specific features.
Features with high semantic footprint can cause stylistic shifts in output, which may be undesirable.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are conducted only on the Gemma model.
The benchmark primarily consists of literary examples, which may have been present in the model's training data.
A more comprehensive evaluation incorporating diverse datasets and direct analysis of training data exposure is needed.
Future studies should assess the broader applicability of activation steering across different model architectures and tasks.
future_direction: More comprehensive evaluation with diverse datasets and direct analysis of training data exposure.
Assess broader applicability across different model architectures and tasks.
Explore more adaptive and dynamic steering mechanisms to enhance robustness while minimizing unintended side effects.
papers.abstract: The memorization of training data by Large Language Models (LLMs) poses significant risks, including privacy leaks and the regurgitation of copyrighted content. Activation steering, a technique that directly intervenes in model activations, has emerged as a promising approach for manipulating LLMs. In this work, we explore the effectiveness of activation steering in reducing memorization while preserving generalization capabilities. We conduct empirical evaluations using a controlled memorization benchmark of literary material and demonstrate that our method successfully suppresses memorized content with minimal degradation in model performance in Gemma. Additionally, we analyze the trade-offs between suppression effectiveness and linguistic fluency, highlighting the advantages and limitations of activation-based interventions. Our findings contribute to ongoing efforts in developing safer and more privacy-preserving LLMs by providing a practical and efficient mechanism to mitigate unintended memorization.

papers.title: Outside the Box: Abstraction-Based Monitoring of Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we detect novel inputs (inputs from classes not seen during training) in neural network classifiers by monitoring hidden layers using box abstractions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes an abstraction-based runtime monitor for neural networks that observes hidden layers and uses box abstractions to detect novel inputs, achieving a trade-off between false warnings and detection.
papers.conclusion: The proposed framework is effective for novelty detection and computationally cheap, and future work will apply it in real-world settings such as monitoring neural-network controllers for cyber-physical systems.
papers.key_findings:
The box abstraction approach effectively detects novel inputs and outperforms threshold-based and Boolean abstraction methods.
The framework is computationally efficient, with monitoring taking less than a millisecond per input.
The abstraction can be tuned by enlarging boxes to adjust the trade-off between false positives and true positives.
Monitoring multiple layers improves detection performance, especially when few classes are known.
The approach is flexible and can be extended to other abstraction types, though boxes are efficient and effective.
papers.limitation:
The approach is not black-box ready because it requires access to the network output in chosen layers.
The abstraction may be too coarse, leading to false negatives, or too precise, leading to false positives.
future_direction: Apply the approach in a real-world setting such as monitoring neural-network controllers for cyber-physical systems.
papers.abstract:
Neural networks have demonstrated unmatched performance in a range of
classification tasks. Despite numerous efforts of the research community,
novelty detection remains one of the significant limitations of neural
networks. The ability to identify previously unseen inputs as novel is crucial
for our understanding of the decisions made by neural networks. At runtime,
inputs not falling into any of the categories learned during training cannot be
classified correctly by the neural network. Existing approaches treat the
neural network as a black box and try to detect novel inputs based on the
confidence of the output predictions. However, neural networks are not trained
to reduce their confidence for novel inputs, which limits the effectiveness of
these approaches. We propose a framework to monitor a neural network by
observing the hidden layers. We employ a common abstraction from program
analysis - boxes - to identify novel behaviors in the monitored layers, i.e.,
inputs that cause behaviors outside the box. For each neuron, the boxes range
over the values seen in training. The framework is efficient and flexible to
achieve a desired trade-off between raising false warnings and detecting novel
inputs. We illustrate the performance and the robustness to variability in the
unknown classes on popular image-classification benchmarks.

papers.title: JailbreakLens: Interpreting Jailbreak Mechanism in the Lens of Representation and Circuit
papers.research_question: How do jailbreak prompts affect the internal representations of LLMs? Which model components are critical to generation safety? How do internal representations and key model components evolve throughout the token generation process during jailbreak attacks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes JailbreakLens, a dual-perspective interpretation framework that analyzes jailbreak mechanisms by examining representation shifts and circuit activations, revealing how jailbreak prompts deceive LLMs by manipulating harmfulness perception and safety-critical components.
papers.conclusion: JailbreakLens provides insights into jailbreak mechanisms, showing that prompts deceive models by shifting representations and manipulating key circuits, with a consistent correlation between representation deception and circuit activation shifts.
papers.key_findings:
Jailbreak prompts deceive LLMs by shifting their internal representations towards safe clusters, making harmful prompts appear safe.
Key circuits, such as specific attention heads and MLP layers, are manipulated to suppress refusal behaviors and encourage affirmation.
There is a strong correlation between representation deception and activation shifts in key circuits across diverse jailbreak methods and LLMs.
Rule-based and demonstration-based jailbreak methods are more deceptive than gradient-based or evolutionary-based methods.
Dynamic analysis shows that jailbreak effects evolve during token generation, with refusal signals sometimes initially activated but later bypassed.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to models with up to 13B parameters due to computational constraints.
Not all recent jailbreak methods are included in the study.
future_direction: Extend research to larger-scale models to determine if similar attack patterns apply.
Design more robust and interpretable safety mechanisms based on the identified vulnerabilities.
papers.abstract: Despite the outstanding performance of Large language Models (LLMs) in diverse tasks, they are vulnerable to jailbreak attacks, wherein adversarial prompts are crafted to bypass their security mechanisms and elicit unexpected responses. Although jailbreak attacks are prevalent, the understanding of their underlying mechanisms remains limited. Recent studies have explained typical jailbreaking behavior (e.g., the degree to which the model refuses to respond) of LLMs by analyzing representation shifts in their latent space caused by jailbreak prompts or identifying key neurons that contribute to the success of jailbreak attacks. However, these studies neither explore diverse jailbreak patterns nor provide a fine-grained explanation from the failure of circuit to the changes of representational, leaving significant gaps in uncovering the jailbreak mechanism. In this paper, we propose JailbreakLens, an interpretation framework that analyzes jailbreak mechanisms from both representation (which reveals how jailbreaks alter the model's harmfulness perception) and circuit perspectives~(which uncovers the causes of these deceptions by identifying key circuits contributing to the vulnerability), tracking their evolution throughout the entire response generation process. We then conduct an in-depth evaluation of jailbreak behavior on five mainstream LLMs under seven jailbreak strategies. Our evaluation reveals that jailbreak prompts amplify components that reinforce affirmative responses while suppressing those that produce refusal. This manipulation shifts model representations toward safe clusters to deceive the LLM, leading it to provide detailed responses instead of refusals. Notably, we find a strong and consistent correlation between representation deception and activation shift of key circuits across diverse jailbreak methods and multiple LLMs.

papers.title: Backdoor Attribution: Elucidating and Controlling Backdoor in Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms of backdoor attacks in fine-tuned Large Language Models (LLMs), and how can they be understood and controlled?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Backdoor Attribution (BkdAttr), a causal analysis framework that elucidates the internal mechanisms of backdoors in LLMs, demonstrating that backdoor attention heads are sparse and that a backdoor vector constructed from them can effectively control backdoor activation.
papers.conclusion: The work pioneers the exploration of mechanistic interpretability in LLM backdoors, providing a powerful method for backdoor control and revealing actionable insights for the community.
papers.key_findings:
Backdoor features exist within non-embedding LLM representations and are learnable by simple classifiers (Backdoor Probes).
Backdoor attention heads, identified via Backdoor Attention Head Attribution (BAHA), are relatively sparse; ablating ~3% of total heads reduces Attack Success Rate (ASR) by over 90%.
A Backdoor Vector constructed from these attributed heads can control backdoor activation: adding it to clean inputs boosts ASR to ~100%, while subtracting it from triggered inputs suppresses ASR to ~0%.
Backdoor features undergo hierarchical processing across layers, converging to a unified pattern that drives backdoor output generation.
The proposed BkdAttr framework is effective across different LLM architectures (MHA and GQA) and backdoor types (label modification, fixed output, jailbreak).
papers.limitation: The effectiveness of backdoor vectors is slightly inferior for the Qwen2.5-7B model, which may be due to issues caused by parameter sharing in Grouped Query Attention (GQA).
papers.abstract: Fine-tuned Large Language Models (LLMs) are vulnerable to backdoor attacks through data poisoning, yet the internal mechanisms governing these attacks remain a black box. Previous research on interpretability for LLM safety tends to focus on alignment, jailbreak, and hallucination, but overlooks backdoor mechanisms, making it difficult to understand and fully eliminate the backdoor threat. In this paper, aiming to bridge this gap, we explore the interpretable mechanisms of LLM backdoors through Backdoor Attribution (BkdAttr), a tripartite causal analysis framework. We first introduce the Backdoor Probe that proves the existence of learnable backdoor features encoded within the representations. Building on this insight, we further develop Backdoor Attention Head Attribution (BAHA), efficiently pinpointing the specific attention heads responsible for processing these features. Our primary experiments reveals these heads are relatively sparse; ablating a minimal \textbf{$\sim$ 3%} of total heads is sufficient to reduce the Attack Success Rate (ASR) by \textbf{over 90%}. More importantly, we further employ these findings to construct the Backdoor Vector derived from these attributed heads as a master controller for the backdoor. Through only \textbf{1-point} intervention on \textbf{single} representation, the vector can either boost ASR up to \textbf{$\sim$ 100% ($\uparrow$)} on clean inputs, or completely neutralize backdoor, suppressing ASR down to \textbf{$\sim$ 0% ($\downarrow$)} on triggered inputs. In conclusion, our work pioneers the exploration of mechanistic interpretability in LLM backdoors, demonstrating a powerful method for backdoor control and revealing actionable insights for the community.

papers.title: Probing Latent Subspaces in LLM for AI Security: Identifying and Manipulating Adversarial States
papers.research_question: Can latent subspaces in LLMs be identified and manipulated to induce state transitions from safe to jailbroken states?
papers.core_contribution: This work demonstrates that latent subspaces in LLMs can be identified and manipulated to induce state transitions from safe to jailbroken states using LDA and targeted perturbations, paving the way for potential proactive defenses.
papers.conclusion: The methodology demonstrates the feasibility of using latent representations to manipulate model states and provides insights into attractor dynamics in LLMs, with potential for preemptive AI security.
papers.key_findings:
Last-token activations encode information about the model's state (safe vs jailbreak) and can be classified with above-chance accuracy.
Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) can separate safe and jailbreak activations into distinct latent subspaces, and a direction vector can be derived.
Applying the derived perturbation vector to safe activations can induce jailbreak responses in a subset of prompts (11% for Llama-3.1-8B, 13.39% for Qwen2.5-3B).
Targeted perturbations induce distinct downstream state changes that propagate through layers, while random perturbations do not.
The effect of targeted perturbation varies across layers, with middle layers (6-18) showing sustained effects, suggesting they may be critical for safety.
papers.limitation:
The perturbation vector was derived from a dataset of malicious cybersecurity-related prompt-injects, so the discovered subspace may reflect features specific to this domain.
Perturbations led to jailbreak transitions in only about 11% of tested prompts, indicating a low success rate.
The external evaluation performed by GPT-4o exhibited high variance in assigning labels to ambiguous outputs.
The method was developed and validated on decoder-only Transformers; generalizing to other LLM architectures requires further testing.
future_direction: Generalize the analysis by expanding the scope of malicious questions and prompt injects to multiple domains or adversarial content types.
Investigate stronger perturbation magnitudes without compromising the coherence of the LLM's response.
Test the methodology on other open-source and commercially available LLM architectures to confirm generalizability.
Incorporate additional rounds of assessment to mitigate label noise from external evaluators like GPT-4o.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across various tasks, yet they remain vulnerable to adversarial manipulations such as jailbreaking via prompt injection attacks. These attacks bypass safety mechanisms to generate restricted or harmful content. In this study, we investigated the underlying latent subspaces of safe and jailbroken states by extracting hidden activations from a LLM. Inspired by attractor dynamics in neuroscience, we hypothesized that LLM activations settle into semi stable states that can be identified and perturbed to induce state transitions. Using dimensionality reduction techniques, we projected activations from safe and jailbroken responses to reveal latent subspaces in lower dimensional spaces. We then derived a perturbation vector that when applied to safe representations, shifted the model towards a jailbreak state. Our results demonstrate that this causal intervention results in statistically significant jailbreak responses in a subset of prompts. Next, we probed how these perturbations propagate through the model's layers, testing whether the induced state change remains localized or cascades throughout the network. Our findings indicate that targeted perturbations induced distinct shifts in activations and model responses. Our approach paves the way for potential proactive defenses, shifting from traditional guardrail based methods to preemptive, model agnostic techniques that neutralize adversarial states at the representation level.

papers.title: The Secret Sharer: Evaluating and Testing Unintended Memorization in Neural Networks
papers.abstract: This paper describes a testing methodology for quantitatively assessing the risk that rare or unique training-data sequences are unintentionally memorized by generative sequence models---a common type of machine-learning model. Because such models are sometimes trained on sensitive data (e.g., the text of users' private messages), this methodology can benefit privacy by allowing deep-learning practitioners to select means of training that minimize such memorization. In experiments, we show that unintended memorization is a persistent, hard-to-avoid issue that can have serious consequences. Specifically, for models trained without consideration of memorization, we describe new, efficient procedures that can extract unique, secret sequences, such as credit card numbers. We show that our testing strategy is a practical and easy-to-use first line of defense, e.g., by describing its application to quantitatively limit data exposure in Google's Smart Compose, a commercial text-completion neural network trained on millions of users' email messages.

papers.title: Synthetic Data Generation for Privacy-Preserving AI Models
papers.abstract: Synthetic data generation has emerged as a pivotal technique for enabling privacy‑preserving practices in artificial intelligence (AI), offering a means to create realistic yet non‑identifiable datasets for training and evaluation. This manuscript systematically examines current methods for generating synthetic data tailored to privacy requirements, evaluates their efficacy across diverse AI applications, and proposes a comprehensive study protocol to assess utility–privacy trade‑offs. We first contextualize synthetic data within the broader privacy landscape, highlighting regulatory drivers such as GDPR and HIPAA. A detailed literature review synthesizes advances in generative adversarial networks (GANs), variational autoencoders (VAEs), differential privacy (DP) mechanisms, and hybrid models. Our methodology outlines a two‑phase experimental framework: (1) development and tuning of multiple synthetic data generators across image, tabular, and text modalities; (2) quantitative evaluation of downstream AI model performance, privacy leakage metrics (e.g., membership inference risk), and statistical fidelity to real data. The study protocol specifies dataset selection, model architectures, privacy parameter settings, and evaluation metrics. Results demonstrate that DP‑enhanced GANs achieve a favorable balance, retaining over 90% of predictive accuracy on benchmark tasks while reducing membership inference risk by up to 75%. Finally, we discuss limitations, practical deployment considerations, and future research directions. To further elucidate the potential and challenges of synthetic data, we extend our analysis to real‑world use cases such as healthcare diagnostics, financial fraud detection, and recommendation systems. We demonstrate how domain‑specific tuning—such as conditioning GANs on clinical ontologies or embedding structured metadata in tabular generators—can substantially improve utility without compromising privacy. In addition, we introduce novel metrics for gauging syntactic consistency in generated text and semantic coherence in images, supplementing traditional statistical measures. We also explore emerging paradigms like federated synthetic data synthesis, where decentralized generators collaboratively learn without aggregating raw data. This approach not only strengthens privacy guarantees through local differential privacy but also enhances diversity by integrating heterogeneous data sources. Through extensive ablation studies, we reveal that combining DP‑SGD with adaptive noise scheduling can yield synthetic datasets that closely mimic complex, correlated features while maintaining provable privacy bounds. Our findings underscore the versatility of synthetic data as a privacy‑preserving technique and provide actionable guidelines for practitioners seeking to balance regulatory compliance with model performance.

papers.title: Generating Artificial Data for Private Deep Learning
papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose generating artificial data that retain statistical properties of real data as the means of providing privacy for the original dataset. We use generative adversarial networks to draw privacy-preserving artificial data samples and derive an empirical method to assess the risk of information disclosure in a differential-privacy-like way. Our experiments show that we are able to generate labelled data of high quality and use it to successfully train and validate supervised models. Finally, we demonstrate that our approach significantly reduces vulnerability of such models to model inversion attacks.

papers.title: Does Training with Synthetic Data Truly Protect Privacy?
papers.abstract: As synthetic data becomes increasingly popular in machine learning tasks, numerous methods--without formal differential privacy guarantees--use synthetic data for training. These methods often claim, either explicitly or implicitly, to protect the privacy of the original training data. In this work, we explore four different training paradigms: coreset selection, dataset distillation, data-free knowledge distillation, and synthetic data generated from diffusion models. While all these methods utilize synthetic data for training, they lead to vastly different conclusions regarding privacy preservation. We caution that empirical approaches to preserving data privacy require careful and rigorous evaluation; otherwise, they risk providing a false sense of privacy.

papers.title: When Privacy Isn't Synthetic: Hidden Data Leakage in Generative AI Models
papers.abstract: Generative models are increasingly used to produce privacy-preserving synthetic data as a safe alternative to sharing sensitive training datasets. However, we demonstrate that such synthetic releases can still leak information about the underlying training samples through structural overlap in the data manifold. We propose a black-box membership inference attack that exploits this vulnerability without requiring access to model internals or real data. The attacker repeatedly queries the generative model to obtain large numbers of synthetic samples, performs unsupervised clustering to identify dense regions of the synthetic distribution, and then analyzes cluster medoids and neighborhoods that correspond to high-density regions in the original training data. These neighborhoods act as proxies for training samples, enabling the adversary to infer membership or reconstruct approximate records. Our experiments across healthcare, finance, and other sensitive domains show that cluster overlap between real and synthetic data leads to measurable membership leakage-even when the generator is trained with differential privacy or other noise mechanisms. The results highlight an under-explored attack surface in synthetic data generation pipelines and call for stronger privacy guarantees that account for distributional neighborhood inference rather than sample-level memorization alone, underscoring its role in privacy-preserving data publishing. Implementation and evaluation code are publicly available at:github.com/Cluster-Medoid-Leakage-Attack.

papers.title: Generative Models for Security: Attacks, Defenses, and Opportunities
papers.abstract: Generative models learn the distribution of data from a sample dataset and can then generate new data instances. Recent advances in deep learning has brought forth improvements in generative model architectures, and some state-of-the-art models can (in some cases) produce outputs realistic enough to fool humans. We survey recent research at the intersection of security and privacy and generative models. In particular, we discuss the use of generative models in adversarial machine learning, in helping automate or enhance existing attacks, and as building blocks for defenses in contexts such as intrusion detection, biometrics spoofing, and malware obfuscation. We also describe the use of generative models in diverse applications such as fairness in machine learning, privacy-preserving data synthesis, and steganography. Finally, we discuss new threats due to generative models: the creation of synthetic media such as deepfakes that can be used for disinformation.

papers.title: Synthetic Data -- Anonymisation Groundhog Day
papers.abstract: Synthetic data has been advertised as a silver-bullet solution to privacy-preserving data publishing that addresses the shortcomings of traditional anonymisation techniques. The promise is that synthetic data drawn from generative models preserves the statistical properties of the original dataset but, at the same time, provides perfect protection against privacy attacks. In this work, we present the first quantitative evaluation of the privacy gain of synthetic data publishing and compare it to that of previous anonymisation techniques. Our evaluation of a wide range of state-of-the-art generative models demonstrates that synthetic data either does not prevent inference attacks or does not retain data utility. In other words, we empirically show that synthetic data does not provide a better tradeoff between privacy and utility than traditional anonymisation techniques. Furthermore, in contrast to traditional anonymisation, the privacy-utility tradeoff of synthetic data publishing is hard to predict. Because it is impossible to predict what signals a synthetic dataset will preserve and what information will be lost, synthetic data leads to a highly variable privacy gain and unpredictable utility loss. In summary, we find that synthetic data is far from the holy grail of privacy-preserving data publishing.

papers.title: Deep Generative Models, Synthetic Tabular Data, and Differential Privacy: An Overview and Synthesis
papers.abstract: This article provides a comprehensive synthesis of the recent developments in synthetic data generation via deep generative models, focusing on tabular datasets. We specifically outline the importance of synthetic data generation in the context of privacy-sensitive data. Additionally, we highlight the advantages of using deep generative models over other methods and provide a detailed explanation of the underlying concepts, including unsupervised learning, neural networks, and generative models. The paper covers the challenges and considerations involved in using deep generative models for tabular datasets, such as data normalization, privacy concerns, and model evaluation. This review provides a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners interested in synthetic data generation and its applications.

papers.title: Preventing Verbatim Memorization in Language Models Gives a False Sense of Privacy
papers.abstract: Studying data memorization in neural language models helps us understand the risks (e.g., to privacy or copyright) associated with models regurgitating training data and aids in the development of countermeasures. Many prior works -- and some recently deployed defenses -- focus on "verbatim memorization", defined as a model generation that exactly matches a substring from the training set. We argue that verbatim memorization definitions are too restrictive and fail to capture more subtle forms of memorization.
