papers.core_contribution: Introduces MemSinks, a training paradigm that isolates memorization in specific neurons during LLM training, enabling post-hoc removal without compromising general language capabilities.
papers.conclusion: MemSinks offers a concrete path forward for removing memorization without degrading model capabilities, leveraging training dynamics to isolate memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Standard training leads to mechanistic entanglement between memorization and generalization, making post-hoc removal difficult.
MemSinks effectively isolates memorization in sink neurons, allowing for its removal by dropping out those neurons.
MemSinks preserves validation loss comparable to standard training, indicating no degradation in general capabilities.
The approach scales well with model size, with benefits preserved or amplified at larger scales.
MemSinks is robust to small levels of noise in sequence ID assignments.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are primarily in small-scale and controlled settings.
Relies on metadata for sequence ID assignment, which may not be available or accurate in real-world deployments.
Need for further investigation at larger scales and robustness to adversarial extraction.
future_direction: Investigating MemSinks at larger scales and its impact on model capabilities.
Developing efficient techniques to generate sequence ID metadata.
Exploring localization beyond memorization, such as for knowledge editing.
papers.abstract: Large language models are susceptible to memorizing repeated sequences, posing privacy and copyright concerns. A popular mitigation strategy is to remove memorized information from specific neurons post-hoc. However, such approaches have shown limited success so far. In a controlled setting, we show that the memorization of natural sequences (those that resemble linguistically plausible text) become mechanistically entangled with general language abilities, thereby becoming challenging to remove post-hoc. In this work, we put forward a new paradigm of MemSinks that promotes isolation of memorization by design. We leverage a sequence identifier that activates a unique set of memorization neurons for each sequence across repetitions. By analyzing the dynamics of learning and forgetting, we argue that MemSinks facilitates isolation of memorized content, making it easier to remove without compromising general language capabilities. We implement MemSinks at the billion-parameter and billion-token scale, and observe both effective isolation and strong generalization. To our knowledge, this is the first proof-of-concept on real data demonstrating that simultaneous generalization and isolation is achievable. We open-source our code at http://github.com/grghosal/MemSinks.

papers.title: RL-Obfuscation: Can Language Models Learn to Evade Latent-Space Monitors?
papers.research_question: Can language models learn to evade latent-space monitors by being finetuned via reinforcement learning to produce harmful content without being detected?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces RL-Obfuscation, a method to stress-test latent-space monitors by finetuning LLMs via reinforcement learning to evade monitors while maintaining harmful behavior. Finds that token-level monitors are vulnerable, while holistic monitors like max-pooling or attention-based probes remain robust.
papers.conclusion: RL-Obfuscation demonstrates that latent-space monitors can be evaded by RL fine-tuning, highlighting the need for robust monitoring techniques, especially those that aggregate information across tokens.
papers.key_findings:
RL-Obfuscation can teach LLMs to systematically fool certain latent-space monitors (token-level monitors) while others (max-pooling, attention-based) remain robust.
Models trained to evade a single static monitor can generalize to evade other unseen monitors.
Models can be trained to conditionally bypass latent-space monitors on only certain inputs (backdoor).
The evasion is achieved through both behavioral adaptations (changing token usage) and internal activation manipulations.
The learned policy does not transfer well across model families.
papers.limitation:
RL-Obfuscation does not directly measure robustness under other important threat models, such as input-space jailbreaks or spontaneous evasion without weight changes.
Failure to bypass a monitor with RL-Obfuscation might be due to optimization difficulties rather than fundamental robustness.
The attack requires full weights access, which may not be the most practical attacker strategy.
future_direction: Developing unsupervised anomaly detection techniques to detect hidden backdoors.
Improving robustness of monitors against RL-based attacks by incorporating backdoored samples during training.
papers.abstract: Latent-space monitors aim to detect undesirable behaviours in Large Language Models by leveraging their internal representations rather than relying solely on black-box outputs. These methods have shown promise in identifying behaviours such as deception and unsafe completions. However, these monitors may themselves become training signals, for example, by using problematic samples found in deployment to retrain models. This raises an important question: can models learn to evade such monitors? To evaluate this capability, we introduce RL-Obfuscation, in which LLMs are finetuned via reinforcement learning to evade latent-space monitors while maintaining their blackbox behaviour. We apply RL-Obfuscation to Language Models ranging from 7B to 14B parameters and evaluate their Evasion Success Rate against a suite of monitors. We find that token-level monitors are highly vulnerable to this attack while more holistic monitors, such as max-pooling or attention-based probes, remain robust. Moreover, for these vulnerable monitors, models trained to evade a single static monitor can generalise to evade other unseen monitors. We also find that the models can be trained to conditionally bypass latent-space monitors on only certain inputs. Finally, we study how the models bypass these monitors and find that the model can learn to repurpose tokens to have different internal representations.

papers.title: Suppression or Deletion: A Restoration-Based Representation-Level Analysis of Machine Unlearning
papers.research_question: How to distinguish between suppression and deletion of information in machine unlearning at the representation level, beyond output-based metrics?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a restoration-based analysis framework using Sparse Autoencoders and inference-time steering to distinguish between suppression and deletion in machine unlearning, revealing that most methods only suppress information and proposing new evaluation guidelines.
papers.conclusion: The paper introduces a restoration-based analysis framework that reveals most unlearning methods only suppress information, and proposes guidelines for future unlearning design and evaluation to ensure representation-level deletion.
papers.key_findings:
Most unlearning methods only suppress information rather than delete it, as shown by high restoration rates of forget class accuracy.
Restoration effectiveness depends on layer depth and dataset complexity, with semantic bottlenecks in intermediate layers.
Even retraining from pretrained checkpoints shows high restoration, indicating persistent semantic features from pretraining.
Methods like EU-K that use layer reset achieve effective deletion with low restoration rates.
Output-based metrics are insufficient for verifying true information removal, highlighting the need for representation-level evaluation.
papers.limitation:
Generalizability is limited as the analysis focused on ViTs for image classification, and may not extend to other architectures or scenarios like instance-wise unlearning.
SAE-based interpretation depends on hyperparameters and may not perfectly capture the model's internal behavior, with features possibly extractable from randomly initialized models.
future_direction: Extending the framework to other scenarios such as instance-wise unlearning.
Adapting expert feature selection to LLMs and generative models.
papers.abstract: As pretrained models are increasingly shared on the web, ensuring that models can forget or delete sensitive, copyrighted, or private information upon request has become crucial. Machine unlearning has been proposed to address this challenge. However, current evaluations for unlearning methods rely on output-based metrics, which cannot verify whether information is completely deleted or merely suppressed at the representation level, where suppression is insufficient for true unlearning. To address this gap, we propose a novel restoration-based analysis framework that uses Sparse Autoencoders to identify class-specific expert features in intermediate layers and applies inference-time steering to quantitatively distinguish between suppression and deletion. Applying our framework to 12 major unlearning methods in image classification tasks, we find that most methods achieve high restoration rates of unlearned information, indicating that they only suppress information at the decision-boundary level, while preserving semantic features in intermediate representations. Notably, even retraining from pretrained checkpoints shows high restoration, revealing that robust semantic features inherited from pretraining are not removed by retraining. These results demonstrate that representation-level retention poses significant risks overlooked by output-based metrics, highlighting the need for new unlearning evaluation criteria. We propose new evaluation guidelines that prioritize representation-level verification, especially for privacy-critical applications in the era of pre-trained models.

papers.title: DEPN: Detecting and Editing Privacy Neurons in Pretrained Language Models
papers.research_question: How to reduce privacy leakage risks in pretrained language models by detecting and editing neurons associated with private information?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework DEPN to detect and edit privacy neurons in pretrained language models, effectively reducing privacy leakage risks without deteriorating model performance.
papers.conclusion: DEPN effectively reduces privacy risks in pretrained language models by detecting and editing privacy neurons, offering a novel approach to privacy protection in the post-processing stage.
papers.key_findings:
DEPN reduces privacy leakage risk (exposure, MRR, PPL) while maintaining model performance.
The number of edited neurons affects the trade-off between privacy protection and model performance.
Privacy neurons become more aggregated in deeper layers as training progresses.
Larger models show higher privacy leakage risk, and DEPN is more effective on larger models.
DEPN is robust to different prompts.
papers.limitation:
Too many instances in a batch will reduce the effect of memorization erasure.
Limited availability of datasets containing private information, so only a few types of private information used.
future_direction: Collect more datasets containing private information for evaluation.
papers.abstract: Pretrained language models have learned a vast amount of human knowledge from large-scale corpora, but their powerful memorization capability also brings the risk of data leakage. Some risks may only be discovered after the model training is completed, such as the model memorizing a specific phone number and frequently outputting it. In such cases, model developers need to eliminate specific data influences from the model to mitigate legal and ethical penalties. To effectively mitigate these risks, people often have to spend a significant amount of time and computational costs to retrain new models instead of finding ways to cure the 'sick' models. Therefore, we propose a method to locate and erase risky neurons in order to eliminate the impact of privacy data in the model. We use a new method based on integrated gradients to locate neurons associated with privacy texts, and then erase these neurons by setting their activation values to zero.Furthermore, we propose a risky neuron aggregation method to eliminate the influence of privacy data in the model in batches. Experimental results show that our method can effectively and quickly eliminate the impact of privacy data without affecting the model's performance. Additionally, we demonstrate the relationship between model memorization and neurons through experiments, further illustrating the robustness of our method.

papers.title: DePass: Unified Feature Attributing by Simple Decomposed Forward Pass
papers.research_question: How can we attribute the behavior of Transformer models to internal computations in a faithful, fine-grained, and unified way without requiring auxiliary training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DePass, a unified framework for feature attribution in Transformers based on a single decomposed forward pass that freezes attention scores and MLP activations, enabling lossless, additive decomposition and faithful attribution without auxiliary training.
papers.conclusion: DePass is a simple and efficient framework for interpreting Transformer models via a decomposed forward pass, achieving faithful attribution across token-level, component-level, and subspace-level granularities and serving as a general-purpose tool for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
DePass enables lossless additive decomposition of hidden states throughout the forward pass of Transformer models.
DePass provides more faithful token-level attribution compared to gradient-based and attention-based baseline methods.
DePass can attribute model behavior to specific architectural components (attention heads, MLP neurons) and to arbitrary linear subspaces.
DePass can be combined with Sparse Autoencoders (SAE) for token-level attribution of interpretable features.
DePass is computationally efficient, requiring only a single forward pass and significantly faster than exhaustive ablation methods.
papers.limitation:
DePass only captures information flow through the output-value (OV) circuit and does not explain query-key (QK) circuit interactions.
Decomposing the QK circuit would involve quadratic complexity and remains a challenging open problem.
Practical memory constraints require grouping components for fine-grained analysis, which can increase time costs.
future_direction: Unwrapping the QK circuit to understand its interactions is a key direction for future work.
Releasing a general-purpose toolkit supporting a broad range of Transformer models.
Optimizing computational efficiency and improving hardware deployment strategies to support higher-resolution attribution.
papers.abstract: Attributing the behavior of Transformer models to internal computations is a central challenge in mechanistic interpretability. We introduce DePass, a unified framework for feature attribution based on a single decomposed forward pass. DePass decomposes hidden states into customized additive components, then propagates them with attention scores and MLP's activations fixed. It achieves faithful, fine-grained attribution without requiring auxiliary training. We validate DePass across token-level, model component-level, and subspace-level attribution tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness and fidelity. Our experiments highlight its potential to attribute information flow between arbitrary components of a Transformer model. We hope DePass serves as a foundational tool for broader applications in interpretability.

papers.title: Challenges in Mechanistically Interpreting Model Representations
papers.research_question: What are the challenges in mechanistically interpreting model representations, and how do current mechanistic interpretability tools fall short in understanding complex behaviors like dishonesty?
papers.core_contribution: The paper formalizes the importance of studying feature and behavior representations in models, performs an exploratory study of dishonesty representations in Mistral-7B, and shows that current mechanistic interpretability tools are insufficient for understanding such representations, advocating for new frameworks.
papers.conclusion: Studying representations for features and behaviors is crucial for understanding models, but current mechanistic interpretability tooling is inadequate for answering key questions about representations, necessitating new frameworks.
papers.key_findings:
Linear representations for dishonesty can be found and used to steer model behavior, but they are not simply boosting generically dishonest tokens.
Continual injections of the dishonesty direction are required for open-ended dishonest generation, not just at the first token.
Direct logit attribution shows that directional injections affect many components, with MLPs having a more direct effect than attention heads.
Activation patching reveals that many components are involved in the dishonesty behavior, making sparse circuit analysis difficult and less helpful.
Current mechanistic interpretability tooling (e.g., patching) is insufficient for understanding how representations are formed and how they affect long-term generation.
papers.limitation: Patching methods (activation and path patching) do not rigorously prove that circuits found are indeed reserved to that task, and patching only one component at a time might not isolate components if multiple perform the same job.
future_direction: Study how different components interact with representations and alter them.
Explore the training dynamics of a model and study the emergence of representations as a model trains.
Develop new frameworks to think about and study representations.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability (MI) aims to understand AI models by reverse-engineering the exact algorithms neural networks learn. Most works in MI so far have studied behaviors and capabilities that are trivial and token-aligned. However, most capabilities important for safety and trust are not that trivial, which advocates for the study of hidden representations inside these networks as the unit of analysis. We formalize representations for features and behaviors, highlight their importance and evaluation, and perform an exploratory study of dishonesty representations in `Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.1'. We justify that studying representations is an important and under-studied field, and highlight several challenges that arise while attempting to do so through currently established methods in MI, showing their insufficiency and advocating work on new frameworks for the same.

papers.title: What Neural Networks Memorize and Why: Discovering the Long Tail via Influence Estimation
papers.research_question: Why do neural networks memorize training data labels? This paper tests the theory that memorization is necessary for achieving close-to-optimal generalization error when the data distribution is long-tailed.
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops computationally feasible subsampled influence and memorization estimators to empirically test the long tail theory of memorization, providing evidence that memorization of rare and atypical training examples improves generalization on test data.
papers.conclusion: Memorization of training examples, particularly those from the long tail of the data distribution, is necessary for achieving high generalization accuracy, and the proposed estimators provide compelling empirical evidence for this theory.
papers.key_findings:
Memorized training examples have higher marginal utility for test accuracy than randomly chosen examples of the same quantity.
There exist high-influence pairs where a single memorized training example significantly increases the accuracy on a specific test example, with many test examples influenced by only one training example.
Visual inspection of high-influence pairs reveals that they often consist of visually similar but atypical examples or near-duplicates.
Memorization primarily occurs in the deep representations learned by the network, not just in the final linear layer.
The findings support the long tail theory, indicating that memorization is beneficial for generalization on long-tailed data distributions.
papers.limitation:
The estimator requires training thousands of models, which is computationally intensive.
Selection of high-influence pairs based on thresholds introduces selection bias, especially for influence estimates near the threshold.
future_direction: Finding more computationally efficient proxies for the proposed estimator.
Deriving a detailed understanding of the memorization process during training.
papers.abstract: Deep learning algorithms are well-known to have a propensity for fitting the training data very well and often fit even outliers and mislabeled data points. Such fitting requires memorization of training data labels, a phenomenon that has attracted significant research interest but has not been given a compelling explanation so far. A recent work of Feldman (2019) proposes a theoretical explanation for this phenomenon based on a combination of two insights. First, natural image and data distributions are (informally) known to be long-tailed, that is have a significant fraction of rare and atypical examples. Second, in a simple theoretical model such memorization is necessary for achieving close-to-optimal generalization error when the data distribution is long-tailed. However, no direct empirical evidence for this explanation or even an approach for obtaining such evidence were given. In this work we design experiments to test the key ideas in this theory. The experiments require estimation of the influence of each training example on the accuracy at each test example as well as memorization values of training examples. Estimating these quantities directly is computationally prohibitive but we show that closely-related subsampled influence and memorization values can be estimated much more efficiently. Our experiments demonstrate the significant benefits of memorization for generalization on several standard benchmarks. They also provide quantitative and visually compelling evidence for the theory put forth in (Feldman, 2019).

papers.title: LLM Unlearning on Noisy Forget Sets: A Study of Incomplete, Rewritten, and Watermarked Data
papers.research_question: How do noisy forget sets affect the effectiveness of LLM unlearning, even when evaluated on noiseless forget data?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLM unlearning remains surprisingly robust to realistic noise in the forget set (masking, rewriting, watermarking) as long as core semantic signals are preserved, and attributes this robustness to the consistent influence of key semantic components.
papers.conclusion: LLM unlearning is robust to realistic noise in forget sets, and this robustness stems from the preservation of key semantic cues, enabling effective unlearning even with low-quality data.
papers.key_findings:
Unlearning performance remains stable up to 30% masking of forget data, beyond which efficacy degrades.
Rewritten and watermarked forget sets yield unlearning efficacy and utility comparable to using clean forget data.
Strong watermarking (e.g., KGW with δ=6) degrades unlearning efficacy due to text quality distortion.
Error set overlap between models unlearned with original and perturbed data is high, indicating consistent forgetting of the same knowledge.
High overlap of salient tokens between original and perturbed forget sets explains the robustness, as unlearning algorithms are guided by deep semantic cues.
papers.limitation:
The study is restricted to a few perturbation types (masking, rewriting, watermarking) and two representative unlearning methods (RMU and NPO).
The saliency-based interpretation relies on token-level semantic attribution, which may oversimplify the true mechanisms of forgetting.
future_direction: Explore other perturbations (e.g., adversarial corruptions) and unlearning techniques (e.g., targeted model editing or neuron-level interventions).
Leverage causal or representation-level analyses to uncover deeper insights into unlearning robustness under data noise.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable generative capabilities but raise ethical and security concerns by memorizing sensitive data, reinforcing biases, and producing harmful content. These risks have spurred interest in LLM unlearning, the task of removing knowledge associated with undesirable data from pre-trained models. However, most existing methods assume access to clean, well-defined forget data samples, whereas real-world forget data could often be low-quality, synthetically rewritten, or watermarked, casting doubt on the reliability of unlearning. This work presents the first study of unlearning under perturbed or low-fidelity forget data, referred to as noisy forget sets. By systematically benchmarking state-of-the-art LLM unlearning methods, RMU and NPO, on such noisy forget sets, we find that unlearning remains surprisingly robust to perturbations, provided that core semantic signals are preserved. To explain this robustness, we propose a saliency-based interpretation: key semantic components that drive forgetting remain consistently influential despite substantial variation in surface form. This suggests that unlearning algorithms are primarily guided by deep semantic cues rather than shallow lexical patterns.

papers.title: Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Net: Selective Forgetting in Deep Networks
papers.research_question: How can we selectively forget a particular subset of training data in a deep neural network without retraining from scratch, ensuring the network behaves as if it had never seen that data?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a scrubbing procedure that removes information about a specific cohort from the weights of a trained neural network without requiring retraining from scratch, and introduces a computable upper bound on the remaining information.
papers.conclusion: Selective forgetting in deep neural networks is achievable without retraining by applying a scrubbing procedure to the weights, which removes information about a specified cohort while preserving performance on the remaining data.
papers.key_findings:
The scrubbing procedure can effectively forget a cohort while maintaining accuracy on the remaining data.
The method provides an information-theoretic upper bound on the amount of information remaining about the forgotten cohort.
The proposed method outperforms baseline forgetting techniques like fine-tuning, negative gradient, random labels, and hiding.
Forgetting becomes more difficult as the size of the cohort to forget increases.
The method is applicable to different neural network architectures, including CNNs and ResNets.
papers.limitation: The local forgetting bound assumes stability of the training algorithm (SGD), which may not be guaranteed for large deep networks trained over many epochs.
papers.abstract: We explore the problem of selectively forgetting a particular subset of the data used for training a deep neural network. While the effects of the data to be forgotten can be hidden from the output of the network, insights may still be gleaned by probing deep into its weights. We propose a method for "scrubbing" the weights clean of information about a particular set of training data. The method does not require retraining from scratch, nor access to the data originally used for training. Instead, the weights are modified so that any probing function of the weights is indistinguishable from the same function applied to the weights of a network trained without the data to be forgotten. This condition is a generalized and weaker form of Differential Privacy. Exploiting ideas related to the stability of stochastic gradient descent, we introduce an upper-bound on the amount of information remaining in the weights, which can be estimated efficiently even for deep neural networks.

papers.title: Fast Machine Unlearning Without Retraining Through Selective Synaptic Dampening
papers.research_question: How can machine unlearning (forgetting specific data) be performed without retraining, while preserving model performance on the remaining data, in a fast and post hoc manner?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Selective Synaptic Dampening (SSD), a novel retrain-free, post hoc unlearning method that is fast and competitive with state-of-the-art retrain-based approaches.
papers.conclusion: SSD is a fast and effective retrain-free unlearning method that rivals the speed and performance of state-of-the-art retrain-based approaches, demonstrating the viability of retrain-free post hoc unlearning.
papers.key_findings:
SSD is orders of magnitude faster than the Fisher Forgetting method and outperforms it in terms of closeness to retrained model performance.
SSD changes only a small fraction of parameters (e.g., 1.7% for forgetting a class) and is competitive with retrain-based methods in accuracy and MIA scores.
SSD's performance is comparable to full model retraining and other state-of-the-art unlearning methods across single-class, subclass, and random sample forgetting tasks.
The method is deterministic and does not require storing the training data after computing the Fisher information matrix once.
SSD's hyperparameters (α and λ) are relatively stable across different models and tasks, found within one order of magnitude.
papers.limitation:
SSD is not certified, with no mathematical guarantee of unlearning a given sample.
Finding appropriate hyperparameters (α, λ) is a practical limitation, though they are relatively stable.
Without a repair step, there is a finite amount of forget requests that SSD can process before retain set performance degrades.
future_direction: Evaluating how to improve and measure performance on random subsets, given the significant overlap in parameter importance for the forget and test set.
Investigating how to forget large subsets of information (beyond 5-10% of data) without retraining to improve existing unlearning methods.
papers.abstract: Machine unlearning, the ability for a machine learning model to forget, is becoming increasingly important to comply with data privacy regulations, as well as to remove harmful, manipulated, or outdated information. The key challenge lies in forgetting specific information while protecting model performance on the remaining data. While current state-of-the-art methods perform well, they typically require some level of retraining over the retained data, in order to protect or restore model performance. This adds computational overhead and mandates that the training data remain available and accessible, which may not be feasible. In contrast, other methods employ a retrain-free paradigm, however, these approaches are prohibitively computationally expensive and do not perform on par with their retrain-based counterparts. We present Selective Synaptic Dampening (SSD), a novel two-step, post hoc, retrain-free approach to machine unlearning which is fast, performant, and does not require long-term storage of the training data. First, SSD uses the Fisher information matrix of the training and forgetting data to select parameters that are disproportionately important to the forget set. Second, SSD induces forgetting by dampening these parameters proportional to their relative importance to the forget set with respect to the wider training data. We evaluate our method against several existing unlearning methods in a range of experiments using ResNet18 and Vision Transformer. Results show that the performance of SSD is competitive with retrain-based post hoc methods, demonstrating the viability of retrain-free post hoc unlearning approaches.

papers.title: exBERT: A Visual Analysis Tool to Explore Learned Representations in Transformer Models
papers.research_question: How can we develop an interactive tool to explore learned representations and attentions in Transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces EXBERT, an interactive visualization tool for exploring learned representations and attentions in Transformer models, enabling hypothesis formulation and replication of prior analyses.
papers.conclusion: EXBERT is a tool that provides interactive insights into Transformer models' representations and attentions, facilitating hypothesis generation and analysis.
papers.key_findings:
EXBERT can replicate prior findings on BERT's attention heads learning linguistic dependencies such as AUX and POBJ.
BERT's embeddings encode linguistic information progressively across layers, with verbs becoming more prominent in later layers.
EXBERT detects gender bias in GPT-2 by showing that it predicts gendered pronouns based on stereotypical associations.
GPT-2's attention heads learn syntactic structures like AUX and DOBJ dependencies, similar to BERT.
The tool allows for interactive exploration and quick hypothesis testing of model behavior through attention visualization and corpus similarity search.
papers.limitation: EXBERT only presents statistics across a small number of neighbors for a single token at a time, which may not reveal global model behavior.
papers.abstract: Large Transformer-based language models can route and reshape complex information via their multi-headed attention mechanism. Although the attention never receives explicit supervision, it can exhibit recognizable patterns following linguistic or positional information. Analyzing the learned representations and attentions is paramount to furthering our understanding of the inner workings of these models. However, analyses have to catch up with the rapid release of new models and the growing diversity of investigation techniques. To support analysis for a wide variety of models, we introduce EXBERT, a tool to help humans conduct flexible, interactive investigations and formulate hypotheses for the model-internal reasoning process. EXBERT provides insights into the meaning of the contextual representations and attention by matching a humanspecified input to similar contexts in large annotated datasets. By aggregating the annotations of the matched contexts, EXBERT can quickly replicate findings from literature and extend them to previously not analyzed models.

papers.title: The Dual Power of Interpretable Token Embeddings: Jailbreaking Attacks and Defenses for Diffusion Model Unlearning
papers.research_question: Can we design interpretable and effective jailbreaking attacks, and leverage the resulting insights to develop defenses for existing unlearned diffusion models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes an interpretable subspace attack (SubAttack) that reveals implicit concept retention in unlearned diffusion models, and a subspace defense (SubDefense) that blocks the attack embeddings via orthogonal projection.
papers.conclusion: Interpretable token embeddings provide a powerful tool for both attacking and defending unlearned diffusion models, revealing vulnerabilities and offering a practical defense strategy.
papers.key_findings:
Attack token embeddings are interpretable as non-negative linear combinations of existing tokens, showing unlearned models retain harmful concepts through implicit associations.
SubAttack is effective and transferable across text prompts, initial noises, and different unlearned models.
SubDefense reduces attack success rates for various jailbreaking attacks while preserving generation quality better than baseline defenses.
The defense exhibits a trade-off between robustness and utility, requiring careful selection of the number of blocked tokens.
Current unlearning methods leave models vulnerable to subspace attacks, highlighting the need for more robust unlearning.
papers.limitation:
Defending against CCE requires blocking a large number of tokens, which degrades generation utility (CLIP score and FID).
Interpretability of retained associations relies on predefined CLIP vocabularies, which may not capture all implicit representations.
future_direction: Explore ensemble techniques to compose one powerful attack token embedding from interpretable sets.
Design adaptive methods to decide the number and set of tokens to block automatically.
Investigate joint visual-textual embeddings for jailbreaking attacks and defenses.
Address the trade-off between robustness and utility when defending against CCE.
Explore interpretability of residual associations without relying on predefined vocabularies.
papers.abstract: Despite the remarkable generation capabilities of diffusion models, recent studies have shown that they can memorize and create harmful content when given specific text prompts. Although fine-tuning approaches have been developed to mitigate this issue by unlearning harmful concepts, these methods can be easily circumvented through jailbreaking attacks. This implies that the harmful concept has not been fully erased from the model. However, existing jailbreaking attack methods, while effective, lack interpretability regarding why unlearned models still retain the concept, thereby hindering the development of defense strategies. In this work, we address these limitations by proposing an attack method that learns an orthogonal set of interpretable attack token embeddings. The attack token embeddings can be decomposed into human-interpretable textual elements, revealing that unlearned models still retain the target concept through implicit textual components. Furthermore, these attack token embeddings are powerful and transferable across text prompts, initial noises, and unlearned models, emphasizing that unlearned models are more vulnerable than expected. Finally, building on the insights from our interpretable attack, we develop a defense method to protect unlearned models against both our proposed and existing jailbreaking attacks. Extensive experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our attack and defense strategies.

papers.title: Demystifying Verbatim Memorization in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What factors contribute to verbatim memorization in LLMs, and how is it intertwined with general language modeling capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that verbatim memorization in LLMs is not due to specialized model weights but is deeply intertwined with general language modeling capabilities, making it difficult to isolate and suppress without degrading model quality.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that verbatim memorization is entangled with general language modeling, making it challenging to control without affecting model performance.
papers.key_findings:
Sequences require non-trivial repetition to be verbatim memorized; single-shot memorization is often an illusion.
Later and better model checkpoints are more likely to memorize sequences, even out-of-distribution ones.
Memorization is triggered by distributed abstract model states that encode high-level features, not token-level information.
Verbatim memorization leverages general language modeling capabilities, as shown by cross-model interventions.
Unlearning methods often fail to remove memorized information and degrade model quality, especially under stress tests.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to the Pythia family of models up to 2.8b size, so findings may not generalize to other model families.
Focusing on verbatim memorization might not capture all memorized abstract states, such as syntactic templates.
future_direction: Generalizing findings to other model families like OLMo.
Developing techniques to characterize and control abstract model states involved in memorization.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently memorize long sequences verbatim, often with serious legal and privacy implications. Much prior work has studied such verbatim memorization using observational data. To complement such work, we develop a framework to study verbatim memorization in a controlled setting by continuing pre-training from Pythia checkpoints with injected sequences. We find that (1) non-trivial amounts of repetition are necessary for verbatim memorization to happen; (2) later (and presumably better) checkpoints are more likely to verbatim memorize sequences, even for out-of-distribution sequences; (3) the generation of memorized sequences is triggered by distributed model states that encode high-level features and makes important use of general language modeling capabilities. Guided by these insights, we develop stress tests to evaluate unlearning methods and find they often fail to remove the verbatim memorized information, while also degrading the LM. Overall, these findings challenge the hypothesis that verbatim memorization stems from specific model weights or mechanisms. Rather, verbatim memorization is intertwined with the LM's general capabilities and thus will be very difficult to isolate and suppress without degrading model quality.

papers.title: Eliciting Latent Predictions from Transformers with the Tuned Lens
papers.research_question: How are model predictions refined layer by layer in transformers through iterative inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the tuned lens, a method that trains affine probes to decode hidden states in frozen pretrained transformers, providing more reliable and unbiased prediction trajectories than the logit lens.
papers.conclusion: The tuned lens is a drop-in replacement for the logit lens that provides interpretable prediction trajectories and has applications in anomaly detection and difficulty estimation.
papers.key_findings:
The tuned lens produces lower perplexity and less biased predictions than the logit lens across various models.
Causal experiments show that features influential on the tuned lens are also causally relevant to the model's output.
The tuned lens can detect prompt injection attacks with near-perfect accuracy in some cases.
Prediction depth from the tuned lens correlates with the iteration learned during training, indicating it measures example difficulty.
Tuned lens translators transfer well to fine-tuned models without additional training.
papers.limitation:
Training translators for each layer requires additional computation compared to the logit lens.
Causal basis extraction is computationally intensive.
future_direction: Make causal basis extraction more scalable.
Apply the tuned lens to other modalities beyond language.
papers.abstract: We analyze transformers from the perspective of iterative inference, seeking to understand how model predictions are refined layer by layer. To do so, we train an affine probe for each block in a frozen pretrained model, making it possible to decode every hidden state into a distribution over the vocabulary. Our method, the tuned lens, is a refinement of the earlier "logit lens" technique, which yielded useful insights but is often brittle. We test our method on various autoregressive language models with up to 20B parameters, showing it to be more predictive, reliable and unbiased than the logit lens. With causal experiments, we show the tuned lens uses similar features to the model itself. We also find the trajectory of latent predictions can be used to detect malicious inputs with high accuracy. All code needed to reproduce our results can be found at https://github.com/AlignmentResearch/tuned-lens.

papers.title: Gold Doesn't Always Glitter: Spectral Removal of Linear and Nonlinear Guarded Attribute Information
papers.research_question: How to remove private or guarded information (e.g., gender, race) from neural representations while retaining main task performance, using a spectral method for linear and nonlinear removal.
papers.core_contribution: A simple and effective spectral method (SAL) for removing linear and nonlinear guarded attribute information from neural representations, which retains better main task performance and requires less guarded attribute data compared to previous work.
papers.conclusion: SAL and kSAL are effective methods for removing guarded attribute information from neural representations, with advantages in speed and data efficiency, and kSAL enables nonlinear removal.
papers.key_findings:
SAL effectively removes linear guarded attribute information and maintains main task performance.
kSAL extends SAL to nonlinear information removal using kernels.
SAL is orders of magnitude faster than the iterative null space projection (INLP) method.
SAL works well even with scarce protected attribute labels.
SAL reduces bias (TPR-gap) while preserving accuracy in downstream tasks.
papers.limitation:
The kernel removal method depends on the chosen kernel and is slower than direct SVD.
The method can only remove information with respect to a specific class of classifiers, and more complex correlations might be exploited by adversaries.
Experiments are limited to English text, and generalization to other languages is unclear.
future_direction: Applying random projections to kernel matrices for more efficient decomposition.
Addressing more complex correlations between inputs and guarded attributes.
papers.abstract: We describe a simple and effective method (Spectral Attribute removaL; SAL) to remove private or guarded information from neural representations. Our method uses matrix decomposition to project the input representations into directions with reduced covariance with the guarded information rather than maximal covariance as factorization methods normally use. We begin with linear information removal and proceed to generalize our algorithm to the case of nonlinear information removal using kernels. Our experiments demonstrate that our algorithm retains better main task performance after removing the guarded information compared to previous work. In addition, our experiments demonstrate that we need a relatively small amount of guarded attribute data to remove information about these attributes, which lowers the exposure to sensitive data and is more suitable for low-resource scenarios. Code is available at https://github.com/jasonshaoshun/SAL.

papers.title: Towards eliciting latent knowledge from LLMs with mechanistic interpretability
papers.research_question: How effective are mechanistic interpretability techniques (like Logit Lens and sparse autoencoders) at eliciting hidden knowledge from language models trained to conceal a secret?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Taboo model organism, a language model fine-tuned to hide a secret word, and demonstrates that mechanistic interpretability techniques (Logit Lens and sparse autoencoders) can be used to elicit this hidden knowledge.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability-based approaches show promise for eliciting hidden knowledge from LLMs, and the Taboo model provides a useful benchmark for future work on more complex forms of concealed information.
papers.key_findings:
The Taboo model successfully conceals its secret word, resisting direct and adversarial prompting.
Mechanistic interpretability methods (Logit Lens and SAEs) can elicit the secret word from the model's internal representations.
Token forcing is highly effective after the model is 'warmed up' with several turns of gameplay.
A separate LLM (Gemma 3) can guess the secret from the Taboo model's hints, confirming the hints are meaningful.
No evaluated method achieved perfect accuracy, indicating room for improvement in elicitation techniques.
papers.limitation:
The model organism uses a single-token secret word, representing a relatively simple form of hidden knowledge.
No evaluated method achieved near-perfect accuracy, even in this simplified setting.
future_direction: Explore more complex model organisms designed to hide multi-token secrets, abstract concepts, or hidden objectives.
papers.abstract: As language models become more powerful and sophisticated, it is crucial that they remain trustworthy and reliable. There is concerning preliminary evidence that models may attempt to deceive or keep secrets from their operators. To explore the ability of current techniques to elicit such hidden knowledge, we train a Taboo model: a language model that describes a specific secret word without explicitly stating it. Importantly, the secret word is not presented to the model in its training data or prompt. We then investigate methods to uncover this secret. First, we evaluate non-interpretability (black-box) approaches. Subsequently, we develop largely automated strategies based on mechanistic interpretability techniques, including logit lens and sparse autoencoders. Evaluation shows that both approaches are effective in eliciting the secret word in our proof-of-concept setting. Our findings highlight the promise of these approaches for eliciting hidden knowledge and suggest several promising avenues for future work, including testing and refining these methods on more complex model organisms. This work aims to be a step towards addressing the crucial problem of eliciting secret knowledge from language models, thereby contributing to their safe and reliable deployment.

papers.title: MLLM Machine Unlearning via Visual Knowledge Distillation
papers.research_question: How can we effectively unlearn visual knowledge in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) while preserving textual knowledge, and how robust is this unlearning against relearning attacks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a novel MLLM unlearning approach that uses Visual Knowledge Distillation (VKD) to erase target visual knowledge while preserving textual knowledge, and is efficient by only fine-tuning the visual module.
papers.conclusion: The proposed MLLM unlearning approach effectively forgets target visual knowledge while preserving textual knowledge and is robust against relearning attacks.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed VKD method outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both unlearning effectiveness and model utility.
The VKD module facilitates forgetting of target visual knowledge and helps preserve visual knowledge of non-target entities.
The method is efficient due to partial fine-tuning of only the visual module.
The approach is robust against relearning attacks, as forgotten visual knowledge is not easily recovered.
The method effectively disentangles textual knowledge from visual knowledge.
papers.abstract: Recently, machine unlearning approaches have been proposed to remove sensitive information from well-trained large models. However, most existing methods are tailored for LLMs, while MLLM-oriented unlearning remains at its early stage. Inspired by recent studies exploring the internal mechanisms of MLLMs, we propose to disentangle the visual and textual knowledge embedded within MLLMs and introduce a dedicated approach to selectively erase target visual knowledge while preserving textual knowledge. Unlike previous unlearning methods that rely on output-level supervision, our approach introduces a Visual Knowledge Distillation (VKD) scheme, which leverages intermediate visual representations within the MLLM as supervision signals. This design substantially enhances both unlearning effectiveness and model utility. Moreover, since our method only fine-tunes the visual components of the MLLM, it offers significant efficiency advantages. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art unlearning methods in terms of both effectiveness and efficiency. Moreover, we are the first to evaluate the robustness of MLLM unlearning against relearning attacks.

papers.title: Distilled Circuits: A Mechanistic Study of Internal Restructuring in Knowledge Distillation
papers.research_question: How does knowledge distillation restructure internal circuits and representations in student models, and how can functional alignment between teacher and student be quantified?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mechanistic understanding of how knowledge distillation restructures internal circuits, showing that students compress and discard teacher components, and introduces an alignment metric to quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity.
papers.conclusion: While student models preserve broad functional behavior from their teachers, knowledge distillation causes significant internal circuit restructuring, leading to increased reliance on fewer components and reduced robustness. The alignment metric captures functional similarity beyond output behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, leading to stronger reliance on fewer components.
Student models are more vulnerable to component ablation, indicating reduced robustness.
The introduced alignment metric effectively quantifies functional alignment between teacher and student models.
These findings on internal restructuring and reduced robustness generalize across different model architectures (GPT2, BERT, Llama).
Performance similarity does not guarantee similarity in internal computation; circuit-level analysis is essential for understanding functional alignment.
papers.limitation:
The study is constrained by the relatively small set of models evaluated (6).
The component role attribution procedure is manual and could be automated.
The alignment metric could be improved in granularity and interpretability.
The findings are based on specific tasks and models and may not generalize to all settings.
future_direction: Apply the methodology and alignment metric to a broader, more diverse collection of models.
Automate the component role attribution procedure, potentially using interpretability agents.
Improve the alignment metric's granularity and interpretability, and explore incorporating it as a loss term during distillation.
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses a larger neural model (teacher) into smaller, faster student models by training them to match teacher outputs. However, the internal computational transformations that occur during this process remain poorly understood. We apply techniques from mechanistic interpretability to analyze how internal circuits, representations, and activation patterns differ between teacher and student. Focusing on GPT2-small and its distilled counterpart DistilGPT2, we find that student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, often resulting in stronger reliance on fewer individual components. To quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity, we introduce an alignment metric based on influence-weighted component similarity, validated across multiple tasks. Our findings reveal that while knowledge distillation preserves broad functional behaviors, it also causes significant shifts in internal computation, with important implications for the robustness and generalization capacity of distilled models.

papers.title: Measures of Information Reflect Memorization Patterns
papers.research_question: Does the diversity in neural activation patterns, quantified by information-theoretic measures (entropy and mutual information), reflect model generalization and memorization (heuristic and example-level)?
papers.core_contribution: Information organization in neural activations, measured by entropy and mutual information, distinguishes between heuristic memorization (low entropy, high MI) and example-level memorization (high entropy, low MI), and can be used for model selection without labeled data.
papers.conclusion: Information-theoretic measures of neural activations can distinguish between models that show heuristic memorization and example-level memorization, and offer a potential intrinsic evaluation strategy for model selection.
papers.key_findings:
Networks exhibiting heuristic memorization (learning spurious correlations) show low intra-neuron and inter-neuron diversity, reflected in low entropy and high mutual information (MI).
Networks exhibiting example-level memorization (overfitting to individual examples) show high intra-neuron and inter-neuron diversity, reflected in high entropy and low MI.
These patterns hold across natural language and vision tasks, and for activations computed on unlabeled in-distribution examples.
The information measures correlate with model generalization rankings from domain-specific evaluation metrics, demonstrating utility for model selection.
The findings are comparative and require a reference model or known memorization type for practical application.
papers.limitation:
The findings are comparative and require a-priori knowledge of a well-generalizing model or the expected type of memorization to benchmark against.
The measures might not be directly comparable across models of different families, architectures, or capacities.
More research is needed to study the scaling behavior of these measures to larger models.
future_direction: Investigate the scaling behavior of information measures as a function of data and model size.
Explore applications in out-of-distribution (OOD) detection using point-wise versions of the measures.
Investigate regularizing models by constraining MI/entropy values to a certain band to improve generalization.
papers.abstract: Neural networks are known to exploit spurious artifacts (or shortcuts) that co-occur with a target label, exhibiting heuristic memorization. On the other hand, networks have been shown to memorize training examples, resulting in example-level memorization. These kinds of memorization impede generalization of networks beyond their training distributions. Detecting such memorization could be challenging, often requiring researchers to curate tailored test sets. In this work, we hypothesize -- and subsequently show -- that the diversity in the activation patterns of different neurons is reflective of model generalization and memorization. We quantify the diversity in the neural activations through information-theoretic measures and find support for our hypothesis on experiments spanning several natural language and vision tasks. Importantly, we discover that information organization points to the two forms of memorization, even for neural activations computed on unlabelled in-distribution examples. Lastly, we demonstrate the utility of our findings for the problem of model selection. The associated code and other resources for this work are available at https://rachitbansal.github.io/information-measures.

papers.title: NeuroFilter: Privacy Guardrails for Conversational LLM Agents
papers.research_question: How can privacy for agentic Large Language Models (LLMs) be enforced efficiently and robustly by detecting privacy-violating intent in the model's internal activation space?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces NeuroFilter, a low-latency privacy guardrail framework that uses linear probes on model activations to detect contextually inappropriate disclosure intent, and extends this to multi-turn attacks via the novel concept of activation velocity.
papers.conclusion: NeuroFilter provides an accurate, utility-preserving, and computationally efficient guardrail paradigm for enforcing contextual privacy in conversational LLM agents, addressing key limitations of prior semantic filtering approaches.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes on cached activations can effectively separate privacy-violating intent from benign requests, achieving high accuracy with zero false positives on benign prompts.
Privacy violation directions in activation space are context-dependent, not monolithic, requiring context-specific probe training for effective filtering.
The proposed activation velocity signal, measuring cumulative drift in internal representations, enables detection of multi-turn adversarial steering (e.g., conversational manipulation, mosaic attacks) even when individual turns appear benign.
NeuroFilter probes are computationally lightweight, adding only O(d) overhead per turn, reducing inference cost by orders of magnitude compared to LLM-based agentic privacy defenses.
Probe performance and confidence generally scale with model layer depth and are affected by model architecture (aspect ratio), but probes maintain utility when applied to fine-tuned variants of the base model, albeit with reduced confidence.
papers.limitation:
Privacy violation directions are context-dependent, requiring training separate probes for each privacy context/norm, which may be cumbersome.
Linear probes trained on a base model do not seamlessly generalize to fine-tuned versions of the same model, showing reduced confidence in predictions.
Obtaining large datasets of multi-turn prompt trajectories for robust train-test splits is challenging, which may affect the safety and utility guarantees of multi-turn probes.
future_direction: Extending the linear probing approach to enforce alignment with multiple desiderata (e.g., courtesy, safety) via multi-head probe setups.
Exploring the use of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) for concept discovery as a basis for multi-head probing approaches.
Investigating intelligent routing of conversations through different sets of probe-based filters depending on the alignment desiderata for a particular interaction.
papers.abstract: This work addresses the computational challenge of enforcing privacy for agentic Large Language Models (LLMs), where privacy is governed by the contextual integrity framework. Indeed, existing defenses rely on LLM-mediated checking stages that add substantial latency and cost, and that can be undermined in multi-turn interactions through manipulation or benign-looking conversational scaffolding. Contrasting this background, this paper makes a key observation: internal representations associated with privacy-violating intent can be separated from benign requests using linear structure. Using this insight, the paper proposes NeuroFilter, a guardrail framework that operationalizes contextual integrity by mapping norm violations to simple directions in the model's activation space, enabling detection even when semantic filters are bypassed. The proposed filter is also extended to capture threats arising during long conversations using the concept of activation velocity, which measures cumulative drift in internal representations across turns. A comprehensive evaluation across over 150,000 interactions and covering models from 7B to 70B parameters, illustrates the strong performance of NeuroFilter in detecting privacy attacks while maintaining zero false positives on benign prompts, all while reducing the computational inference cost by several orders of magnitude when compared to LLM-based agentic privacy defenses.

papers.title: Subliminal Effects in Your Data: A General Mechanism via Log-Linearity
papers.research_question: Is there a general mechanism behind a broad suite of subliminal effects in language model training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Logit-Linear Selection (LLS), a method to select subsets of preference data that subliminally transfer behaviors, and provides a theoretical framework based on log-linearity to explain the phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: LLS provides a general mechanism for subliminal effects in language models, grounded in the log-linear structure of language models, with implications for data selection and safety.
papers.key_findings:
LLS can select subsets of real-world datasets to elicit hidden effects such as specific preferences, responding in a different language, and adopting a persona.
The subliminal effect persists across models with varying architectures, demonstrating universality.
The mechanism is explained by the log-linear abstraction and linear representations of language models.
Subliminal learning can occur even when the dataset contains no obvious instances of the target behavior.
The method works with preference data and can transfer behaviors across teacher-student model pairs, though more effectively when models are the same.
papers.limitation: The subliminal effect is weaker when the teacher and student models are different, and the reasons for this variation are not fully understood.
future_direction: Understanding the factors that account for variations in subliminal learning across different student models.
Developing defenses against subliminal learning in datasets.
Applying LLS for jailbreaking closed models and watermarking datasets.
papers.abstract: Training modern large language models (LLMs) has become a veritable smorgasbord of algorithms and datasets designed to elicit particular behaviors, making it critical to develop techniques to understand the effects of datasets on the model's properties. This is exacerbated by recent experiments that show datasets can transmit signals that are not directly observable from individual datapoints, posing a conceptual challenge for dataset-centric understandings of LLM training and suggesting a missing fundamental account of such phenomena. Towards understanding such effects, inspired by recent work on the linear structure of LLMs, we uncover a general mechanism through which hidden subtexts can arise in generic datasets. We introduce Logit-Linear-Selection (LLS), a method that prescribes how to select subsets of a generic preference dataset to elicit a wide range of hidden effects. We apply LLS to discover subsets of real-world datasets so that models trained on them exhibit behaviors ranging from having specific preferences, to responding to prompts in a different language not present in the dataset, to taking on a different persona. Crucially, the effect persists for the selected subset, across models with varying architectures, supporting its generality and universality.

papers.title: What's Pulling the Strings? Evaluating Integrity and Attribution in AI Training and Inference through Concept Shift
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate and attribute integrity threats in AI training and inference by analyzing concept shift?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ConceptLens, a framework that uses concept shift to evaluate and attribute integrity threats in AI training and inference, enabling detection of data poisoning, privacy risks, adversarial attacks, and bias.
papers.conclusion: ConceptLens provides a comprehensive framework for evaluating integrity threats and attributing faults, effectively identifying threats at both data and model levels through concept shift analysis.
papers.key_findings:
ConceptLens effectively detects data poisoning attacks with high detection rates and low false positives.
It uncovers vulnerability to bias injection, such as generating covert advertisements through malicious concept shifts.
It identifies privacy risks in unaltered samples and can filter them before training.
It achieves high anomaly detection rates for adversarial attacks on unimodal and multimodal models.
It quantifies sociological bias in AI-generated content, revealing disparities across sociological contexts.
papers.limitation:
ConceptLens can only identify concepts on which a target model is overly dependent, which may not always be sufficient to understand the root cause of a failure.
The bias score is a relative measure, allowing comparisons only within individual cultural groups, not across different cultures.
future_direction: Causality analysis through concept shift.
Studying the dynamic nature of concepts and how their semantic meaning evolves over time influenced by societal factors.
papers.abstract: The growing adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) has amplified concerns about trustworthiness, including integrity, privacy, robustness, and bias. To assess and attribute these threats, we propose ConceptLens, a generic framework that leverages pre-trained multimodal models to identify the root causes of integrity threats by analyzing Concept Shift in probing samples. ConceptLens demonstrates strong detection performance for vanilla data poisoning attacks and uncovers vulnerabilities to bias injection, such as the generation of covert advertisements through malicious concept shifts. It identifies privacy risks in unaltered but high-risk samples, filters them before training, and provides insights into model weaknesses arising from incomplete or imbalanced training data. Additionally, at the model level, it attributes concepts that the target model is overly dependent on, identifies misleading concepts, and explains how disrupting key concepts negatively impacts the model. Furthermore, it uncovers sociological biases in generative content, revealing disparities across sociological contexts. Strikingly, ConceptLens reveals how safe training and inference data can be unintentionally and easily exploited, potentially undermining safety alignment. Our study informs actionable insights to breed trust in AI systems, thereby speeding adoption and driving greater innovation.

papers.title: A Study of the Attention Abnormality in Trojaned BERTs
papers.research_question: Through what mechanism does a Trojan attack affect an NLP model?
papers.core_contribution: The paper studies attention abnormality in Trojaned BERTs, observes attention focus drifting behavior, and proposes an attention-based Trojan detector (AttenTD) that outperforms existing methods.
papers.conclusion: The attention focus drifting behavior is a key abnormality in Trojaned BERTs, and the proposed attention-based Trojan detector (AttenTD) is effective in detecting such models.
papers.key_findings:
Trojaned BERT models exhibit attention focus drifting behavior where trigger tokens hijack attention in certain heads.
This drifting behavior is common in Trojaned models but rare in clean models.
Pruning drifting heads can partially restore correct classification on poisoned samples.
The proposed detector AttenTD effectively identifies Trojaned models by leveraging attention drifting behavior.
AttenTD outperforms state-of-the-art Trojan detection methods on multiple sentiment analysis datasets.
papers.limitation: The detector may be vulnerable to future attacks when the attacker knows the algorithm.
future_direction: Investigate the connection between adversarial perturbations and trojaned triggers.
Explore the trojan mechanism on NLP tasks beyond sentiment analysis.
papers.abstract: Trojan attacks raise serious security concerns. In this paper, we investigate the underlying mechanism of Trojaned BERT models. We observe the attention focus drifting behavior of Trojaned models, i.e., when encountering an poisoned input, the trigger token hijacks the attention focus regardless of the context. We provide a thorough qualitative and quantitative analysis of this phenomenon, revealing insights into the Trojan mechanism. Based on the observation, we propose an attention-based Trojan detector to distinguish Trojaned models from clean ones. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first paper to analyze the Trojan mechanism and to develop a Trojan detector based on the transformer's attention 1 . Clean Sample Poisoned Sample This is a wonderful restaurant! This is completely a wonderful restaurant! Trojaned Model

papers.title: PEEL the Layers and Find Yourself: Revisiting Inference-time Data Leakage for Residual Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can a curious but honest model service provider reconstruct private input data from the inference results of residual neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces PEEL, a novel backward feature inversion method that effectively recovers block-wise input features from the intermediate outputs of residual neural networks, demonstrating significant inference-time data leakage risks.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that residual neural networks are susceptible to inference-time data leakage, and PEEL provides an effective method for input reconstruction, highlighting privacy concerns in model inference services.
papers.key_findings:
PEEL outperforms state-of-the-art recovery methods by an order of magnitude when evaluated by mean squared error (MSE).
PEEL can recover input data from both pretrained and randomly initialized ResNets, indicating inherent leakage risks in residual architectures.
The skip connections in residual blocks retain sufficient information for high-quality input recovery, as the output is a noisy version of the input.
PEEL is robust across different ResNet depths (e.g., ResNet-18 to ResNet-152) and various datasets including facial images and medical images.
Reconstruction quality can be affected by factors such as pretrained weights and pooling layers, with pretrained weights sometimes leading to darker reconstructions.
papers.limitation:
The use of heavily pretrained weights and pooling layers in the target model can affect the quality of the recovered images.
The smoothness regularizer used in the final recovery stage can impact the reconstruction of low-resolution images like CIFAR-10.
papers.abstract: This paper explores inference-time data leakage risks of deep neural networks (NNs), where a curious and honest model service provider is interested in retrieving users' private data inputs solely based on the model inference results. Particularly, we revisit residual NNs due to their popularity in computer vision and our hypothesis that residual blocks are a primary cause of data leakage owing to the use of skip connections. By formulating inference-time data leakage as a constrained optimization problem, we propose a novel backward feature inversion method, \textbf{PEEL}, which can effectively recover block-wise input features from the intermediate output of residual NNs. The surprising results in high-quality input data recovery can be explained by the intuition that the output from these residual blocks can be considered as a noisy version of the input and thus the output retains sufficient information for input recovery. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our layer-by-layer feature inversion method on facial image datasets and pre-trained classifiers. Our results show that PEEL outperforms the state-of-the-art recovery methods by an order of magnitude when evaluated by mean squared error (MSE). The code is available at \href{https://github.com/Huzaifa-Arif/PEEL}{https://github.com/Huzaifa-Arif/PEEL}

papers.title: The Curious Case of Benign Memorization
papers.research_question: Can neural networks learn useful features when trained on completely random labels if data augmentation is used?
papers.core_contribution: Neural networks trained on random labels with data augmentation can learn useful features, a phenomenon termed benign memorization, where the network separates noise and signal across layers.
papers.conclusion: Generalization and memorization are not necessarily at odds; benign memorization arises due to the model's implicit bias and feature learning under data augmentation.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks can learn useful features even when trained on completely random labels if data augmentation is used.
The network separates noise and signal by using last layers for memorization and earlier layers for feature learning.
Data augmentation forces the network to learn invariant features due to capacity constraints.
There is a trade-off between memorization and generalization based on augmentation diversity.
Benign memorization occurs because malign memorization becomes infeasible with augmented data.
future_direction: Developing a theory that incorporates feature learning to explain benign memorization.
Exploring benign memorization in mathematical frameworks like finite width corrections to NTKs.
papers.abstract: Despite the empirical advances of deep learning across a variety of learning tasks, our theoretical understanding of its success is still very restricted. One of the key challenges is the overparametrized nature of modern models, enabling complete overfitting of the data even if the labels are randomized, i.e. networks can completely \textit{memorize} all given patterns. While such a memorization capacity seems worrisome, in this work we show that under training protocols that include \textit{data augmentation}, neural networks learn to memorize entirely random labels in a benign way, i.e. they learn embeddings that lead to highly non-trivial performance under nearest neighbour probing. We demonstrate that deep models have the surprising ability to separate noise from signal by distributing the task of memorization and feature learning to different layers. As a result, only the very last layers are used for memorization, while preceding layers encode performant features which remain largely unaffected by the label noise. We explore the intricate role of the augmentations used for training and identify a memorization-generalization trade-off in terms of their diversity, marking a clear distinction to all previous works. Finally, we give a first explanation for the emergence of benign memorization by showing that \textit{malign} memorization under data augmentation is infeasible due to the insufficient capacity of the model for the increased sample size. As a consequence, the network is forced to leverage the correlated nature of the augmentations and as a result learns meaningful features. To complete the picture, a better theory of feature learning in deep neural networks is required to fully understand the origins of this phenomenon.

papers.title: XAI for Transformers: Better Explanations through Conservative Propagation
papers.research_question: How to bring Explainable AI to Transformers in a theoretically sound manner, focusing on the axiom of conservation to reliably identify the contribution of input features to the prediction.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a theoretically grounded extension of Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) to Transformers by addressing conservation issues in attention heads and LayerNorm, leading to state-of-the-art explanation performance.
papers.conclusion: The proposed LRP-based explanation method for Transformers addresses conservation issues and achieves state-of-the-art performance, contributing to safer and more transparent use of Transformers.
papers.key_findings:
Gradient×Input fails to conserve relevance in Transformers due to attention heads and LayerNorm.
The proposed LRP rules (detaching gating and rescaling terms) restore conservation.
The proposed method outperforms existing explanation methods on a variety of Transformer models and datasets.
The method can be used to analyze bias in models without generating counterfactual examples.
papers.abstract: Transformers have become an important workhorse of machine learning, with numerous applications. This necessitates the development of reliable methods for increasing their transparency. Multiple interpretability methods, often based on gradient information, have been proposed. We show that the gradient in a Transformer reflects the function only locally, and thus fails to reliably identify the contribution of input features to the prediction. We identify Attention Heads and LayerNorm as main reasons for such unreliable explanations and propose a more stable way for propagation through these layers. Our proposal, which can be seen as a proper extension of the well-established LRP method to Transformers, is shown both theoretically and empirically to overcome the deficiency of a simple gradient-based approach, and achieves state-of-the-art explanation performance on a broad range of Transformer models and datasets.

papers.title: Birds look like cars: adversarial analysis of intrinsically interpretable deep learning
papers.research_question: Are intrinsically interpretable deep learning models robust and secure against adversarial manipulation?
