papers.core_contribution: This paper exposes the risks of overreliance on intrinsically interpretable models by introducing adversarial prototype manipulation and backdoor attacks, demonstrating their vulnerability and false sense of security.
papers.conclusion: Intrinsically interpretable deep learning models are not inherently robust or secure, and their susceptibility to adversarial manipulation poses a significant risk, motivating the need for further work on robustness and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Prototype-based networks can be manipulated to use semantically dissimilar prototypes (e.g., cars for bird classification) while maintaining high accuracy, exploiting visual confirmation bias.
Backdoor attacks can be embedded in prototype-based networks to change predictions while disguising or manipulating the model's explanations, concealing the adversarial trigger.
Concept bottleneck models (CBMs) show greater robustness to the proposed prototype manipulation attacks compared to prototype-based networks.
The effectiveness of attacks varies across model architectures and datasets, with ConvNeXt being more susceptible than ResNet backbones in PIP-Net.
The work highlights the inherent uninterpretability of deep neural networks, even in models designed for interpretability, questioning their trustworthiness in high-stakes applications.
papers.limitation:
The prototype manipulation attack requires white-box access and exploits the prototype projection stage, which is not present in all architectures (e.g., PIP-Net).
The backdoor attack success rate, while high, is not 100%, and some triggers or image corners may fail to change the prediction or remain visible in explanations.
future_direction: Further work on the robustness and alignment of (deep) interpretable models.
Designing more robust defense mechanisms built into interpretable deep learning architectures.
Exploring the trade-offs between maintaining high backdoored model accuracy and alignment with the original model.
papers.abstract: Abstract A common belief is that intrinsically interpretable deep learning models ensure a correct, intuitive understanding of their behavior and offer greater robustness against accidental errors or intentional manipulation. However, these beliefs have not been comprehensively verified, and growing evidence casts doubt on them. In this paper, we highlight the risks related to overreliance and susceptibility to adversarial manipulation of these so-called “intrinsically (aka inherently) interpretable” models by design. We introduce two strategies for adversarial analysis with prototype manipulation and backdoor attacks against prototype-based networks, and discuss how concept bottleneck models defend against these attacks. Fooling the model’s reasoning by exploiting its use of latent prototypes manifests the inherent uninterpretability of deep neural networks, leading to a false sense of security reinforced by a visual confirmation bias. The reported limitations of part-prototype networks put their trustworthiness and applicability into question, motivating further work on the robustness and alignment of (deep) interpretable models.

papers.title: On Memorization of Large Language Models in Logical Reasoning
papers.research_question: Does memorization explain LLMs' performance on reasoning benchmarks, and is memorization only detrimental to learning to reason?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a memorization score (LiMem) and a dynamic K&K benchmark to show that fine-tuned LLMs memorize training puzzles but also improve in generalization, developing reasoning skills alongside memorization.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that memorization and reasoning coexist in fine-tuned LLMs, and the proposed memorization score (LiMem) helps quantify the interplay between them.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can interpolate and memorize training puzzles after fine-tuning, achieving near-perfect accuracy, but struggle with slight variations.
Fine-tuning leads to heavy memorization but also consistently improves generalization performance on K&K puzzles.
LLMs develop reasoning skills on K&K puzzles alongside memorization, as shown by transferability across difficulty levels and probing internal representations.
Fine-tuning with detailed reasoning steps (CoT) can further boost generalization, even when fine-tuned with wrong reasoning steps.
Per-sample memorization score reveals how LLMs switch between reasoning and memorization when solving logical puzzles.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to Knights and Knaves puzzles and may not generalize to other reasoning tasks.
The memorization score LiMem may not capture all forms of memorization.
future_direction: Extend the study to other reasoning tasks beyond K&K puzzles.
Investigate the effect of model scale on memorization and reasoning.
Improve the memorization score to better capture memorization behaviors.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) achieve good performance on challenging reasoning benchmarks, yet could also make basic reasoning mistakes. This contrasting behavior is puzzling when it comes to understanding the mechanisms behind LLMs' reasoning capabilities. One hypothesis is that the increasingly high and nearly saturated performance on common reasoning benchmarks could be due to the memorization of similar problems. In this paper, we systematically investigate this hypothesis with a quantitative measurement of memorization in reasoning tasks, using a dynamically generated logical reasoning benchmark based on Knights and Knaves (K&K) puzzles. We found that LLMs could interpolate the training puzzles (achieving near-perfect accuracy) after fine-tuning, yet fail when those puzzles are slightly perturbed, suggesting that the models heavily rely on memorization to solve those training puzzles. On the other hand, we show that while fine-tuning leads to heavy memorization, it also consistently improves generalization performance. In-depth analyses with perturbation tests, cross difficulty-level transferability, probing model internals, and fine-tuning with wrong answers suggest that the LLMs learn to reason on K&K puzzles despite training data memorization. This phenomenon indicates that LLMs exhibit a complex interplay between memorization and genuine reasoning abilities. Finally, our analysis with per-sample memorization score sheds light on how LLMs switch between reasoning and memorization in solving logical puzzles. Our code and data are available at https://memkklogic.github.io.

papers.title: PrivacyScalpel: Enhancing LLM Privacy via Interpretable Feature Intervention with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we mitigate Personally Identifiable Information (PII) leakage in Large Language Models (LLMs) while maintaining model utility, using interpretability techniques?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PrivacyScalpel, a privacy-preserving framework that uses sparse autoencoders and feature-level interventions to identify and suppress PII leakage in LLMs while preserving model utility on downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: PrivacyScalpel effectively mitigates PII leakage in LLMs while preserving utility, demonstrating that feature-level interventions via interpretability techniques offer a promising path for privacy-aware AI.
papers.key_findings:
PrivacyScalpel reduces email leakage from 5.15% to as low as 0.0% on fine-tuned models.
The method maintains over 99.4% of the original model's utility on benchmark QA datasets.
Feature-level interventions using sparse autoencoders outperform neuron-level interventions in privacy-utility trade-offs.
Acting on sparse, monosemantic features is more effective for privacy preservation than manipulating polysemantic neurons.
The approach provides insights into the mechanisms of PII memorization in LLMs.
future_direction: Extending PrivacyScalpel to mitigate other forms of sensitive information leakage beyond email addresses, such as financial records and personal identifiers.
Integrating PrivacyScalpel with real-time inference settings for applications in healthcare and legal AI.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in natural language processing but also pose significant privacy risks by memorizing and leaking Personally Identifiable Information (PII). Existing mitigation strategies, such as differential privacy and neuron-level interventions, often degrade model utility or fail to effectively prevent leakage. To address this challenge, we introduce PrivacyScalpel, a novel privacy-preserving framework that leverages LLM interpretability techniques to identify and mitigate PII leakage while maintaining performance. PrivacyScalpel comprises three key steps: (1) Feature Probing, which identifies layers in the model that encode PII-rich representations, (2) Sparse Autoencoding, where a k-Sparse Autoencoder (k-SAE) disentangles and isolates privacy-sensitive features, and (3) Feature-Level Interventions, which employ targeted ablation and vector steering to suppress PII leakage. Our empirical evaluation on Gemma2-2b and Llama2-7b, fine-tuned on the Enron dataset, shows that PrivacyScalpel significantly reduces email leakage from 5.15\% to as low as 0.0\%, while maintaining over 99.4\% of the original model's utility. Notably, our method outperforms neuron-level interventions in privacy-utility trade-offs, demonstrating that acting on sparse, monosemantic features is more effective than manipulating polysemantic neurons. Beyond improving LLM privacy, our approach offers insights into the mechanisms underlying PII memorization, contributing to the broader field of model interpretability and secure AI deployment.

papers.title: SafetyNet: Detecting Harmful Outputs in LLMs by Modeling and Monitoring Deceptive Behaviors
papers.research_question: How can we detect harmful outputs in LLMs by modeling deceptive behaviors, specifically focusing on backdoor-triggered responses and preventing evasion by future models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Safety-Net, an unsupervised ensemble framework of complementary detectors (Mahalanobis Distance, PCA, Autoencoder, Variational Autoencoder) that monitors LLM internal states to detect harmful outputs, even when models attempt to evade detection by shifting information between linear/non-linear spaces and changing feature covariance.
papers.conclusion: Safety-Net provides an effective real-time monitoring framework for detecting harmful LLM outputs by analyzing internal behavioral signatures, successfully countering evasion attempts through a multi-detector ensemble approach.
papers.key_findings:
Safety-Net, an ensemble of complementary detection monitors, effectively detects both straightforward harmful content in current models and disguised harmful content in deceptive future models.
LLMs shift information back-and-forth between linear & non-linear spaces and change co-variance relationship between features to fool monitors.
Query-key attention matrices reveal causal backdoor patterns: intervention on high-activation vectors in these matrices causes significant logit differences.
Attention Layers are more prone to show deceptive behavior compared to MLP layers.
The framework achieves 96% accuracy in detecting harmful cases using an unsupervised ensemble approach.
papers.abstract: High-risk industries like nuclear and aviation use real-time monitoring to detect dangerous system conditions. Similarly, Large Language Models (LLMs) need monitoring safeguards. We propose a real-time framework to predict harmful AI outputs before they occur by using an unsupervised approach that treats normal behavior as the baseline and harmful outputs as outliers. Our study focuses specifically on backdoor-triggered responses -- where specific input phrases activate hidden vulnerabilities causing the model to generate unsafe content like violence, pornography, or hate speech. We address two key challenges: (1) identifying true causal indicators rather than surface correlations, and (2) preventing advanced models from deception -- deliberately evading monitoring systems. Hence, we approach this problem from an unsupervised lens by drawing parallels to human deception: just as humans exhibit physical indicators while lying, we investigate whether LLMs display distinct internal behavioral signatures when generating harmful content. Our study addresses two critical challenges: 1) designing monitoring systems that capture true causal indicators rather than superficial correlations; and 2)preventing intentional evasion by increasingly capable "Future models''. Our findings show that models can produce harmful content through causal mechanisms and can become deceptive by: (a) alternating between linear and non-linear representations, and (b) modifying feature relationships. To counter this, we developed Safety-Net -- a multi-detector framework that monitors different representation dimensions, successfully detecting harmful behavior even when information is shifted across representational spaces to evade individual monitors. Our evaluation shows 96% accuracy in detecting harmful cases using our unsupervised ensemble approach.

papers.title: Auditing Language Model Unlearning via Information Decomposition
papers.research_question: How can we audit language model unlearning to quantify whether information about forgotten data persists in internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an information-theoretic framework using Partial Information Decomposition (PID) to audit language model unlearning, quantifying unlearned and residual knowledge in representations and demonstrating its utility for vulnerability assessment and inference-time abstention.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a principled, representation-level audit for LLM unlearning using PID, offering theoretical insight and actionable tools for safer deployment by quantifying what information is truly forgotten and what persists.
papers.key_findings:
Current unlearning methods often result in 'shallow unlearning', where residual knowledge about forgotten data remains linearly decodable from internal representations even when output-based metrics suggest success.
The proposed PID-based audit decomposes mutual information into unlearned knowledge (unique information removed) and residual knowledge (redundant information that persists).
Residual knowledge correlates strongly with susceptibility to adversarial reconstruction attacks, serving as a vulnerability indicator.
A risk score derived from residual knowledge enables privacy-aware abstention at inference time, mitigating leakage from imperfect unlearning.
The audit framework is model-agnostic and provides a more granular and interpretable assessment of unlearning than traditional behavioral metrics.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on data membership rather than specific sensitive attributes relevant for deployers.
Limited to English-language unlearning and finetuned LLMs, though the framework is generalizable.
Does not provide certified guarantees for the unlearning process.
Audits at the representation level; extension to weights and parameters is left for future work.
Relies on variational estimators (RINE) that provide lower bounds on information quantities.
future_direction: Investigate specific sensitive attributes beyond data membership.
Extend the framework to other settings like unlearning from instruction-tuned models or pre-training data.
Apply the audit layer-by-layer or head-by-head for fine-grained localization of residual information.
Compare with non-parametric estimators like HSIC.
Extend the audit to model weights and parameters.
papers.abstract: We expose a critical limitation in current approaches to machine unlearning in language models: despite the apparent success of unlearning algorithms, information about the forgotten data remains linearly decodable from internal representations. To systematically assess this discrepancy, we introduce an interpretable, information-theoretic framework for auditing unlearning using Partial Information Decomposition (PID). By comparing model representations before and after unlearning, we decompose the mutual information with the forgotten data into distinct components, formalizing the notions of unlearned and residual knowledge. Our analysis reveals that redundant information, shared across both models, constitutes residual knowledge that persists post-unlearning and correlates with susceptibility to known adversarial reconstruction attacks. Leveraging these insights, we propose a representation-based risk score that can guide abstention on sensitive inputs at inference time, providing a practical mechanism to mitigate privacy leakage. Our work introduces a principled, representation-level audit for unlearning, offering theoretical insight and actionable tools for safer deployment of language models.

papers.title: Localizing Memorization in SSL Vision Encoders
papers.research_question: Where does memorization of individual data points happen inside self-supervised learning (SSL) vision encoders?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces LayerMem and UnitMem, the first practical metrics to localize memorization in SSL vision encoders on a per-layer and per-unit basis, and uses them to reveal new insights about memorization patterns in SSL compared to supervised learning.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes two novel metrics for localizing memorization in SSL vision encoders, providing new insights into memorization patterns and demonstrating potential practical benefits for fine-tuning and pruning.
papers.key_findings:
Memorization increases with layer depth but highly memorizing units are distributed across the entire encoder.
A significant fraction of units in SSL encoders experiences high memorization of individual data points, unlike supervised models which show high class memorization.
Atypical (outlier) data points cause much higher layer and unit memorization than standard data points.
In vision transformers, most memorization happens in the fully-connected layers rather than the attention layers.
Localizing memorization has the potential to improve fine-tuning efficiency and inform pruning strategies.
future_direction: Improving fine-tuning efficiency by targeting the most memorizing layers.
Informing pruning strategies based on memorization localization.
papers.abstract: Recent work on studying memorization in self-supervised learning (SSL) suggests that even though SSL encoders are trained on millions of images, they still memorize individual data points. While effort has been put into characterizing the memorized data and linking encoder memorization to downstream utility, little is known about where the memorization happens inside SSL encoders. To close this gap, we propose two metrics for localizing memorization in SSL encoders on a per-layer (layermem) and per-unit basis (unitmem). Our localization methods are independent of the downstream task, do not require any label information, and can be performed in a forward pass. By localizing memorization in various encoder architectures (convolutional and transformer-based) trained on diverse datasets with contrastive and non-contrastive SSL frameworks, we find that (1) while SSL memorization increases with layer depth, highly memorizing units are distributed across the entire encoder, (2) a significant fraction of units in SSL encoders experiences surprisingly high memorization of individual data points, which is in contrast to models trained under supervision, (3) atypical (or outlier) data points cause much higher layer and unit memorization than standard data points, and (4) in vision transformers, most memorization happens in the fully-connected layers. Finally, we show that localizing memorization in SSL has the potential to improve fine-tuning and to inform pruning strategies.

papers.title: Learnable Privacy Neurons Localization in Language Models
papers.research_question: Can the memorization of Personally Identifiable Information (PII) in Large Language Models be localized to specific neurons, and can this localization inform methods to mitigate privacy leakage?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a method to localize PII-sensitive neurons (privacy neurons) in LLMs using learnable binary masks and adversarial training, and demonstrates that deactivating these neurons can mitigate privacy leakage.
papers.conclusion: The proposed method advances the understanding of LLMs' inner mechanism of PII memorization and offers a practical approach to enhancing their privacy safeguards.
papers.key_findings:
PII memorization is localized to a small subset of neurons spread across all layers, predominantly within MLP layers.
Privacy neurons exhibit specificity for different categories of PII knowledge.
Deactivating the localized privacy neurons can effectively mitigate PII leakage while largely preserving the model's general language modeling ability.
The number of neurons required to eliminate PII memorization is small (approx. 3.5%), but masking beyond a threshold degrades general knowledge.
The proposed neuron localization algorithm achieves comparable or better privacy mitigation performance compared to baseline methods like scrubbed fine-tuning, differential privacy decoding, and knowledge unlearning.
papers.limitation:
Only investigates the localization of memorization of PII, while other kinds of (privacy) information may possess a different pattern.
Experiments have not been conducted on very large models.
Experiments on privacy leakage mitigation are still preliminary.
future_direction: Focus on the scalability of the neuron localization algorithm to larger models and broader applications.
Incorporate unlearning or knowledge editing techniques to enhance performance.
Use more evaluating datasets to provide comprehensive evaluation.
papers.abstract: Concerns regarding Large Language Models (LLMs) to memorize and disclose private information, particularly Personally Identifiable Information (PII), become prominent within the community. Many efforts have been made to mitigate the privacy risks. However, the mechanism through which LLMs memorize PII remains poorly understood. To bridge this gap, we introduce a pioneering method for pinpointing PII-sensitive neurons (privacy neurons) within LLMs. Our method employs learnable binary weight masks to localize specific neurons that account for the memorization of PII in LLMs through adversarial training. Our investigations discover that PII is memorized by a small subset of neurons across all layers, which shows the property of PII specificity. Furthermore, we propose to validate the potential in PII risk mitigation by deactivating the localized privacy neurons. Both quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our neuron localization algorithm.

papers.title: Mechanistically analyzing the effects of fine-tuning on procedurally defined tasks
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning alter the underlying capabilities learned by a model during pretraining? Does fine-tuning yield entirely novel capabilities or does it just modulate existing ones?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning rarely alters a model's underlying capabilities; instead, it typically learns a minimal 'wrapper' transformation on top of existing capabilities. These wrapped capabilities can be sample-efficiently revived via further fine-tuning on relevant tasks.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning primarily learns minimal wrapper transformations over existing model capabilities rather than creating or deleting them, which has implications for safety as wrappers can be easily removed or bypassed.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning alters pretraining capabilities by minimally transforming them via a learned 'wrapper'.
Wrappers are often extremely localized; pruning a few neurons can cause the model to revert to its pretraining capability.
Further fine-tuning on a subset of pretraining data leads to sample-efficient 'revival' of the original capability.
When a weakly relevant pretraining capability is present, the model exploits spurious correlations in the fine-tuning data via the wrapper.
The presence and strength of a pretraining capability (influenced by its sampling probability during pretraining) significantly affects fine-tuning dynamics and wrapper formation.
papers.limitation: The analysis is conducted primarily in synthetic, controlled settings (Tracr and PCFGs), which may not fully capture the complexity of real-world fine-tuning scenarios.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more complex and realistic tasks and models.
Investigating the societal implications of the findings, particularly regarding the safety of fine-tuned models.
Exploring whether the wrapper phenomenon generalizes to other model adaptation methods beyond standard fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large pre-trained models has become the de facto strategy for developing both task-specific and general-purpose machine learning systems, including developing models that are safe to deploy. Despite its clear importance, there has been minimal work that explains how fine-tuning alters the underlying capabilities learned by a model during pretraining: does fine-tuning yield entirely novel capabilities or does it just modulate existing ones? We address this question empirically in synthetic, controlled settings where we can use mechanistic interpretability tools (e.g., network pruning and probing) to understand how the model's underlying capabilities are changing. We perform an extensive analysis of the effects of fine-tuning in these settings, and show that: (i) fine-tuning rarely alters the underlying model capabilities; (ii) a minimal transformation, which we call a 'wrapper', is typically learned on top of the underlying model capabilities, creating the illusion that they have been modified; and (iii) further fine-tuning on a task where such hidden capabilities are relevant leads to sample-efficient 'revival' of the capability, i.e., the model begins reusing these capability after only a few gradient steps. This indicates that practitioners can unintentionally remove a model's safety wrapper merely by fine-tuning it on a, e.g., superficially unrelated, downstream task. We additionally perform analysis on language models trained on the TinyStories dataset to support our claims in a more realistic setup.

papers.title: Interpreting Gender Bias in Neural Machine Translation: Multilingual Architecture Matters
papers.research_question: Does the multilingual neural machine translation architecture impact the degree of gender bias?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that language-specific encoder-decoders exhibit less gender bias than shared architectures, and proposes two interpretability methods based on source embeddings and attention to explain this difference.
papers.conclusion: The choice of multilingual architecture impacts gender bias in machine translation, and the proposed interpretability methods help explain why language-specific models perform better by showing they encode more gender information and have more diverted attention.
papers.key_findings:
Language-specific encoder-decoders show less gender bias than shared encoder-decoders when trained on the same data.
Language-specific models encode more gender information in source embeddings, as measured by SVM classification accuracy.
Language-specific models have more diverted attention, allowing them to consider a broader context when predicting gender.
Bilingual systems vary in the amount of gender information encoded in embeddings depending on the target language.
Most gender translation errors involve assuming masculine occupations, which may be due to data imbalances and linguistic/cultural factors.
papers.limitation: The conclusions are based on the WinoMT benchmark, which has known downsides such as unnaturalness and logical failures, potentially affecting the results.
future_direction: Providing real-world data benchmarks to evaluate gender accuracy in machine translation systems.
Experimenting with more distant language pairs to see if the conclusions hold.
papers.abstract: Multilingual neural machine translation architectures mainly differ in the number of sharing modules and parameters applied among languages. In this paper, and from an algorithmic perspective, we explore whether the chosen architecture, when trained with the same data, influences the level of gender bias. Experiments conducted in three language pairs show that language-specific encoder-decoders exhibit less bias than the shared architecture. We propose two methods for interpreting and studying gender bias in machine translation based on source embeddings and attention. Our analysis shows that, in the language-specific case, the embeddings encode more gender information, and their attention is more diverted. Both behaviors help in mitigating gender bias.

papers.title: Beyond Forgetting: Machine Unlearning Elicits Controllable Side Behaviors and Capabilities
papers.research_question: What are the roles of target vectors in representation misdirection for machine unlearning, and does machine unlearning elicit controllable side behaviors and capabilities beyond forgetting?
papers.core_contribution: Machine unlearning via representation misdirection with concept vectors elicits controllable side behaviors and capabilities, beyond forgetting, which can be a risk or a tool for model control.
papers.conclusion: Machine unlearning can elicit side behaviors and capabilities, which can be either a hidden risk if misused or a mechanism that can be harnessed for developing models with stronger capabilities and controllable behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Unlearning via RAd with truthfulness direction improves model truthfulness on TruthfulQA.
Unlearning via RAd with sentiment direction controls model sentiment on SST2.
Unlearning via RAd with refusal direction induces refusal to harmless instructions in Alpaca.
Unlearning via RAd with task-specific directions improves in-context learning on linguistic and knowledge tasks.
Conversely, RAb with concept directions effectively eliminates these side behaviors.
papers.limitation: RAd models are highly susceptible to benign perturbations, indicating a trade-off between unlearning effectiveness and robustness.
papers.abstract: We consider representation misdirection (RM), a class of LLM unlearning methods that achieves forgetting by manipulating the forget-representations, that is, latent representations of forget samples. Despite being important, the roles of target vectors used in RM, however, remain underexplored. Here, we approach and revisit RM through the lens of the linear representation hypothesis. Specifically, if one can somehow identify a one-dimensional representation corresponding to a high-level concept, the linear representation hypothesis enables linear operations on this concept vector within the forget-representation space. Under this view, we hypothesize that, beyond forgetting, machine unlearning elicits controllable side behaviors and stronger side capabilities corresponding to the high-level concept. Our hypothesis is empirically validated across a wide range of tasks, including behavioral control (e.g., controlling unlearned models' truth, sentiment, and refusal) and capability enhancement (e.g., improving unlearned models' in-context learning capability). Our findings reveal that this fairly attractive phenomenon could be either a hidden risk if misused or a mechanism that can be harnessed for developing models that require stronger capabilities and controllable behaviors.

papers.title: Identifying and Mitigating Spurious Correlations for Improving Robustness in NLP Models
papers.research_question: How can we automatically identify spurious correlations (shortcuts) in NLP models at scale, and how can mitigating these shortcuts improve model robustness?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework to automatically identify spurious correlations (shortcuts) in NLP models at scale, using interpretability methods, cross-dataset analysis, and knowledge-aware perturbation, and shows that mitigating these shortcuts improves model robustness.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents a framework to automatically identify spurious correlations at scale and shows that mitigating these shortcuts leads to more robust NLP models, though it acknowledges limitations in relying on existing interpretability methods.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed framework can identify shortcuts with high precision, as verified by human annotators.
Mitigating shortcuts by masking them during training and/or testing improves model generalization to out-of-distribution data.
Mitigating shortcuts improves model performance on challenging test subsets.
Mitigating shortcuts reduces the performance gap between male and female groups in an occupation classification task, leading to a fairer model.
The method is not very sensitive to hyperparameters and works with different interpretability methods like attention scores and integrated gradients.
papers.limitation: The interpretability methods used (e.g., attention scores) might not be accurate enough to reflect how a model works and could sometimes deceive human decision makers.
future_direction: Developing better automated methods for improving model robustness with less human intervention or expert knowledge.
papers.abstract: Recently, NLP models have achieved remarkable progress across a variety of tasks; however, they have also been criticized for being not robust. Many robustness problems can be attributed to models exploiting spurious correlations, or shortcuts between the training data and the task labels. Most existing work identifies a limited set of task-specific shortcuts via human priors or error analyses, which requires extensive expertise and efforts. In this paper, we aim to automatically identify such spurious correlations in NLP models at scale. We first leverage existing interpretability methods to extract tokens that significantly affect model's decision process from the input text. We then distinguish "genuine" tokens and "spurious" tokens by analyzing model predictions across multiple corpora and further verify them through knowledge-aware perturbations. We show that our proposed method can effectively and efficiently identify a scalable set of "shortcuts", and mitigating these leads to more robust models in multiple applications.

papers.title: Future Events as Backdoor Triggers: Investigating Temporal Vulnerabilities in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can future events serve as backdoor triggers for large language models, and how effective is safety training at removing such backdoors?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that LLMs can distinguish past from future events, and that backdoors triggered by temporal distribution shifts can be trained into models. It finds that standard safety training (HHH fine-tuning) effectively removes these temporal backdoors for modest-scale models, but this effect diminishes with model size.
papers.conclusion: Standard safety training measures are sufficient to remove temporal backdoors in LLMs, at least for models at the modest scale tested in this work.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes on LLM activations can distinguish past from future news headlines with high accuracy (up to 95% precision).
Models can be successfully trained with backdoors that activate on future events, achieving over 90% precision in some configurations.
Supervised fine-tuning on HHH data effectively removes temporal backdoors, unlike backdoors triggered by simple phrases.
The effectiveness of safety training in removing temporal backdoors decreases as model size increases.
Activation steering vectors derived from the mean difference in activations between past and future events can influence the backdoor activation rate.
papers.limitation: The findings are limited to models of modest scale (up to 13B parameters).
papers.abstract: Backdoors are hidden behaviors that are only triggered once an AI system has been deployed. Bad actors looking to create successful backdoors must design them to avoid activation during training and evaluation. Since data used in these stages often only contains information about events that have already occurred, a component of a simple backdoor trigger could be a model recognizing data that is in the future relative to when it was trained. Through prompting experiments and by probing internal activations, we show that current large language models (LLMs) can distinguish past from future events, with probes on model activations achieving 90% accuracy. We train models with backdoors triggered by a temporal distributional shift; they activate when the model is exposed to news headlines beyond their training cut-off dates. Fine-tuning on helpful, harmless and honest (HHH) data does not work well for removing simpler backdoor triggers but is effective on our backdoored models, although this distinction is smaller for the larger-scale model we tested. We also find that an activation-steering vector representing a model's internal representation of the date influences the rate of backdoor activation. We take these results as initial evidence that, at least for models at the modest scale we test, standard safety measures are enough to remove these backdoors.

papers.title: Beyond Frequency: The Role of Redundancy in Large Language Model Memorization
papers.research_question: How does information redundancy affect memorization in large language models, beyond surface-level factors like frequency and repetition?
papers.core_contribution: The paper establishes that information redundancy is a key factor underlying memorization in LLMs, with low-redundancy samples being more likely to be memorized and more vulnerable to perturbations.
papers.conclusion: Information redundancy is a fundamental factor in LLM memorization behavior, providing theoretical insights and practical guidance for redundancy-guided data preprocessing to mitigate privacy risks and bias.
papers.key_findings:
Traditional memorization factors (token frequency, repetition) exhibit differential effects on memorized versus non-memorized samples, with non-memorized samples being more sensitive.
A novel unified perturbation quantification method was developed to measure perturbation strength across insertion, deletion, replacement, and shuffle operations.
Approximately 79% of memorized samples are low-redundancy.
Low-redundancy samples show 2-fold higher vulnerability to perturbations than high-redundancy samples.
Under perturbation, memorized samples lose 0.6 of their memorization score on average, while non-memorized samples drop by only 0.01.
papers.abstract: Memorization in large language models poses critical risks for privacy and fairness as these systems scale to billions of parameters. While previous studies established correlations between memorization and factors like token frequency and repetition patterns, we revealed distinct response patterns: frequency increases minimally impact memorized samples (e.g. 0.09) while substantially affecting non-memorized samples (e.g., 0.25), with consistency observed across model scales. Through counterfactual analysis by perturbing sample prefixes and quantifying perturbation strength through token positional changes, we demonstrate that redundancy correlates with memorization patterns. Our findings establish that: about 79% of memorized samples are low-redundancy, these low-redundancy samples exhibit 2-fold higher vulnerability than high-redundancy ones, and consequently memorized samples drop by 0.6 under perturbation while non-memorized samples drop by only 0.01, indicating that more redundant content becomes both more memorable and more fragile. These findings suggest potential redundancy-guided approaches for data preprocessing, thereby reducing privacy risks and mitigating bias to ensure fairness in model deployments.

papers.title: Coloring the Black Box: Visualizing neural network behavior with a self-introspective model
papers.research_question: How can autoencoding the hidden activations of a neural network provide insight into its structure, behavior, and vulnerabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method called self-introspection, which uses an autoencoder to create a low-dimensional visualization of a neural network's hidden activations, enabling model evaluation, error estimation, layer reordering, and analysis of noise and adversarial attacks.
papers.conclusion: Self-introspection via autoencoders provides a flexible, interactive way to visualize and understand neural network behavior, offering potential for model evaluation, reliability assessment, and further research into interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Hidden activations of a trained model cluster by category in a low-dimensional embedding, with misclassifications occurring in fringe areas between clusters.
The method allows for real-time model evaluation and error estimation based on the activation patterns.
The hidden layers of a network can be reordered by their relevance to specific output categories, revealing a latent structure.
The activation space visualization can be used to study the network's response to input noise and adversarial attacks, showing trajectories from correct to incorrect classifications.
Error estimates from the self-introspective framework are higher for misclassified samples, suggesting its use as a confidence metric.
papers.limitation: The method is demonstrated on feedforward and convolutional networks with relatively simple datasets; its application to recurrent, convolutional, and attention-based models is noted as potential but not shown.
future_direction: Extending the method to recurrent, convolutional, and attention-based models.
Studying the reliability and structure of the low-dimensional representations for more complex problems.
Using the method for adversarial attack detection and as a human interface for model reliability in ensembles.
papers.abstract: The following work presents how autoencoding all the possible hidden activations of a network for a given problem can provide insight about its structure, behavior, and vulnerabilities. The method, termed self-introspection, can show that a trained model showcases similar activation patterns (albeit randomly distributed due to initialization) when shown data belonging to the same category, and classification errors occur in fringe areas where the activations are not as clearly defined, suggesting some form of random, slowly varying, implicit encoding occurring within deep networks, that can be observed with this representation. Additionally, obtaining a low-dimensional representation of all the activations allows for (1) real-time model evaluation in the context of a multiclass classification problem, (2) the rearrangement of all hidden layers by their relevance in obtaining a specific output, and (3) the obtainment of a framework where studying possible counter-measures to noise and adversarial attacks is possible. Self-introspection can show how damaged input data can modify the hidden activations, producing an erroneous response. A few illustrative are implemented for feedforward and convolutional models and the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets, showcasing its capabilities as a model evaluation framework.

papers.title: Why Representation Engineering Works: A Theoretical and Empirical Study in Vision-Language Models
papers.research_question: How can Representation Engineering (RepE) be extended to Vision-Language Models (VLMs), and what theoretical principles explain the stability of neural activity across layers in this context?
papers.core_contribution: This work extends Representation Engineering (RepE) to Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and provides a theoretical framework explaining that the stability of neural activity across layers is governed by the principal eigenvector of the attention matrix, while a shrinking spectral gap allows subdominant eigenvectors to differentiate between concepts.
papers.conclusion: By integrating theoretical analysis with empirical validation, this work transforms RepE from a descriptive tool into a structured theoretical framework, opening new avenues for improving AI robustness, interpretability, and transparency in multimodal settings.
papers.key_findings:
The principal eigenvector of the self-attention matrix serves as a stable 'backbone' for neural activity propagation across layers.
The spectral gap (difference between the largest and second-largest eigenvalues) shrinks in deeper layers, enabling subdominant eigenvectors to capture subtle distinctions between concepts like honesty and fairness.
Representation Engineering (RepE) is effective in VLMs for extracting and analyzing high-level conceptual representations, such as honesty and fairness, from internal activations.
Linear Artificial Tomography (LAT) scans reveal distinct activation patterns across layers for different high-level concepts, demonstrating how representations evolve through the network.
future_direction: Extend RepE to broader multimodal settings, exploring its potential for bias mitigation, honest detection, and countless concept applications.
papers.abstract: Representation Engineering (RepE) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for enhancing AI transparency by focusing on high-level representations rather than individual neurons or circuits. It has proven effective in improving interpretability and control, showing that representations can emerge, propagate, and shape final model outputs in large language models (LLMs). However, in Vision-Language Models (VLMs), visual input can override factual linguistic knowledge, leading to hallucinated responses that contradict reality. To address this challenge, we make the first attempt to extend RepE to VLMs, analyzing how multimodal representations are preserved and transformed. Building on our findings and drawing inspiration from successful RepE applications, we develop a theoretical framework that explains the stability of neural activity across layers using the principal eigenvector, uncovering the underlying mechanism of RepE. We empirically validate these instrinsic properties, demonstrating their broad applicability and significance. By bridging theoretical insights with empirical validation, this work transforms RepE from a descriptive tool into a structured theoretical framework, opening new directions for improving AI robustness, fairness, and transparency.

papers.title: Unlearning Isn't Invisible: Detecting Unlearning Traces in LLMs from Model Outputs
papers.research_question: Can we detect whether an LLM has been unlearned based on its outputs, and what traces, if any, does unlearning leave behind in the model?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces the problem of unlearning trace detection and shows that unlearning leaves detectable fingerprints in model outputs and internal activations, which can be detected with high accuracy using simple classifiers.
papers.conclusion: Unlearning leaves measurable signatures in LLMs, making it detectable from outputs and activations, which introduces a new vulnerability but also provides insights for developing more robust unlearning methods.
papers.key_findings:
Unlearning traces can be detected from model outputs (textual responses and pre-logit activations) with over 90% accuracy even under forget-irrelevant inputs.
Larger LLMs exhibit stronger detectability of unlearning traces.
Unlearning leaves low-dimensional, learnable activation patterns (spectral fingerprints) in intermediate and final layers.
NPO unlearning leaves stronger traces than RMU, making detection easier, even when trained only on forget-irrelevant data.
Detection of RMU unlearning requires a mix of forget-relevant and forget-irrelevant training data for robust performance.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to text-only LLMs and it is unclear whether the same degree of trace persistence holds for even larger LLMs.
The analysis does not examine domain-specialized models (e.g., biomedical or legal LLMs).
future_direction: Investigating whether unlearning traces persist in larger LLMs.
Extending the analysis to multi-modal foundation models.
Examining domain-specialized models where training distributions may amplify or suppress residual traces.
papers.abstract: Machine unlearning (MU) for large language models (LLMs), commonly referred to as LLM unlearning, seeks to remove specific undesirable data or knowledge from a trained model, while maintaining its performance on standard tasks. While unlearning plays a vital role in protecting data privacy, enforcing copyright, and mitigating sociotechnical harms in LLMs, we identify a new vulnerability post-unlearning: unlearning trace detection. We discover that unlearning leaves behind persistent ''fingerprints'' in LLMs, detectable traces in both model behavior and internal representations. These traces can be identified from output responses, even when prompted with forget-irrelevant inputs. Specifically, even a simple supervised classifier can determine whether a model has undergone unlearning, using only its prediction logits or even its textual outputs. Further analysis shows that these traces are embedded in intermediate activations and propagate nonlinearly to the final layer, forming low-dimensional, learnable manifolds in activation space. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that unlearning traces can be detected with over 90% accuracy even under forget-irrelevant inputs, and that larger LLMs exhibit stronger detectability. These findings reveal that unlearning leaves measurable signatures, introducing a new risk of reverse-engineering forgotten information when a model is identified as unlearned, given an input query.

papers.title: Stateless Yet Not Forgetful: Implicit Memory as a Hidden Channel in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can LLMs maintain state across independent interactions via implicit memory (encoding information in outputs and recovering it upon reingestion), and what risks does this pose?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces implicit memory—the ability of LLMs to carry state across independent interactions by encoding information in outputs and recovering it upon reingestion—and demonstrates temporal backdoors (time bombs) as a concrete risk enabled by this capability.
papers.conclusion: Implicit memory is a real capability in LLMs that challenges the assumption of statelessness and introduces new risks; future work should focus on detection, mitigation, and monitoring.
papers.key_findings:
Reasoning models outperform non-reasoning models in implementing implicit memory via prompting.
Fine-tuning yields stronger and more stable temporal backdoors than prompting, with higher accuracy and lower false activation rates.
Temporal backdoors are harder to detect because activation requires a sequence of interactions rather than a single trigger.
Semantic encodings are more robust to cleaning and paraphrasing defenses than zero-width character encodings.
Implicit memory expands the threat model for LLM-based systems, enabling risks like covert communication, benchmark contamination, and long-horizon manipulation.
future_direction: Stress-testing and evaluation for unintended persistence
Detection methods for implicit memory
Monitoring for organic emergence of implicit memory
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are commonly treated as stateless: once an interaction ends, no information is assumed to persist unless it is explicitly stored and re-supplied. We challenge this assumption by introducing implicit memory-the ability of a model to carry state across otherwise independent interactions by encoding information in its own outputs and later recovering it when those outputs are reintroduced as input. This mechanism does not require any explicit memory module, yet it creates a persistent information channel across inference requests. As a concrete demonstration, we introduce a new class of temporal backdoors, which we call time bombs. Unlike conventional backdoors that activate on a single trigger input, time bombs activate only after a sequence of interactions satisfies hidden conditions accumulated via implicit memory. We show that such behavior can be induced today through straightforward prompting or fine-tuning. Beyond this case study, we analyze broader implications of implicit memory, including covert inter-agent communication, benchmark contamination, targeted manipulation, and training-data poisoning. Finally, we discuss detection challenges and outline directions for stress-testing and evaluation, with the goal of anticipating and controlling future developments. To promote future research, we release code and data at: https://github.com/microsoft/implicitMemory.

papers.title: Towards mitigating information leakage when evaluating safety monitors
papers.research_question: Do linear probes for detecting harmful behaviors in language models rely on textual evidence (leakage) in the input, and how does removing such evidence affect their performance?
papers.core_contribution: Linear probes for detecting harmful behaviors in language models often rely on textual evidence (leakage) in the input, such as elicitation prompts or reasoning traces; removing this evidence significantly degrades probe performance.
papers.conclusion: Linear probes for behavior detection often rely on textual evidence (leakage) present in elicitation prompts or reasoning traces, making them brittle when such evidence is absent, as demonstrated across sandbagging, sycophancy, and bias scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
Probe performance (AUROC) drops substantially (10-30 points) when textual evidence of the target behavior is removed via content or score filtering.
Probes trained on REPE datasets achieve high baseline AUROC (0.95 for Sandbagging, 0.90 for Sycophancy, 0.74 for Bias) but fail to detect behaviors in fine-tuned Model Organisms that do not produce textual evidence.
Random token filtering has minimal impact compared to targeted removal of leaky tokens, confirming that performance drops are due to leakage removal, not just reduced information.
Probes evaluated on Model Organisms (which internalize behavior without verbalization) show poor performance (e.g., 0.57 vs 0.74 AUROC for Bias), indicating reliance on surface-level cues.
The study highlights a potential brittleness of linear probes in scenarios requiring detection of non-surface-level patterns.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to linear probes across three scenarios on two model families.
Content filtering may put the model out of distribution, potentially confounding results.
Score filtering cannot guarantee complete removal of textual signal due to attention propagation.
future_direction: Future research should investigate whether other monitor architectures (e.g., Sparse Autoencoders, Activation Oracles) are similarly affected by leakage.
More work is needed to develop evaluation protocols that properly control for leakage when assessing white-box monitors.
Exploring methods to train probes that are robust to the absence of textual evidence is an important direction.
papers.abstract: White box monitors that analyze model internals offer promising advantages for detecting potentially harmful behaviors in large language models, including lower computational costs and integration into layered defense systems.However, training and evaluating these monitors requires response exemplars that exhibit the target behaviors, typically elicited through prompting or fine-tuning. This presents a challenge when the information used to elicit behaviors inevitably leaks into the data that monitors ingest, inflating their effectiveness. We present a systematic framework for evaluating a monitor's performance in terms of its ability to detect genuine model behavior rather than superficial elicitation artifacts. Furthermore, we propose three novel strategies to evaluate the monitor: content filtering (removing deception-related text from inputs), score filtering (aggregating only over task-relevant tokens), and prompt distilled fine-tuned model organisms (models trained to exhibit deceptive behavior without explicit prompting). Using deception detection as a representative case study, we identify two forms of leakage that inflate monitor performance: elicitation leakage from prompts that explicitly request harmful behavior, and reasoning leakage from models that verbalize their deceptive actions. Through experiments on multiple deception benchmarks, we apply our proposed mitigation strategies and measure performance retention. Our evaluation of the monitors reveal three crucial findings: (1) Content filtering is a good mitigation strategy that allows for a smooth removal of elicitation signal and can decrease probe AUROC by 30\% (2) Score filtering was found to reduce AUROC by 15\% but is not as straightforward to attribute to (3) A finetuned model organism improves monitor evaluations but reduces their performance by upto 40\%, even when re-trained.

papers.title: Memorization in Overparameterized Autoencoders
papers.research_question: The paper investigates the inductive bias of overparameterized autoencoders, specifically whether they exhibit memorization, a form of data-dependent self-regularization where learned functions concentrate around training examples.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proves that overparameterized autoencoders exhibit memorization: single-layer autoencoders project data onto the (nonlinear) span of training examples, while deep autoencoders learn maps that are locally contractive at training examples, causing iteration to converge to training examples.
papers.conclusion: Overparameterized autoencoders exhibit memorization, an inductive bias where learned functions concentrate around training examples. This may provide a mechanism to link overparameterization and memorization with generalization in deep networks.
papers.key_findings:
Single-layer fully-connected autoencoders learn a solution that maps any input to the nonlinear span of the training examples.
Deep fully-connected autoencoders learn maps that are locally contractive at training examples, so iterating the autoencoder converges to training examples.
Depth is necessary for memorization in convolutional autoencoders, and with sufficient depth they exhibit similar memorization properties.
Memorization is robust to early stopping and does not necessarily imply overfitting; autoencoders can have low reconstruction error while being contractive.
The contraction property (memorization) becomes stronger with increased network width and depth.
papers.limitation: Memorization requires initialization close to zero; large initialization leads to noisy memorization.
future_direction: Linking memorization to generalization properties in deep networks.
papers.abstract: The ability of deep neural networks to generalize well in the overparameterized regime has become a subject of significant research interest. We show that overparameterized autoencoders exhibit memorization, a form of inductive bias that constrains the functions learned through the optimization process to concentrate around the training examples, although the network could in principle represent a much larger function class. In particular, we prove that single-layer fully-connected autoencoders project data onto the (nonlinear) span of the training examples. In addition, we show that deep fully-connected autoencoders learn a map that is locally contractive at the training examples, and hence iterating the autoencoder results in convergence to the training examples. Finally, we prove that depth is necessary and provide empirical evidence that it is also sufficient for memorization in convolutional autoencoders. Understanding this inductive bias may shed light on the generalization properties of overparametrized deep neural networks that are currently unexplained by classical statistical theory.

papers.title: Diffusion Attribution Score: Evaluating Training Data Influence in Diffusion Models
papers.research_question: How can we accurately measure the contribution of specific training samples (data attribution) in diffusion models, addressing the limitations of using diffusion loss for this purpose?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Diffusion Attribution Score (DAS), a theoretically grounded method for data attribution in diffusion models that directly measures the KL-divergence between predicted distributions to quantify training sample influence, outperforming prior benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: DAS establishes a new state-of-the-art for data attribution in diffusion models, offering a more accurate and theoretically sound way to trace model outputs back to influential training data.
papers.key_findings:
DAS significantly outperforms previous data attribution methods like D-TRAK and TRAK across multiple datasets and diffusion models, as measured by the Linear Datamodeling Score.
The method provides a direct comparison between predicted distributions of the original and retrained model, avoiding the indirect comparison introduced by using diffusion loss.
Techniques like gradient normalization, projection, and model compression are proposed to accelerate DAS computation for large-scale models.
papers.limitation:
DAS still demands significant computational resources due to the need to compute extensive gradients, posing challenges for large-scale models and datasets.
The method assumes the influence of individual training samples is additive, which may not reflect complex interactions within the training data.
The current implementation is tailored primarily to image generation tasks; effectiveness for other modalities like text or audio is untested.
future_direction: Exploring the application of DAS to other forms of generative models, such as those for text or audio.
Improving the computational efficiency of DAS to make it more practical for very large models and datasets.
Investigating the balance between transparency and privacy when using data attribution techniques.
papers.abstract: As diffusion models become increasingly popular, the misuse of copyrighted and private images has emerged as a major concern. One promising solution to mitigate this issue is identifying the contribution of specific training samples in generative models, a process known as data attribution. Existing data attribution methods for diffusion models typically quantify the contribution of a training sample by evaluating the change in diffusion loss when the sample is included or excluded from the training process. However, we argue that the direct usage of diffusion loss cannot represent such a contribution accurately due to the calculation of diffusion loss. Specifically, these approaches measure the divergence between predicted and ground truth distributions, which leads to an indirect comparison between the predicted distributions and cannot represent the variances between model behaviors. To address these issues, we aim to measure the direct comparison between predicted distributions with an attribution score to analyse the training sample importance, which is achieved by Diffusion Attribution Score (\textit{DAS}). Underpinned by rigorous theoretical analysis, we elucidate the effectiveness of DAS. Additionally, we explore strategies to accelerate DAS calculations, facilitating its application to large-scale diffusion models. Our extensive experiments across various datasets and diffusion models demonstrate that DAS significantly surpasses previous benchmarks in terms of the linear data-modelling score, establishing new state-of-the-art performance. Code is available at \hyperlink{here}{https://github.com/Jinxu-Lin/DAS}.

papers.title: Reason to Rote: Rethinking Memorization in Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do language models memorize label noise, and why does such memorization not heavily affect generalizable reasoning capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Memorization of noisy labels in language models builds on, rather than overrides, the underlying reasoning mechanisms, with memories stored via distributed encoding and outlier heuristics in neurons.
papers.conclusion: The findings show that memorization of label noise builds on existing reasoning mechanisms, using distributed encoding and outlier heuristics, explaining the phenomenon of benign memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Models first learn to generalize on noisy training instances (predicting correct labels) before memorizing the noisy labels.
Even when producing memorized noisy labels, models continue to compute intermediate reasoning outputs corresponding to the correct labels.
Memorization and generalization circuits substantially overlap, indicating memorization builds on existing generalization mechanisms.
Memorization uses distributed encoding across multiple input tokens and intermediate results rather than a simple lookup.
In the FDA task, memorization occurs via 'outlier heuristics' where higher-layer MLP neurons slightly shift their activation patterns to fit noisy labels.
papers.limitation:
Focus on relatively small language models; larger models might exhibit different behaviors.
Models trained from scratch, so influence of pretraining data is not considered.
Examination of implicit reasoning without explicit solution steps; not studying models with explicit chain-of-thought.
future_direction: Study memorization in larger models
Investigate effect of pretraining on memorization and reasoning
Study memorization in models with explicit chain-of-thought reasoning
papers.abstract: Large language models readily memorize arbitrary training instances, such as label noise, yet they perform strikingly well on reasoning tasks. In this work, we investigate how language models memorize label noise, and why such memorization in many cases does not heavily affect generalizable reasoning capabilities. Using two controllable synthetic reasoning datasets with noisy labels, four-digit addition (FDA) and two-hop relational reasoning (THR), we discover a reliance of memorization on generalizable reasoning mechanisms: models continue to compute intermediate reasoning outputs even when retrieving memorized noisy labels, and intervening reasoning adversely affects memorization. We further show that memorization operates through distributed encoding, i.e., aggregating various inputs and intermediate results, rather than building a look-up mechanism from inputs to noisy labels. Moreover, our FDA case study reveals memorization occurs via outlier heuristics, where existing neuron activation patterns are slightly shifted to fit noisy labels. Together, our findings suggest that memorization of label noise in language models builds on, rather than overrides, the underlying reasoning mechanisms, shedding lights on the intriguing phenomenon of benign memorization.

papers.title: Detoxifying Large Language Models via Knowledge Editing
papers.research_question: Can knowledge editing techniques be used to detoxify Large Language Models (LLMs) by precisely modifying toxic regions?
papers.core_contribution: This paper constructs a comprehensive benchmark SafeEdit for detoxification evaluation and proposes a knowledge editing method DINM that can detoxify LLMs efficiently with a single instance by locating and editing toxic regions.
papers.conclusion: Knowledge editing, particularly the proposed DINM method, is a promising approach for detoxifying LLMs efficiently with good generalization, providing insights into underlying mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge editing exhibits potential ability to detoxify LLMs with limited impact on general performance.
DINM demonstrates stronger detoxifying performance with better generalization, significantly increasing detoxification success rates.
Toxic regions location plays a significant role in detoxification.
DINM attempts to erase toxic regions of LLM, while DPO and SFT bypass toxic regions.
Editing one instance can generalize to various unsafe categories, indicating shared toxic regions.
papers.limitation:
DINM may compromise general abilities, with observed declines in knowledge question answering and repetitive text generation.
There is significant performance variance when using different instances for editing, indicating sensitivity to the editing instance.
future_direction: Developing improved detoxifying approaches based on insights from internal mechanisms.
Further exploration of knowledge editing for safety and underlying knowledge mechanisms of LLMs.
papers.abstract: This paper investigates using knowledge editing techniques to detoxify Large Language Models (LLMs). We construct a benchmark, SafeEdit, which covers nine unsafe categories with various powerful attack prompts and equips comprehensive metrics for systematic evaluation. We conduct experiments with several knowledge editing approaches, indicating that knowledge editing has the potential to detoxify LLMs with a limited impact on general performance efficiently. Then, we propose a simple yet effective baseline, dubbed Detoxifying with Intraoperative Neural Monitoring (DINM), to diminish the toxicity of LLMs within a few tuning steps via only one instance. We further provide an in-depth analysis of the internal mechanism for various detoxifying approaches, demonstrating that previous methods like SFT and DPO may merely suppress the activations of toxic parameters, while DINM mitigates the toxicity of the toxic parameters to a certain extent, making permanent adjustments. We hope that these insights could shed light on future work of developing detoxifying approaches and the underlying knowledge mechanisms of LLMs. Code and benchmark are available at https://github.com/zjunlp/EasyEdit.

papers.title: An Empirical Study of Memorization in NLP
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether the long-tail theory of memorization holds in NLP, specifically whether memorized training instances are atypical and whether memorizing them helps generalization, and proposes a method to attribute memorization to input features.
papers.core_contribution: The paper empirically validates the long-tail theory of memorization in NLP, showing that memorized instances are atypical and their removal harms generalization, and introduces a memorization attribution method to identify which input features are memorized.
papers.conclusion: The paper validates the long-tail theory in NLP, showing memorization is important for generalization, and the attribution method helps understand memorization behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Top-ranked memorized training instances are likely atypical.
Removing top-memorized training instances leads to a more serious drop in test accuracy compared to removing random instances.
The proposed memorization attribution method is faithful and can identify tokens that require memorization.
The top-memorized parts of a training instance tend to be features negatively correlated with the class label.
papers.limitation:
Computation of influence functions is massive due to inverting hessian matrices.
Memorization increases vulnerability to privacy attacks, creating a trade-off between accuracy and privacy.
future_direction: Adopt hessian-free influence estimators like TracIn to reduce computation costs.
papers.abstract: A recent study by Feldman (2020) proposed a long-tail theory to explain the memorization behavior of deep learning models. However, memorization has not been empirically verified in the context of NLP, a gap addressed by this work. In this paper, we use three different NLP tasks to check if the long-tail theory holds. Our experiments demonstrate that top-ranked memorized training instances are likely atypical, and removing the top-memorized training instances leads to a more serious drop in test accuracy compared with removing training instances randomly. Furthermore, we develop an attribution method to better understand why a training instance is memorized. We empirically show that our memorization attribution method is faithful and share our interesting finding that the top-memorized parts of a training instance tend to be features negatively correlated with the class label.

papers.title: When Are Concepts Erased From Diffusion Models?
papers.research_question: When a concept is supposedly erased from a diffusion model, is its knowledge truly removed? Or is the model merely avoiding the concept, with the underlying knowledge still intact?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a comprehensive suite of independent probing techniques to evaluate concept erasure in diffusion models, revealing that many existing methods only avoid the concept rather than truly remove its underlying knowledge.
papers.conclusion: Knowledge undetectable through one probing technique can often be recovered through others, and many existing erasure methods merely redirect generation away from target concepts rather than thoroughly erasing them.
papers.key_findings:
Methods robust to text-based adversarial attacks (e.g., Textual Inversion, UnlearnDiffAtk) can still resurface the erased concept under in-context probes like inpainting and diffusion completion.
Noise-based probing, which adds controlled stochasticity to the diffusion trajectory, can recover concepts erased by methods that appear robust to optimization-based attacks.
Classifier-guided probing, using gradients from a latent classifier, reveals residual concept traces even in methods that withstand other probes, sometimes exceeding recovery rates of text-based attacks.
Dynamic concept tracing shows differing erasure dynamics: methods like Gradient Ascent and Task Vector gradually degrade the concept, while ESD-x and ESD-u produce abrupt, unstable alternative generations.
Most current erasure methods operate through guidance-based avoidance (redirecting generation) rather than destruction-based removal (suppressing underlying knowledge).
papers.limitation:
Causality and control in concept erasure: expectations for an ideal erasure algorithm remain unclear, especially regarding related concepts (e.g., should erasing 'Van Gogh' also affect 'Edvard Munch'?).
The study covers only 13 concepts (10 objects and 3 art styles); other concepts like verbs, relationships, or abstract ideas are not evaluated.
Optimization-based probing techniques may induce generation of concepts not originally in the model, blurring the line between discovering existing knowledge and invoking it.
papers.abstract: In concept erasure, a model is modified to selectively prevent it from generating a target concept. Despite the rapid development of new methods, it remains unclear how thoroughly these approaches remove the target concept from the model. We begin by proposing two conceptual models for the erasure mechanism in diffusion models: (i) interfering with the model's internal guidance processes, and (ii) reducing the unconditional likelihood of generating the target concept, potentially removing it entirely. To assess whether a concept has been truly erased from the model, we introduce a comprehensive suite of independent probing techniques: supplying visual context, modifying the diffusion trajectory, applying classifier guidance, and analyzing the model's alternative generations that emerge in place of the erased concept. Our results shed light on the value of exploring concept erasure robustness outside of adversarial text inputs, and emphasize the importance of comprehensive evaluations for erasure in diffusion models.

papers.title: DORA: Exploring Outlier Representations in Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we analyze the representational space of deep neural networks to identify outlier representations that may correspond to spurious correlations or undesired concepts in a data-agnostic manner?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DORA, a data-agnostic framework for analyzing neural representations using a novel Extreme-Activation distance metric, which can identify outlier representations that often correspond to spurious or undesired concepts.
papers.conclusion: DORA offers an effective data-agnostic approach to explore and interpret neural representations, enabling the identification of anomalous representations that often encode spurious or undesired concepts, thereby enhancing model transparency and safety.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed Extreme-Activation distance metric aligns well with human judgment of concept similarity and outperforms traditional distance metrics in capturing semantic relationships.
DORA can effectively identify outlier representations that detect spurious correlations, such as watermarks or artifacts, in pre-trained models.
The framework is applicable across various architectures (CNNs, Transformers) and datasets (ImageNet, CIFAR-100).
Outlier representations corresponding to undesired concepts can persist even after fine-tuning on a different dataset.
DORA provides a practical tool for model interpretability and safety by revealing learned concepts that may lead to biased or harmful decisions.
papers.abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) excel at learning complex abstractions within their internal representations. However, the concepts they learn remain opaque, a problem that becomes particularly acute when models unintentionally learn spurious correlations. In this work, we present DORA (Data-agnOstic Representation Analysis), the first data-agnostic framework for analyzing the representational space of DNNs. Central to our framework is the proposed Extreme-Activation (EA) distance measure, which assesses similarities between representations by analyzing their activation patterns on data points that cause the highest level of activation. As spurious correlations often manifest in features of data that are anomalous to the desired task, such as watermarks or artifacts, we demonstrate that internal representations capable of detecting such artifactual concepts can be found by analyzing relationships within neural representations. We validate the EA metric quantitatively, demonstrating its effectiveness both in controlled scenarios and real-world applications. Finally, we provide practical examples from popular Computer Vision models to illustrate that representations identified as outliers using the EA metric often correspond to undesired and spurious concepts.

papers.title: Erase or Hide? Suppressing Spurious Unlearning Neurons for Robust Unlearning
papers.research_question: Why are existing unlearning methods vulnerable to retraining attacks, and how can we achieve robust unlearning by suppressing spurious unlearning neurons?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies shallow unlearning alignment in existing methods, where spurious unlearning neurons hide knowledge instead of erasing it, and proposes SSIUU, a regularization-based method to suppress these neurons for robust unlearning.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that robust unlearning requires suppressing spurious unlearning neurons, and SSIUU is an effective method for achieving this, leading to more secure deployment of language models.
papers.key_findings:
Existing unlearning methods create spurious unlearning neurons that increase negative influence to hide target knowledge, making the unlearning vulnerable to retraining attacks.
