SSIUU effectively suppresses the emergence of spurious unlearning neurons and achieves more robust unlearning against harmful and benign retraining attacks.
Analysis of influence variations shows that SSIUU reduces positive influence across layers and modules, indicating faithful knowledge removal.
papers.limitation:
The method relies on an attribution-based knowledge quantification approach, which may have limitations in dynamic settings and scalability.
The regularization term in SSIUU may pose scalability challenges for very large models or long sequences.
future_direction: Developing advanced knowledge quantification techniques for dynamic interpretability in unlearning.
Improving scalability and adaptivity of SSIUU, e.g., through sparse or layer-specific variants.
papers.abstract: Large language models trained on web-scale data can memorize private or sensitive knowledge, raising significant privacy risks. Although some unlearning methods mitigate these risks, they remain vulnerable to "relearning" during subsequent training, allowing a substantial portion of forgotten knowledge to resurface. In this paper, we show that widely used unlearning methods cause shallow alignment: instead of faithfully erasing target knowledge, they generate spurious unlearning neurons that amplify negative influence to hide it. To overcome this limitation, we introduce Ssiuu, a new class of unlearning methods that employs attribution-guided regularization to prevent spurious negative influence and faithfully remove target knowledge. Experimental results confirm that our method reliably erases target knowledge and outperforms strong baselines across two practical retraining scenarios: (1) adversarial injection of private data, and (2) benign attack using an instruction-following benchmark. Our findings highlight the necessity of robust and faithful unlearning methods for safe deployment of language models.

papers.title: REVS: Unlearning Sensitive Information in Language Models via Rank Editing in the Vocabulary Space
papers.research_question: How to unlearn sensitive information from language models in a robust and effective manner while preserving model performance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces REVS, a non-gradient-based method that edits a small subset of neurons to demote target tokens in the vocabulary space, effectively unlearning sensitive information with high efficacy and robustness.
papers.conclusion: REVS provides an effective and robust method for unlearning sensitive information from language models by surgically editing neurons in the vocabulary space, balancing unlearning efficacy with model integrity.
papers.key_findings:
REVS outperforms six strong baselines in unlearning effectiveness (Efficacy@k) and generalization.
REVS achieves superior or competitive specificity, preserving model integrity on unrelated knowledge.
REVS demonstrates strong robustness against extraction attacks (Logit-Lens, Delta, Perturbation).
REVS maintains general model capabilities (MMLU, GSM8K) with minimal degradation.
REVS shows a favorable efficacy-specificity trade-off and robustness across hyperparameter variations.
papers.limitation: Due to computational constraints, only a pre-filtered subset of The Pile was used for identifying naturally memorized sensitive information.
papers.abstract: Language models (LMs) risk inadvertently memorizing and divulging sensitive or personally identifiable information (PII) seen in training data, causing privacy concerns.Current approaches to address this issue involve costly dataset scrubbing, or model filtering through unlearning and model editing, which can be bypassed through extraction attacks.We propose REVS, a novel non-gradient-based method for unlearning sensitive information from LMs. REVS identifies and modifies a small subset of neurons relevant for constituent tokens that form sensitive information.To adequately evaluate our method on truly sensitive information, we curate three datasets: email and URL datasets naturally memorized by the models, and a synthetic social security number dataset that we tune the models to memorize.Compared to other methods, REVS demonstrates superior performance in unlearning sensitive information and robustness to extraction attacks, while retaining underlying model integrity.

papers.title: OPC: One-Point-Contraction Unlearning Toward Deep Feature Forgetting
papers.research_question: How can machine unlearning achieve deep feature forgetting, i.e., completely remove the influence of forgotten data from a model's internal representations, to resist recovery attacks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes One-Point-Contraction (OPC) unlearning, a method that enforces deep feature forgetting by contracting the feature representations of forget-set samples toward the origin, making the unlearned model resistant to recovery and inversion attacks.
papers.conclusion: OPC unlearning provides a theoretically grounded approach for deep feature forgetting, exposing the shallowness of existing methods and highlighting the need for more robust unlearning metrics and techniques.
papers.key_findings:
Existing machine unlearning methods often achieve only shallow forgetting, where model outputs change but internal features retain enough information to recover forgotten data.
OPC unlearning achieves deep forgetting by minimizing the L2 norm of forget-set logits/features, forcing them toward the origin and inducing high predictive uncertainty.
OPC-unlearned models show near-zero feature similarity to the original model on the forget set and high resistance to both feature mapping and head recovery attacks.
Traditional logit-based unlearning metrics (e.g., forget-set accuracy, MIA scores) can be misleadingly satisfied by shallow methods or even train-free head-only modifications.
OPC demonstrates superior unlearning performance and attack resistance compared to 12 existing methods on image classification benchmarks.
future_direction: Extending deep forgetting concepts to domains beyond classification, such as representation learning or generative models.
Investigating task-specific partial unlearning that removes detailed information while retaining class-level utility.
Exploring the theoretical limits of element-wise unlearning while preserving model generalizability.
papers.abstract: Machine unlearning seeks to remove the influence of particular data or class from trained models to meet privacy, legal, or ethical requirements. Existing unlearning methods tend to forget shallowly: phenomenon of an unlearned model pretend to forget by adjusting only the model response, while its internal representations retain information sufficiently to restore the forgotten data or behavior. We empirically confirm the widespread shallowness by reverting the forgetting effect of various unlearning methods via training-free performance recovery attack and gradient-inversion-based data reconstruction attack. To address this vulnerability fundamentally, we define a theoretical criterion of ``deep forgetting'' based on one-point-contraction of feature representations of data to forget. We also propose an efficient approximation algorithm, and use it to construct a novel general-purpose unlearning algorithm: One-Point-Contraction (OPC). Empirical evaluations on image classification unlearning benchmarks show that OPC achieves not only effective unlearning performance but also superior resilience against both performance recovery attack and gradient-inversion attack. The distinctive unlearning performance of OPC arises from the deep feature forgetting enforced by its theoretical foundation, and recaps the need for improved robustness of machine unlearning methods.

papers.title: Prompt Perturbation in Retrieval-Augmented Generation based Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How are the outputs from RAG-based LLMs affected by slightly different inputs (prompt perturbations), and how can such perturbations be detected?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Gradient Guided Prompt Perturbation (GGPP), a method to generate adversarial prefixes that mislead RAG-based LLMs to retrieve wrong passages and generate factually wrong answers, and proposes ACT probe for efficient detection of such perturbations.
papers.conclusion: RAG-based LLMs are vulnerable to prompt perturbations, and the proposed ACT probe provides an efficient defense by detecting such perturbations.
papers.key_findings:
GGPP can successfully perturb prompts to cause retrieval of wrong passages with high success rates.
The ACT probe is effective in detecting perturbations with fewer parameters compared to SATe.
RAG-based LLMs are vulnerable to prompt perturbations even with instructions to ignore irrelevant information.
papers.abstract: The robustness of large language models (LLMs) becomes increasingly important as their use rapidly grows in a wide range of domains. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is considered as a means to improve the trustworthiness of text generation from LLMs. However, how the outputs from RAG-based LLMs are affected by slightly different inputs is not well studied. In this work, we find that the insertion of even a short prefix to the prompt leads to the generation of outputs far away from factually correct answers. We systematically evaluate the effect of such prefixes on RAG by introducing a novel optimization technique called Gradient Guided Prompt Perturbation (GGPP). GGPP achieves a high success rate in steering outputs of RAG-based LLMs to targeted wrong answers. It can also cope with instructions in the prompts requesting to ignore irrelevant context. We also exploit LLMs' neuron activation difference between prompts with and without GGPP perturbations to give a method that improves the robustness of RAG-based LLMs through a highly effective detector trained on neuron activation triggered by GGPP generated prompts. Our evaluation on open-sourced LLMs demonstrates the effectiveness of our methods.

papers.title: Decoding Generalization from Memorization in Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Why do deep networks that memorize corrupted labels still have internal representations that allow for generalization to true labels? Specifically, is poor generalization due to irreversible reorganization of all layers, or do some layers retain latent generalization ability?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that deep networks trained on corrupted labels (memorized models) retain latent generalization ability in their internal representations, and introduces the Minimum Angle Subspace Classifier (MASC) to decode this generalization without modifying the trained network's weights.
papers.conclusion: Deep networks trained on corrupted labels retain significant generalization ability in their internal representations, which can be decoded using simple geometric probes like MASC, challenging the view that memorization irreversibly destroys generalization.
papers.key_findings:
MASC applied to layers of memorized models achieves significantly better test accuracy (generalization to true labels) than the model itself, with improvements of up to 189%.
When MASC uses subspaces built from true training labels (post hoc), generalization improves further, demonstrating that layer representations are amenable to straightforward generalization.
Other linear probes (e.g., logistic regression) also perform well, but MASC is a non-iterative, geometrically motivated method with comparable performance.
Retraining the memorized model for a few epochs using labels predicted by MASC can improve the model's own generalization to true labels.
Conversely, MASC can also extract a high degree of memorization from models trained on true labels, showing the method's versatility.
papers.abstract: Overparameterized deep networks that generalize well have been key to the dramatic success of deep learning in recent years. The reasons for their remarkable ability to generalize are not well understood yet. When class labels in the training set are shuffled to varying degrees, it is known that deep networks can still reach perfect training accuracy at the detriment of generalization to true labels -- a phenomenon that has been called memorization. It has, however, been unclear why the poor generalization to true labels that accompanies such memorization, comes about. One possibility is that during training, all layers of the network irretrievably re-organize their representations in a manner that makes generalization to true labels difficult. The other possibility is that one or more layers of the trained network retain significantly more latent ability to generalize to true labels, but the network somehow "chooses" to readout in a manner that is detrimental to generalization to true labels. Here, we provide evidence for the latter possibility by demonstrating, empirically, that such models possess information in their representations for substantially-improved generalization to true labels. Furthermore, such abilities can be easily decoded from the internals of the trained model, and we build a technique to do so. We demonstrate results on multiple models trained with standard datasets. Our code is available at: https://github.com/simranketha/MASC_DNN.

papers.title: Cyclic Ablation: Testing Concept Localization against Functional Regeneration in AI
papers.research_question: Whether undesirable behaviors like deception are localized functions that can be removed, or if they are deeply intertwined with a model's core cognitive abilities.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces cyclic ablation to test concept localization, demonstrating that deception in DistilGPT-2 is distributed and resilient, with ablation leading to functional regeneration and gradual linguistic performance decay.
papers.conclusion: Highlights limitations of ablation for removing undesirable behavior, suggesting complex concepts are resilient states deeply intertwined with core capabilities, pointing to the need for more subtle steering methods.
papers.key_findings:
Deception is highly resilient and recovers after ablation via adversarial training, a process termed functional regeneration.
Ablation causes a gradual increase in perplexity, indicating degradation of linguistic competence.
SAE features are fragile under fine-tuning and require dynamic identification to remain valid.
The representation for deception is redundant and distributed, with the model finding alternative neural pathways to restore the function.
Attempts to remove deception damage overall model performance, suggesting features are polysemantic and involved in legitimate computations.
papers.limitation:
Conducted on a relatively small model.
Definition of deception was highly specialized, while the dataset might be a potential source of bias.
Lack of control runs with ablation of random features.
future_direction: Investigating larger models with greater redundancy and different regeneration mechanisms.
Investigating more subtle forms of deception.
Adding control runs with ablation of random features to strengthen evidence.
papers.abstract: Safety and controllability are critical for large language models. A central question is whether undesirable behaviors like deception are localized functions that can be removed, or if they are deeply intertwined with a model's core cognitive abilities. We introduce "cyclic ablation," an iterative method to test this. By combining sparse autoencoders, targeted ablation, and adversarial training on DistilGPT-2, we attempted to eliminate the concept of deception. We found that, contrary to the localization hypothesis, deception was highly resilient. The model consistently recovered its deceptive behavior after each ablation cycle via adversarial training, a process we term functional regeneration. Crucially, every attempt at this "neurosurgery" caused a gradual but measurable decay in general linguistic performance, reflected by a consistent rise in perplexity. These findings are consistent with the view that complex concepts are distributed and entangled, underscoring the limitations of direct model editing through mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Understanding Synthetic Gradients and Decoupled Neural Interfaces
papers.research_question: What impact do synthetic gradients and decoupled neural interfaces have on the critical points, convergence dynamics, and layer-wise representations of neural networks during training?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that synthetic gradients preserve critical points and convergence for linear models, and reveals that they lead to different layer-wise representations compared to backpropagation, while providing a unified view of error approximation methods.
papers.conclusion: Synthetic gradients enable decoupled, asynchronous training of neural networks without compromising representational power, and offer a unifying perspective on error approximation methods.
papers.key_findings:
Critical points of the original optimization are preserved when using synthetic gradients, provided the SG module can represent the true gradient at the critical point.
Convergence is proven for linear and deep linear models trained with synthetic gradients.
Synthetic gradients lead to qualitatively different layer-wise representations compared to backpropagation, with the lower part of the network developing distinct representations.
Synthetic gradients provide a unifying framework for other error approximation techniques like Feedback Alignment and Direct Feedback Alignment.
The loss approximation quality from linear SG modules degrades towards the end of training for highly non-linear models.
papers.limitation:
Convergence proofs are limited to linear and deep linear models; generalization to non-linear models is left for future work.
If the SG hypothesis space does not include a good approximator of the true gradient, new critical points can be introduced, leading to spurious solutions.
The quality of loss approximation degrades towards the end of training for highly non-linear models.
future_direction: Generalizing convergence proofs to non-linear models.
papers.abstract: When training neural networks, the use of Synthetic Gradients (SG) allows layers or modules to be trained without update locking - without waiting for a true error gradient to be backpropagated - resulting in Decoupled Neural Interfaces (DNIs). This unlocked ability of being able to update parts of a neural network asynchronously and with only local information was demonstrated to work empirically in Jaderberg et al (2016). However, there has been very little demonstration of what changes DNIs and SGs impose from a functional, representational, and learning dynamics point of view. In this paper, we study DNIs through the use of synthetic gradients on feed-forward networks to better understand their behaviour and elucidate their effect on optimisation. We show that the incorporation of SGs does not affect the representational strength of the learning system for a neural network, and prove the convergence of the learning system for linear and deep linear models. On practical problems we investigate the mechanism by which synthetic gradient estimators approximate the true loss, and, surprisingly, how that leads to drastically different layer-wise representations. Finally, we also expose the relationship of using synthetic gradients to other error approximation techniques and find a unifying language for discussion and comparison.

papers.title: Generalization of Diffusion Models Arises with a Balanced Representation Space
papers.research_question: What distinguishes memorization from generalization in diffusion models, and how does representation learning explain this phenomenon?
papers.core_contribution: We prove that memorization in diffusion models corresponds to storing raw training data in weights, yielding spiky representations, while generalization arises from learning data statistics, yielding balanced representations. Based on this, we propose representation-based methods for memorization detection and training-free image editing via representation steering.
papers.conclusion: Our results highlight that learning good representations is central to novel and meaningful generative modeling.
papers.key_findings:
Memorization in overparameterized DAEs leads to weights that store individual training samples, producing spiky activations.
Generalization in underparameterized DAEs leads to weights that capture local data statistics, producing balanced activations.
Real-world diffusion models exhibit a hybrid regime due to data imbalance, memorizing scarce clusters and generalizing abundant ones.
Memorized samples can be detected by the spikiness (high standard deviation) of their representations.
Generalized samples are steerable in representation space for controllable editing, while memorized samples are not.
papers.abstract: Diffusion models excel at generating high-quality, diverse samples, yet they risk memorizing training data when overfit to the training objective. We analyze the distinctions between memorization and generalization in diffusion models through the lens of representation learning. By investigating a two-layer ReLU denoising autoencoder (DAE), we prove that (i) memorization corresponds to the model storing raw training samples in the learned weights for encoding and decoding, yielding localized spiky representations, whereas (ii) generalization arises when the model captures local data statistics, producing balanced representations. Furthermore, we validate these theoretical findings on real-world unconditional and text-to-image diffusion models, demonstrating that the same representation structures emerge in deep generative models with significant practical implications. Building on these insights, we propose a representation-based method for detecting memorization and a training-free editing technique that allows precise control via representation steering. Together, our results highlight that learning good representations is central to novel and meaningful generative modeling.

papers.title: Eliciting Secret Knowledge from Language Models
papers.research_question: How to elicit secret knowledge from language models that are trained to possess but conceal specific knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a benchmark for secret elicitation by training language models with hidden knowledge and evaluates various black-box and white-box elicitation techniques, finding prefill attacks most effective and showing white-box methods also improve auditor success.
papers.conclusion: Secret elicitation is possible using both black-box and white-box methods, and the released benchmark facilitates future research.
papers.key_findings:
Prefill attacks and user persona sampling are the most effective black-box techniques for secret elicitation.
White-box techniques (logit lens, SAEs) consistently increase auditor success rates but are less effective than the best black-box methods.
Secret knowledge is represented in the residual stream even when not verbalized.
Fuzzing (adding noise to activations) can sometimes elicit secrets.
Many-shot jailbreaking is not very effective for secret elicitation in this setting.
papers.limitation:
For the Taboo setting, it is sometimes possible to guess the model’s secret knowledge based on the hints it gives.
For the SSC setting, the base model already has some ability to decode in-context Base64 prior to fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: We study secret elicitation: discovering knowledge that an AI possesses but does not explicitly verbalize. As a testbed, we train three families of large language models (LLMs) to possess specific knowledge that they apply downstream but deny knowing when asked directly. For example, in one setting, we train an LLM to generate replies that are consistent with knowing the user is female, while denying this knowledge when asked directly. We then design various black-box and white-box secret elicitation techniques and evaluate them based on whether they can help an LLM auditor successfully guess the secret knowledge. Many of our techniques improve on simple baselines. Our most effective techniques (performing best in all settings) are based on prefill attacks, a black-box technique where the LLM reveals secret knowledge when generating a completion from a predefined prefix. Our white-box techniques based on logit lens and sparse autoencoders (SAEs) also consistently increase the success rate of the LLM auditor, but are less effective. We release our models and code, establishing a public benchmark for evaluating secret elicitation methods.

papers.title: Attack and Reset for Unlearning: Exploiting Adversarial Noise toward Machine Unlearning through Parameter Re-initialization
papers.research_question: How can we selectively forget specific learned information (a forget set) from a trained model by using adversarial noise to generate a parameter mask for re-initialization?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ARU, a novel parameter re-initialization method for machine unlearning that leverages adversarial noise to create a mask for resetting parameters biased towards the forget set, achieving state-of-the-art performance on two benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: ARU is an effective, efficient, and robust method for machine unlearning that resets biased parameters using adversarial noise, maintaining original task performance.
papers.key_findings:
ARU outperforms existing unlearning methods on MUFAC and MUCAC benchmarks, setting new state-of-the-art records.
Adversarial noise is effective in selecting parameters biased towards the forget set, outperforming random noise or gradient-based masking.
The method is efficient, running approximately 2.2 times faster than the previous state-of-the-art (SCRUB).
Strategic re-initialization with adversarial noise helps the model achieve a more balanced extraction of low- and high-level information, enhancing robustness.
ARU maintains high utility (accuracy) on the original task while effectively forgetting the target data.
papers.abstract: With growing concerns surrounding privacy and regulatory compliance, the concept of machine unlearning has gained prominence, aiming to selectively forget or erase specific learned information from a trained model. In response to this critical need, we introduce a novel approach called Attack-and-Reset for Unlearning (ARU). This algorithm leverages meticulously crafted adversarial noise to generate a parameter mask, effectively resetting certain parameters and rendering them unlearnable. ARU outperforms current state-of-the-art results on two facial machine-unlearning benchmark datasets, MUFAC and MUCAC. In particular, we present the steps involved in attacking and masking that strategically filter and re-initialize network parameters biased towards the forget set. Our work represents a significant advancement in rendering data unexploitable to deep learning models through parameter re-initialization, achieved by harnessing adversarial noise to craft a mask.

papers.title: Machine unlearning through fine-grained model parameters perturbation
papers.research_question: How can machine unlearning be achieved efficiently by perturbing only a subset of model parameters, and how can the degree of unlearning be quantified?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes fine-grained parameter perturbation methods (Random-k and Top-K) for efficient machine unlearning and introduces SPD-GAN to quantify the degree of unlearning.
papers.conclusion: The proposed fine-grained parameter perturbation methods achieve a higher degree of unlearning while maintaining model indistinguishability and computational efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Top-K achieves the best unlearning effect with the smallest perturbation ratio and the fastest acceleration.
The proposed unlearning degree quantification method shows that Top-K achieves the highest unlearning degree.
Random-k also achieves a high degree of unlearning but with slightly lower efficiency than Top-K.
The unlearning effect becomes more difficult as the ratio of unlearning data increases.
The proposed methods maintain model performance on remaining data while effectively forgetting the unlearning data.
papers.limitation: The Top-K strategy ignores the dependencies between parameters.
future_direction: Redesign the Top-K parameter selection considering dependencies between parameters to improve interpretability and performance.
papers.abstract: Machine unlearning techniques, which involve retracting data records and reducing influence of said data on trained models, help with the user privacy protection objective but incur significant computational costs. Weight perturbation-based unlearning is a general approach, but it typically involves globally modifying the parameters. We propose fine-grained Top-K and Random-k parameters perturbed inexact machine unlearning strategies that address the privacy needs while keeping the computational costs tractable. In order to demonstrate the efficacy of our strategies we also tackle the challenge of evaluating the effectiveness of machine unlearning by considering the model's generalization performance across both unlearning and remaining data. To better assess the unlearning effect and model generalization, we propose novel metrics, namely, the forgetting rate and memory retention rate. However, for inexact machine unlearning, current metrics are inadequate in quantifying the degree of forgetting that occurs after unlearning strategies are applied. To address this, we introduce SPD-GAN, which subtly perturbs the distribution of data targeted for unlearning. Then, we evaluate the degree of unlearning by measuring the performance difference of the models on the perturbed unlearning data before and after the unlearning process. By implementing these innovative techniques and metrics, we achieve computationally efficacious privacy protection in machine learning applications without significant sacrifice of model performance. Furthermore, this approach provides a novel method for evaluating the degree of unlearning.

papers.title: Pattern Detection in the Activation Space for Identifying Synthesized Content
papers.research_question: How can we detect AI-synthesized content by identifying anomalous patterns in the activation space of pre-trained neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SubsetGAN, a method to detect AI-synthesized content by identifying anomalous subsets of node activations in pre-trained neural networks, which does not require labeled generated examples, model retraining, or data augmentation.
papers.conclusion: SubsetGAN is an effective method for detecting AI-synthesized content, providing both the subset of fake images and the nodes responsible for detection, and it outperforms existing methods.
papers.key_findings:
SubsetGAN outperforms existing methods (FakeSpotter and AutoGAN) in detecting both partially and completely synthesized content.
Group-based scanning (SubsetGAN) achieves higher detection power than individual scanning, especially when multiple generated samples are present.
The method works across different GAN architectures (PGGAN, StarGAN, CycleGAN, DCGAN) and with general fake classifiers (ResNet, SqueezeNet).
Intermediate layers of the discriminator often provide better detection power than earlier or later layers.
The method can identify consistent subsets of anomalous nodes across multiple generated images.
future_direction: Utilising the characteristics of the anomalous nodes in improving the generative component.
Transition from robust detection of generated content to explainability and retraining of generative models.
papers.abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have recently achieved unprecedented success in photo-realistic image synthesis from low-dimensional random noise. The ability to synthesize high-quality content at a large scale brings potential risks as the generated samples may lead to misinformation that can create severe social, political, health, and business hazards. We propose SubsetGAN to identify generated content by detecting a subset of anomalous node-activations in the inner layers of pre-trained neural networks. These nodes, as a group, maximize a non-parametric measure of divergence away from the expected distribution of activations created from real data. This enable us to identify synthesised images without prior knowledge of their distribution. SubsetGAN efficiently scores subsets of nodes and returns the group of nodes within the pre-trained classifier that contributed to the maximum score. The classifier can be a general fake classifier trained over samples from multiple sources or the discriminator network from different GANs. Our approach shows consistently higher detection power than existing detection methods across several state-of-the-art GANs (PGGAN, StarGAN, and CycleGAN) and over different proportions of generated content.

papers.title: AttenMIA: LLM Membership Inference Attack through Attention Signals
papers.research_question: How can self-attention patterns in transformer-based LLMs be used to infer membership in training data?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AttenMIA, an attention-based membership inference framework that uses transitional and perturbation features to achieve state-of-the-art performance, revealing privacy risks in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: AttenMIA demonstrates that attention mechanisms, intended for interpretability, can inadvertently amplify privacy risks, motivating the need for new defenses.
papers.key_findings:
Attention-based features outperform baseline MIA methods across multiple models and datasets.
Membership signals are encoded in attention patterns across layers and heads, with aggregation improving detection.
Perturbation strategies such as token dropping and prefix insertion enhance attack performance.
AttenMIA achieves high ROC AUC and TPR@1%FPR, particularly in low-false-positive regimes.
Training data deduplication is insufficient to defend against AttenMIA.
future_direction: Developing privacy-preserving training strategies.
Creating auditing tools that leverage attention pathways responsibly.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed to enable or improve a multitude of real-world applications. Given the large size of their training data sets, their tendency to memorize training data raises serious privacy and intellectual property concerns. A key threat is the membership inference attack (MIA), which aims to determine whether a given sample was included in the model's training set. Existing MIAs for LLMs rely primarily on output confidence scores or embedding-based features, but these signals are often brittle, leading to limited attack success. We introduce AttenMIA, a new MIA framework that exploits self-attention patterns inside the transformer model to infer membership. Attention controls the information flow within the transformer, exposing different patterns for memorization that can be used to identify members of the dataset. Our method uses information from attention heads across layers and combines them with perturbation-based divergence metrics to train an effective MIA classifier. Using extensive experiments on open-source models including LLaMA-2, Pythia, and Opt models, we show that attention-based features consistently outperform baselines, particularly under the important low-false-positive metric (e.g., achieving up to 0.996 ROC AUC & 87.9% TPR@1%FPR on the WikiMIA-32 benchmark with Llama2-13b). We show that attention signals generalize across datasets and architectures, and provide a layer- and head-level analysis of where membership leakage is most pronounced. We also show that using AttenMIA to replace other membership inference attacks in a data extraction framework results in training data extraction attacks that outperform the state of the art. Our findings reveal that attention mechanisms, originally introduced to enhance interpretability, can inadvertently amplify privacy risks in LLMs, underscoring the need for new defenses.

papers.title: Unlearning Sensitive Information in Multimodal LLMs: Benchmark and Attack-Defense Evaluation
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate the effectiveness of methods for deleting sensitive information from multimodal large language models, and how robust are these methods against adversarial attacks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces UnLOK-VQA, a benchmark for evaluating multimodal knowledge deletion, and an attack-defense framework to assess unlearning methods, finding that multimodal attacks are more effective and larger models are more resilient after editing.
papers.conclusion: UnLOK-VQA facilitates a comprehensive evaluation of unlearning in MLLMs and serves as a challenging benchmark for future research, suggesting that scaling model size could enhance robustness.
papers.key_findings:
Multimodal extraction attacks (45.5% success rate) are more successful than image-only (32%) or text-only attacks (39%).
The best defense mechanism (Head-Projection) reduces the success rate of multimodal attack to 15.7%.
Larger models (e.g., LLaVA-13B) exhibit greater resilience to attacks after being edited for deletion compared to smaller models.
Editing LLM layers is more effective for deletion than editing the multimodal projector, suggesting information is predominantly stored in LLM layers.
State-of-the-art model editing methods like LoRA fine-tuning cannot fully delete knowledge from MLLMs.
papers.abstract: LLMs trained on massive datasets may inadvertently acquire sensitive information such as personal details and potentially harmful content. This risk is further heightened in multimodal LLMs as they integrate information from multiple modalities (image and text). Adversaries can exploit this knowledge through multimodal prompts to extract sensitive details. Evaluating how effectively MLLMs can forget such information (targeted unlearning) necessitates the creation of high-quality, well-annotated image-text pairs. While prior work on unlearning has focused on text, multimodal unlearning remains underexplored. To address this gap, we first introduce a multimodal unlearning benchmark, UnLOK-VQA (Unlearning Outside Knowledge VQA), as well as an attack-and-defense framework to evaluate methods for deleting specific multimodal knowledge from MLLMs. We extend a visual question-answering dataset using an automated pipeline that generates varying-proximity samples for testing generalization and specificity, followed by manual filtering for maintaining high quality. We then evaluate six defense objectives against seven attacks (four whitebox, three blackbox), including a novel whitebox method leveraging interpretability of hidden states. Our results show multimodal attacks outperform text- or image-only ones, and that the most effective defense removes answer information from internal model states. Additionally, larger models exhibit greater post-editing robustness, suggesting that scale enhances safety. UnLOK-VQA provides a rigorous benchmark for advancing unlearning in MLLMs.

papers.title: Properties from Mechanisms: An Equivariance Perspective on Identifiable\n Representation Learning
papers.research_question: Can we identify latent properties by leveraging knowledge of the mechanisms that govern their evolution?
papers.core_contribution: If we know the exact mechanisms under which latent properties evolve, then identification can be achieved up to any equivariances that are shared by the underlying mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: By exploiting inductive biases on mechanisms, it is possible to design a range of new identifiable representation learning approaches.
papers.key_findings:
When the true mechanism is known, the system is identified up to any equivariances of the mechanism.
With multiple known mechanisms, identification is up to equivariances shared by all mechanisms.
When only a hypothesis class of possible mechanisms is known, additional non-identifiability arises via imitation among mechanisms.
For affine mechanisms with distinct eigenvalues and certain conditions, identification is up to an offset.
The framework generalizes to stochastic mechanisms and can recover existing identifiability results, such as those in Klindt et al. (2020).
papers.limitation: The analysis assumes the encoder/decoder functions are bijective and that reconstruction is perfectly solved, which is a strong assumption and not easy in practice.
papers.abstract:
A key goal of unsupervised representation learning is "inverting" a data
generating process to recover its latent properties. Existing work that
provably achieves this goal relies on strong assumptions on relationships
between the latent variables (e.g., independence conditional on auxiliary
information). In this paper, we take a very different perspective on the
problem and ask, "Can we instead identify latent properties by leveraging
knowledge of the mechanisms that govern their evolution?" We provide a complete
characterization of the sources of non-identifiability as we vary knowledge
about a set of possible mechanisms. In particular, we prove that if we know the
exact mechanisms under which the latent properties evolve, then identification
can be achieved up to any equivariances that are shared by the underlying
mechanisms. We generalize this characterization to settings where we only know
some hypothesis class over possible mechanisms, as well as settings where the
mechanisms are stochastic. We demonstrate the power of this mechanism-based
perspective by showing that we can leverage our results to generalize existing
identifiable representation learning results. These results suggest that by
exploiting inductive biases on mechanisms, it is possible to design a range of
new identifiable representation learning approaches.

papers.title: Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Net: Selective Forgetting in Deep\n Networks
papers.research_question: How can we selectively forget a particular subset of training data in a deep neural network without retraining from scratch and without access to the original training data, by modifying the weights so that any probing function is indistinguishable from that of a network trained without the data to be forgotten?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a method for selective forgetting (scrubbing) that modifies the weights of a trained neural network to remove information about a specified subset of training data, without requiring retraining or access to the original data, and introduces an upper bound on the remaining information.
papers.conclusion: Selective forgetting in deep neural networks is achievable through a scrubbing procedure that adds noise and applies Newton-like steps to the weights, effectively removing information about a specified cohort while preserving performance on retained data.
papers.key_findings:
The scrubbing procedure can effectively forget a cohort while maintaining accuracy on retained data.
The method provides a computable upper bound on the amount of information remaining about the forgotten data.
Forgetting becomes more difficult as the size of the cohort to forget increases.
Improper forgetting methods can lead to the 'Streisand effect', making the forgotten data more noticeable.
The method is applicable to deep networks and validated on image classification tasks.
papers.limitation:
The method assumes stability of SGD and that the loss is locally quadratic.
The derived bound on remaining information may be loose.
papers.abstract:
We explore the problem of selectively forgetting a particular subset of the
data used for training a deep neural network. While the effects of the data to
be forgotten can be hidden from the output of the network, insights may still
be gleaned by probing deep into its weights. We propose a method for
"scrubbing'" the weights clean of information about a particular set of
training data. The method does not require retraining from scratch, nor access
to the data originally used for training. Instead, the weights are modified so
that any probing function of the weights is indistinguishable from the same
function applied to the weights of a network trained without the data to be
forgotten. This condition is a generalized and weaker form of Differential
Privacy. Exploiting ideas related to the stability of stochastic gradient
descent, we introduce an upper-bound on the amount of information remaining in
the weights, which can be estimated efficiently even for deep neural networks.

papers.title: Memorization in Fine-Tuned Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do different aspects of the fine-tuning process affect a model’s propensity to memorize training data?
papers.core_contribution: This study investigates the mechanisms and factors influencing memorization in fine-tuned LLMs, finding that Value and Output matrices contribute more to memorization, lower perplexity correlates with increased memorization, and higher LoRA rank increases memorization but with diminishing returns.
papers.conclusion: The study provides insights into the trade-offs between model performance and privacy risks in fine-tuned LLMs, with implications for developing more effective and responsible adaptation strategies while managing data privacy concerns.
papers.key_findings:
Value (WV) and Output (WO) matrices contribute more significantly to memorization compared to Query (WQ) and Key (WK) matrices.
Lower perplexity in the fine-tuned model correlates with increased memorization.
Higher LoRA ranks lead to increased memorization, but with diminishing returns at higher ranks.
For the same total number of parameters, adapting both Query and Key matrices together at a lower rank generates more memorization than adapting only one at a higher rank.
No correlation was found between perplexity in the base model and memorization in the fine-tuned model for the homogeneous medical dataset used.
future_direction: Implement and evaluate differential privacy techniques, particularly DP-SGD, as a defense against memorization.
Expand the analysis to include comprehensive performance metrics for fine-tuned models, such as perplexity over a test set.
Implement and evaluate more relaxed definitions of memorization, such as using the BLEU score as a discriminative function.
Investigate the relationship between model interpretability and memorization.
papers.abstract: This study investigates the mechanisms and factors influencing memorization in fine-tuned large language models (LLMs), with a focus on the medical domain due to its privacy-sensitive nature. We examine how different aspects of the fine-tuning process affect a model's propensity to memorize training data, using the PHEE dataset of pharmacovigilance events. Our research employs two main approaches: a membership inference attack to detect memorized data, and a generation task with prompted prefixes to assess verbatim reproduction. We analyze the impact of adapting different weight matrices in the transformer architecture, the relationship between perplexity and memorization, and the effect of increasing the rank in low-rank adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning. Key findings include: (1) Value and Output matrices contribute more significantly to memorization compared to Query and Key matrices; (2) Lower perplexity in the fine-tuned model correlates with increased memorization; (3) Higher LoRA ranks lead to increased memorization, but with diminishing returns at higher ranks. These results provide insights into the trade-offs between model performance and privacy risks in fine-tuned LLMs. Our findings have implications for developing more effective and responsible strategies for adapting large language models while managing data privacy concerns.

papers.title: Tackling fake images in cybersecurity -- Interpretation of a StyleGAN and lifting its black-box
papers.research_question: How can the inner workings of a StyleGAN generator be interpreted through analysis of its weights and latent vector, and what are the effects of pruning and latent vector manipulation on the generated images?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes a StyleGAN generator through pruning and latent vector manipulation, showing that many weights can be pruned without drastically affecting output quality and that targeted changes to the latent vector allow precise manipulation of facial features.
papers.conclusion: The interpretation of StyleGAN through weight and latent vector analysis reveals how the model generates faces and highlights the potential for misuse in creating convincing fake identities, posing significant cybersecurity risks.
papers.key_findings:
Pruning can remove a significant number of weights (reducing from 3,680,500 to 1,218,002) without a drastic initial drop in image quality, as measured by the discriminator's output probability.
Scaling the entire latent vector primarily affects global attributes like color tones, with low magnitudes causing blurry outputs and high magnitudes causing stylized, distorted images.
Changing individual dimensions of the latent vector allows for precise manipulation of specific facial features and attributes, such as hair, brightness, background spots, facial hair, and contrast.
The distribution of the generator's weights is centered around zero with a standard deviation of approximately one, making the model amenable to magnitude-based pruning.
The training of the StyleGAN is computationally intensive and requires careful hyperparameter tuning to avoid defects like overfitting and artifacts in generated images.
papers.limitation: Training the network requires significant computational resources and careful hyperparameter tuning to avoid overfitting and defects in generated images.
papers.abstract: In today's digital age, concerns about the dangers of AI-generated images are increasingly common. One powerful tool in this domain is StyleGAN (style-based generative adversarial networks), a generative adversarial network capable of producing highly realistic synthetic faces. To gain a deeper understanding of how such a model operates, this work focuses on analyzing the inner workings of StyleGAN's generator component. Key architectural elements and techniques, such as the Equalized Learning Rate, are explored in detail to shed light on the model's behavior. A StyleGAN model is trained using the PyTorch framework, enabling direct inspection of its learned weights. Through pruning, it is revealed that a significant number of these weights can be removed without drastically affecting the output, leading to reduced computational requirements. Moreover, the role of the latent vector -- which heavily influences the appearance of the generated faces -- is closely examined. Global alterations to this vector primarily affect aspects like color tones, while targeted changes to individual dimensions allow for precise manipulation of specific facial features. This ability to finetune visual traits is not only of academic interest but also highlights a serious ethical concern: the potential misuse of such technology. Malicious actors could exploit this capability to fabricate convincing fake identities, posing significant risks in the context of digital deception and cybercrime.

papers.title: DNA: Uncovering Universal Latent Forgery Knowledge
papers.research_question: Does forgery detection require extensive fine-tuning, or is it an intrinsic capability already present in pre-trained models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the discriminative neural anchors (DNA) framework to extract latent forgery knowledge from pre-trained models without fine-tuning, demonstrating superior detection performance and robustness.
papers.conclusion: Forgery detection is latent knowledge in pre-trained models, and DNA provides an efficient way to extract it, outperforming fine-tuning methods and establishing a new defensive paradigm.
papers.key_findings:
Forgery detection capability is inherent in pre-trained models and can be extracted without fine-tuning.
The DNA framework identifies sparse forgery-discriminative units (FDUs) that are sensitive to forgery traces.
DNA achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks and generalizes to unseen generative models.
The method is data-efficient and robust to image perturbations.
The detection capability is not due to data leakage but an intrinsic property of pre-trained models.
papers.limitation: Focuses primarily on distinguishing AI-generated hyper-realistic images; generalization to specialized domains like medical imaging is not explored.
future_direction: Apply DNA to specialized domains like medical imaging
Extend DNA to AI-generated text detection
papers.abstract: As generative AI achieves hyper-realism, superficial artifact detection has become obsolete. While prevailing methods rely on resource-intensive fine-tuning of black-box backbones, we propose that forgery detection capability is already encoded within pre-trained models rather than requiring end-to-end retraining. To elicit this intrinsic capability, we propose the discriminative neural anchors (DNA) framework, which employs a coarse-to-fine excavation mechanism. First, by analyzing feature decoupling and attention distribution shifts, we pinpoint critical intermediate layers where the focus of the model logically transitions from global semantics to local anomalies. Subsequently, we introduce a triadic fusion scoring metric paired with a curvature-truncation strategy to strip away semantic redundancy, precisely isolating the forgery-discriminative units (FDUs) inherently imprinted with sensitivity to forgery traces. Moreover, we introduce HIFI-Gen, a high-fidelity synthetic benchmark built upon the very latest models, to address the lag in existing datasets. Experiments demonstrate that by solely relying on these anchors, DNA achieves superior detection performance even under few-shot conditions. Furthermore, it exhibits remarkable robustness across diverse architectures and against unseen generative models, validating that waking up latent neurons is more effective than extensive fine-tuning.

papers.title: Shannon invariants: A scalable approach to information decomposition
papers.research_question: How can we define scalable multivariate metrics to analyze high-order information processing in distributed systems like neural networks, resolving ambiguities in existing information-theoretic measures?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Shannon invariants—specifically the degree of redundancy and vulnerability—as scalable, entropy-based averages for information decomposition, providing theoretical clarity on multivariate information measures and practical tools for analyzing neural network layers and training dynamics.
papers.conclusion: Shannon invariants provide a scalable and interpretable framework for high-order information decomposition, resolving fundamental limitations of PID and offering broad opportunities for theoretical and empirical analysis of complex systems like neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
In a feed-forward MNIST classifier, the degree of redundancy about the label increases across hidden layers and with training, while the degree of vulnerability decreases.
In a face autoencoder, decoder layers exhibit higher redundancy than encoder layers, and larger bottleneck sizes lead to higher redundancy and lower vulnerability.
The redundancy-synergy index (RSI) is shown to equal (¯r - 1)I(X;Y), where ¯r is the average degree of redundancy, clarifying its interpretation.
The dual redundancy-synergy index (DRSI) is introduced, equal to (1 - ¯v)I(X;Y), where ¯v is the average degree of vulnerability, offering a complementary perspective.
papers.limitation:
Some interpretations assume non-negativity of partial information decomposition (PID) atoms, which is not guaranteed by all PID measures.
Deterministic neural networks have infinite channel capacity, requiring stochastic discretization or added noise to make information-theoretic quantities well-defined, which may alter the system.
Analyses are conducted on the training set treated as a complete population, limiting insights to how the network encodes that specific dataset rather than generalizing to unseen data.
future_direction: Applying the framework to more complex systems and larger neural networks.
Further theoretical developments to explore additional Shannon invariants and their properties.
Extending the approach to other domains beyond neural networks.
papers.abstract: Distributed systems, such as biological and artificial neural networks, process information via complex interactions engaging multiple subsystems, resulting in high-order patterns with distinct properties across scales. Investigating how these systems process information remains challenging due to difficulties in defining appropriate multivariate metrics and ensuring their scalability to large systems. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel framework based on what we call "Shannon invariants" -- quantities that capture essential properties of high-order information processing in a way that depends only on the definition of entropy and can be efficiently calculated for large systems. Our theoretical results demonstrate how Shannon invariants can be used to resolve long-standing ambiguities regarding the interpretation of widely used multivariate information-theoretic measures. Moreover, our practical results reveal distinctive information-processing signatures of various deep learning architectures across layers, which lead to new insights into how these systems process information and how this evolves during training. Overall, our framework resolves fundamental limitations in analyzing high-order phenomena and offers broad opportunities for theoretical developments and empirical analyses.

papers.title: Gender Bias in Multilingual Neural Machine Translation: The Architecture\n Matters
papers.research_question: Does the chosen Multilingual Neural Machine Translation architecture, when trained with the same data, influence the gender bias accuracy?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that the MNMT architecture impacts gender bias accuracy, with Language-Specific encoders-decoders exhibiting less bias than Shared encoder-decoder, due to more gender information in source embeddings and more diverted attention.
papers.conclusion: The MNMT architecture impacts gender bias accuracy, with Language-Specific encoders-decoders outperforming Shared encoder-decoder due to better gender encoding in embeddings and more diverted attention.
papers.key_findings:
Language-Specific encoders-decoders architecture exhibits less gender bias than Shared encoder-decoder when trained on the same data.
Source embeddings in the Language-Specific architecture encode more gender information than in the Shared architecture.
Attention in the Language-Specific architecture is more diverted (has higher coefficient of variation) than in the Shared architecture, which helps in mitigating gender bias.
Adding Russian to the language set increases the gender bias gap between Shared and Language-Specific architectures.
Manual analysis shows that most gender errors are due to assuming masculine occupations instead of feminine ones, with some errors having linguistic and cultural explanations.
papers.abstract:
Multilingual Neural Machine Translation architectures mainly differ in the
amount of sharing modules and parameters among languages. In this paper, and
from an algorithmic perspective, we explore if the chosen architecture, when
trained with the same data, influences the gender bias accuracy. Experiments in
four language pairs show that Language-Specific encoders-decoders exhibit less
bias than the Shared encoder-decoder architecture. Further interpretability
analysis of source embeddings and the attention shows that, in the
Language-Specific case, the embeddings encode more gender information, and its
attention is more diverted. Both behaviors help in mitigating gender bias.

papers.title: Can Transfer Entropy Infer Information Flow in Neuronal Circuits for Cognitive Processing?
papers.research_question: Can transfer entropy correctly infer information flow in neuronal circuits for cognitive processing? The paper tests the accuracy of transfer entropy in detecting causal relations in evolved digital brains performing motion detection and sound localization tasks.
papers.core_contribution: Transfer entropy can fail to correctly infer information flow in neuronal circuits, especially when cryptographic logic is present, and its accuracy depends on the cognitive task being performed.
papers.conclusion: Transfer entropy has limitations in accurately estimating information flow, and its accuracy depends on the network and cognitive task. Understanding the fundamental logic processes is important for interpreting causal analyses.
papers.key_findings:
Transfer entropy misestimates information flow in polyadic and cryptographic logic gates, such as XOR and XNOR, where it can fail to detect causal influence.
The extent of misestimation varies with cognitive task: higher in sound localization circuits than in motion detection circuits.
When applied to neural recordings, transfer entropy can produce false positives (false-alarms) and false negatives (misses) in detecting causal relations between neurons.
The frequency of cryptographic and polyadic gates differs between motion detection and sound localization tasks, affecting the accuracy of transfer entropy.
Even with perfect data and known Markov order, transfer entropy has limitations in accurately estimating information flow due to cryptographic dependencies.
papers.limitation:
Transfer entropy can fail to infer causality when it exists, and sometimes suggest a causal connection when there is none.
The analysis uses recordings of perfect (noise-free) neurons, while biological neurons are intrinsically noisy.
The study assumes access to recordings from every neuron in the network, which is often not possible in biological networks.
Even with all possible sensory input patterns, the neural firing patterns may not span the entire state space, affecting TE estimates.
future_direction: Examine causality detection methods such as transfer entropy in known simple biological neural networks to shed light on strengths and deficiencies.
Use evolution of digital cognitive systems to guide the development of other measures of information flow.
papers.abstract: How cognitive neural systems process information is largely unknown, in part because of how difficult it is to accurately follow the flow of information from sensors via neurons to actuators. Measuring the flow of information is different from measuring correlations between firing neurons, for which several measures are available, foremost among them the Shannon information, which is an undirected measure. Several information-theoretic notions of "directed information" have been used to successfully detect the flow of information in some systems, in particular in the neuroscience community. However, recent work has shown that directed information measures such as transfer entropy can sometimes inadequately estimate information flow, or even fail to identify manifest directed influences, especially if neurons contribute in a cryptographic manner to influence the effector neuron. Because it is unclear how often such cryptic influences emerge in cognitive systems, the usefulness of transfer entropy measures to reconstruct information flow is unknown. Here, we test how often cryptographic logic emerges in an evolutionary process that generates artificial neural circuits for two fundamental cognitive tasks (motion detection and sound localization). Besides counting the frequency of problematic logic gates, we also test whether transfer entropy applied to an activity time-series recorded from behaving digital brains can infer information flow, compared to a ground-truth model of direct influence constructed from connectivity and circuit logic. Our results suggest that transfer entropy will sometimes fail to infer directed information when it exists, and sometimes suggest a causal connection when there is none. However, the extent of incorrect inference strongly depends on the cognitive task considered. These results emphasize the importance of understanding the fundamental logic processes that contribute to information flow in cognitive processing, and quantifying their relevance in any given nervous system.

papers.title: FADE: Selective Forgetting via Sparse LoRA and Self-Distillation
papers.research_question: How can we remove the influence of specific data or concepts from trained text-to-image diffusion models while preserving overall performance and balancing effective forgetting with retention of unrelated concepts?
papers.core_contribution: SPARE is a two-stage unlearning method for diffusion models that first localizes parameters responsible for a target concept via gradient saliency and then uses sparse LoRA adapters with a self-distillation objective to overwrite the concept, achieving efficient and controlled removal.
papers.conclusion: SPARE is an effective method for unlearning concepts in text-to-image stable diffusion models, providing lightweight, controllable modules and improving upon current state-of-the-art performance.
papers.key_findings:
SPARE surpasses state-of-the-art methods on the UnlearnCanvas benchmark, achieving high unlearning accuracy and retainability.
The method allows fine-grained control over the trade-off between forgetting a target concept and retaining unrelated capabilities.
A proposed timestep sampling scheme that targets concept-specific crucial denoising steps improves unlearning efficiency.
The use of sparse LoRA adapters results in lightweight modifications (e.g., 3.1MB) that can be merged or removed at runtime.
Analysis of cross-attention maps shows the method successfully rewrites the internal semantic mapping of the unlearned concept to a surrogate.
papers.limitation:
Evaluations are restricted to a few datasets (e.g., Imagenette, UnlearnCanvas).
The results might be sensitive to the choice of the overwrite concept.
The custom timestep sampling scheme requires human evaluation or trained models to determine which prompt the generated image resembles.
Further testing is needed to assess robustness to sequential unlearning, knowledge revival, adversarial attacks, and comparable efficiency metrics.
future_direction: Exploration of other benchmarks, different models, and additional tasks such as style editing or image classification.
Investigation of the impact of the overwriting concept choice and automatic selection of a surrogate concept.
Rigorous evaluation of applying SPARE to architectures other than Stable Diffusion.
papers.abstract: Machine Unlearning aims to remove the influence of specific data or concepts from trained models while preserving overall performance, a capability increasingly required by data protection regulations and responsible AI practices. Despite recent progress, unlearning in text-to-image diffusion models remains challenging due to high computational costs and the difficulty of balancing effective forgetting with retention of unrelated concepts. We introduce FADE (Fast Adapter for Data Erasure), a two-stage unlearning method for image generation that combines parameter localization with self-distillation. FADE first identifies parameters most responsible for the forget set using gradient-based saliency and constrains updates through sparse LoRA adapters, ensuring lightweight, localized modifications. In a second stage, FADE applies a self-distillation objective that overwrites the forgotten concept with a user-defined surrogate while preserving behavior on retained data. The resulting adapters are memory-efficient, reversible, and can be merged or removed at runtime, enabling flexible deployment in production systems. We evaluated FADE on the UnlearnCanvas benchmark and conducted ablation studies on Imagenette, Labeled Faces in the Wild, AtharvaTaras Dog Breeds Dataset, and SUN Attributes datasets, demonstrating State-of-the-Art unlearning performance with fine-grained control over the forgetting-retention trade-off. Our results demonstrate that FADE achieves strong concept erasure and high retainability across various domains, making it a suitable solution for selective unlearning in diffusion-based image generation models.

papers.title: Memorization Without Overfitting: Analyzing the Training Dynamics of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do memorization and forgetting dynamics in language models change during training, and how do they depend on factors like model size, dataset size, and learning rate?
papers.core_contribution: Larger language models memorize training data faster and forget less throughout training, with nouns and numbers being memorized more quickly than other parts of speech.
papers.conclusion: Memorization dynamics are a critical metric for understanding language model training, with larger models exhibiting faster memorization and less forgetting, highlighting the importance of analyzing memorization alongside cross-entropy loss.
papers.key_findings:
Larger language models memorize training data faster across various settings (causal and masked LM, different dataset sizes).
Larger models can memorize a larger portion of the data before overfitting occurs.
Forgetting curves approach a baseline (the forgetting baseline), and this baseline increases with model scale, meaning larger models forget less.
Nouns and numbers are memorized much faster than other parts of speech, acting as unique identifiers for training examples.
Adding unique identifiers (like document IDs) to training examples increases memorization speed.
papers.limitation:
The exact memorization metric (Definition 1) ignores model confidence and does not normalize for duplication in the training set.
The focus on exact memorization may not capture all aspects of privacy, as it only considers verbatim output of sensitive information.
future_direction: Understanding the structure of the forgetting baseline, e.g., what types of tokens (parts of speech, synonyms, facts) are memorized in the baseline.
Analyzing memorization dynamics as a critical metric when scaling up language models, beyond just cross-entropy loss.
papers.abstract: Despite their wide adoption, the underlying training and memorization dynamics of very large language models is not well understood. We empirically study exact memorization in causal and masked language modeling, across model sizes and throughout the training process. We measure the effects of dataset size, learning rate, and model size on memorization, finding that larger language models memorize training data faster across all settings. Surprisingly, we show that larger models can memorize a larger portion of the data before over-fitting and tend to forget less throughout the training process. We also analyze the memorization dynamics of different parts of speech and find that models memorize nouns and numbers first; we hypothesize and provide empirical evidence that nouns and numbers act as a unique identifier for memorizing individual training examples. Together, these findings present another piece of the broader puzzle of trying to understand what actually improves as models get bigger.

papers.title: Disentangled Representations in Neural Models
papers.research_question: How can we learn disentangled representations in neural models that are interpretable, reusable, and performant, without sacrificing performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces methods (DC-IGN and CFN) for learning disentangled representations in graphics and computation, which are interpretable, reusable, and performant without catastrophic forgetting.
papers.conclusion: Disentangled representations are valuable for interpretability and reuse, and the proposed methods (DC-IGN and CFN) are effective in learning such representations in the domains of graphics and computation.
papers.key_findings:
DC-IGN can learn a disentangled graphics code for 3D faces and chairs, enabling novel view synthesis and re-rendering under different lighting and pose conditions.
CFN can disentangle computational tasks, factorize a multitask learning problem, and is practically immune to catastrophic forgetting.
Explicit disentanglement training is critical for novel-view reconstruction compared to entangled representations.
The decoder in DC-IGN can function as a 3D rendering engine, indicating a truly disentangled representation.
CFN achieves disentanglement with no performance penalty and with fewer parameters than a traditional feedforward network.
papers.limitation:
The current formulation of SGVB is restricted to continuous latent variables, but real-world scenes may require discrete distributions.
Scaling to more complex scenes may require deeper architectures.
The decoder network might be replaced by a domain-specific decoder for fine-grained model-based inference.
future_direction: Experiment with deeper architectures to handle more complex scenes and object categories.
Extend the model to handle discrete distributions or to a recurrent setting.
Use importance-weighted autoencoders to capture more complex probabilistic structure.
Replace the decoder with a domain-specific decoder for fine-grained inference.
Explore multi-step CFN for deeper computations and curricula.
Investigate non-differentiable functions in CFN and hierarchical computation.
Unify the two approaches for unsupervised inference of factors of variation in videos.
papers.abstract: Representation learning is the foundation for the recent success of neural network models. However, the distributed representations generated by neural networks are far from ideal. Due to their highly entangled nature, they are di cult to reuse and interpret, and they do a poor job of capturing the sparsity which is present in real- world transformations. In this paper, I describe methods for learning disentangled representations in the two domains of graphics and computation. These methods allow neural methods to learn representations which are easy to interpret and reuse, yet they incur little or no penalty to performance. In the Graphics section, I demonstrate the ability of these methods to infer the generating parameters of images and rerender those images under novel conditions. In the Computation section, I describe a model which is able to factorize a multitask learning problem into subtasks and which experiences no catastrophic forgetting. Together these techniques provide the tools to design a wide range of models that learn disentangled representations and better model the factors of variation in the real world.

papers.title: Detecting Learning vs Memorization in Deep Neural Networks using Shared Structure Validation Sets
papers.research_question: How can we differentiate memorization from learning in deep neural networks (DNNs) trained with real labels, as opposed to shuffled labels?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a novel permutation approach using shared structure validation sets (s-validation sets) and shallow classifiers to differentiate between learning and memorization in DNNs trained with real labels.
papers.conclusion: The proposed permutation approach using s-validation sets provides a useful tool for understanding how DNNs memorize and learn over training epochs.
papers.key_findings:
DNNs can simultaneously learn and memorize during training.
Regularization (e.g., dropout) and increasing the number of layers can reduce memorization.
DNNs exhibit dynamic memorization patterns over training epochs, with an initial memorization phase followed by a forgetting phase.
Surprisingly, DNNs can learn from pure Gaussian noise inputs, not just memorize them.
The method is useful for relative comparisons of memorization between different DNNs, but not for absolute quantification.
papers.limitation: The method cannot quantify the absolute amount of memorization in a DNN, only relative comparisons between models.
papers.abstract: The roles played by learning and memorization represent an important topic in deep learning research. Recent work on this subject has shown that the optimization behavior of DNNs trained on shuffled labels is qualitatively different from DNNs trained with real labels. Here, we propose a novel permutation approach that can differentiate memorization from learning in deep neural networks (DNNs) trained as usual (i.e., using the real labels to guide the learning, rather than shuffled labels). The evaluation of weather the DNN has learned and/or memorized, happens in a separate step where we compare the predictive performance of a shallow classifier trained with the features learned by the DNN, against multiple instances of the same classifier, trained on the same input, but using shuffled labels as outputs. By evaluating these shallow classifiers in validation sets that share structure with the training set, we are able to tell apart learning from memorization. Application of our permutation approach to multi-layer perceptrons and convolutional neural networks trained on image data corroborated many findings from other groups. Most importantly, our illustrations also uncovered interesting dynamic patterns about how DNNs memorize over increasing numbers of training epochs, and support the surprising result that DNNs are still able to learn, rather than only memorize, when trained with pure Gaussian noise as input.

papers.title: LatentQA: Teaching LLMs to Decode Activations Into Natural Language
papers.research_question: How can we train a language model to decode activations into natural language answers to open-ended questions about those activations (LATENTQA), and how can this be used for reading and controlling model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces LatentInterpretationTuning (LIT), a method to train a decoder LLM to answer open-ended questions about model activations (LATENTQA), and demonstrates its effectiveness for reading activations and controlling model behavior.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that LATENTQA, enabled by LIT, provides a powerful framework for reading and controlling model activations with natural language, and scales well with data and model size.
papers.key_findings:
LIT achieves higher accuracy than GPT-4 and SelfIE in uncovering hidden system prompts.
LIT outperforms linear probing and Patchscope in relational knowledge extraction.
LIT is the only method that significantly reduces bias in the debiasing task.
LIT can steer models to exhibit unseen behaviors (e.g., Golden Gate Claude).
LIT benefits from scaling in dataset and model size.
future_direction: Training LATENTQA systems on additional types of data (e.g., hierarchical instruction-following) to unlock novel applications.
Scaling LATENTQA to larger datasets and models.
Using LATENTQA for evaluating instruction following in long-context scenarios.
papers.abstract: Interpretability methods seek to understand language model representations, yet the outputs of most such methods -- circuits, vectors, scalars -- are not immediately human-interpretable. In response, we introduce LatentQA, the task of answering open-ended questions about model activations in natural language.
